title: Fire Extinguisher Promotion Audition

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll prove I deserve to be promoted to "Technical Prima Donna."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think this shows that I'm emotionally unstable and potentially dangerous.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Fooosh

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How was that?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It was good. I'm starting to over-value your technical knowledge already.

setting: The Boss's office
situation: Dilbert announces he will prove he deserves a promotion to 'Technical Prima Donna' and sprays the seated Boss with a fire extinguisher. He asks how that went, and the foam-covered Boss says it was good because he is already starting to over-value Dilbert's technical knowledge.
punchline: Management rewards technical staff who behave in a volatile, dangerous manner by deferring to them, so acting unhinged is the way to win a promotion.
summary: An engineer auditions for a prima donna title by blasting his boss with foam, and the boss responds by feeling more impressed by his expertise.

title: Four Hour Meeting From Hell

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Welcome to the four hour...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Meeting from HELL!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ha ha ha ha ha ha ha

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's rarely a good sign.

setting: Conference room
situation: The Boss opens a long meeting by announcing it as a four hour session. In the next panel he cheerfully declares it the "meeting from hell" with devil horns drawn on his hair, laughing maniacally. Dilbert, sitting with Alice, thinks to himself that a boss gleefully calling his own meeting hellish is not a good omen.
punchline: The Boss cheerfully admits his own meeting will be a hellish ordeal, and Dilbert dryly notes that a manager saying so is rarely good news.
summary: A manager gleefully kicks off an endless meeting by labeling it infernal, leaving his staff dreading what's ahead.

title: Working Like a Dog, Literally

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What are you up to, Ted?

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: I'm working like a dog lately.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'd better not ask.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Scratch scratch

setting: Office cubicle
situation: Dilbert, holding a coffee mug, asks coworker Ted what he is up to. Ted says he has been working like a dog lately, and Dilbert thinks to himself that he'd better not ask for details. In the last panel Ted is at his computer, scratching himself furiously like a dog.
punchline: Ted's idiom about working like a dog turns out to be disturbingly literal, as he scratches himself like a flea-ridden dog at his desk.
summary: A coworker's claim of toiling like a canine is undercut by a visual gag of him scratching at his desk.

title: Dilbert's Ego Fed Sparkling Water

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hi, I'm Dilbert and this is the physical manifestation of my ego.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Splash!!

transcript.speaker: Ego
transcript.text: Worship me, female!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's why I only feed it sparkling water.

setting: A party or social gathering with stools and drinks
situation: Dilbert introduces a small woman to a tiny creature sitting on a stool, which he claims is the physical manifestation of his ego. The woman sprays it with water from her drink, and it swells into a huge, puffy white mass that demands worship. Dilbert explains that this is why he only feeds it sparkling water.
punchline: Dilbert's ego puffs up and becomes obnoxious when fed anything bubbly, which is a literal take on a fizzy drink inflating one's ego, and his smug explanation shows he's weirdly proud of managing it.
summary: A man shows off a pet that embodies his ego, and when it gets splashed it balloons into an arrogant fluffy blob.

title: Dogbert's Newborn Baby Instruction Manual

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What are you doing?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm writing an instruction book for newborn babies.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You don't know anything about babies.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Okay, I'm not an expert, but compared to the people who have babies...

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Which end do I put the cheese steak in?

setting: Office desk with a computer, then a scene with new parents
situation: Dilbert asks Dogbert what he is doing at his computer, and Dogbert says he is writing an instruction book for newborn babies. When Dilbert points out that Dogbert knows nothing about babies, Dogbert argues he is still better informed than actual parents. In the last panel a mother holding a cheese steak sandwich asks her husband, who is cradling the baby, which end to put it in.
punchline: The parents are so clueless that they try to feed the baby a cheese steak and can't even tell which end is the mouth, proving Dogbert's point that even a non-expert knows more than they do.
summary: A dog's self-assured baby manual is vindicated when a confused mother wonders where to insert a sandwich into her infant.

title: The Little Phhbwt Theory

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It took weeks but I've calculated a new theory about the origin of the universe.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: According to my calculations it didn't start with a "Big Bang" at all - it was more of a "phhbwt" sound.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You may be wondering about the practical applications of the "Little Phhbwt" theory.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I was wondering when you'll go away.

setting: Dilbert's home, living room with a boombox
situation: Dilbert holds a long printout and proudly announces a new theory about the origin of the universe while Dogbert lies on a cushion beside a boombox playing music. Dilbert explains that the universe began with a "phhbwt" sound rather than a Big Bang, then starts to discuss practical applications. Dogbert, unimpressed, says he is only wondering when Dilbert will leave.
punchline: Dilbert's weeks of earnest calculation produce a silly theory, and Dogbert bluntly shows he has no interest and just wants Dilbert gone.
summary: After weeks of number crunching, an engineer unveils a goofy cosmic theory, only for his dog to politely ask when the lecture will end.

title: Belt-O-Authority Electric Shock Headbands

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Everybody take one and fasten it securely around your head.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: From time to time I'll use my "Belt-O-Authority" to send you painful electric shocks.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: When our performance is bad?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's one theory, sure.

setting: Office meeting area
situation: The Boss hands out headbands with antennae to his employees and tells them to wear them. He explains he will use a belt-mounted control, his "Belt-O-Authority," to send painful electric shocks to them. Dilbert asks if the shocks are a punishment for bad performance, and the Boss vaguely replies that it's one theory.
punchline: The Boss's shocks have no connection to performance; he will zap people arbitrarily, and his evasive answer admits that his discipline is capricious and abusive.
summary: A manager outfits his staff with shock-delivering headgear and cheerfully declines to promise the zaps will be tied to anything sensible.

title: Dogbert's School for Technology Imbeciles

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Welcome to Dogbert's School for Technology Imbeciles.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You are all easily baffled by simple technology, even though you have normal intelligence otherwise.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Of course, I'm generalizing on that last point.

setting: A classroom or training room where Dogbert addresses a seated audience
situation: Dogbert, holding a pointer, welcomes a group of seated students to his school for people who can't handle technology. He tells them they are baffled by simple technology despite otherwise normal intelligence. In the last panel, the audience looks dazed and one wears a beer shirt, and Dogbert concedes he was generalizing.
punchline: Dogbert admits his claim that they have normal intelligence otherwise was a generalization, since the students plainly look dim, implying they are truly stupid across the board.
summary: A canine instructor insults his dull-looking students by praising their intelligence, then takes it back when he sees how vacant they appear.

title: Boss Shocks Employee Over Memos

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've had enough of those wimpy management techniques like "empowerment" and "quality."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Write a better memo or I'll send a strong shock to your head.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The best part is that it's all subjective.

setting: Office cubicle
situation: The Boss, holding a remote control device, muses that he is done with soft management techniques such as empowerment and quality. He then threatens an employee wearing a head-mounted shock device, telling him to write a better memo or be zapped. The employee is shocked in the last panel while the Boss gleefully notes that the judgment of a 'better' memo is entirely subjective.
punchline: The Boss has found a management technique with total power over employees, since he alone decides what counts as a 'better' memo, so he can shock them whenever he likes.
summary: Fed up with gentle management fads, a gleeful supervisor zaps his subordinate with a head-mounted shock device whenever he judges a memo lacking, an arbitrary standard.

title: Free Therapy From Psychology Students

transcript.speaker: Sign
transcript.text: Free therapy

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why is it free?

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: Our therapists are first year psychology students.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What have I got to lose?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sometimes I have low self-esteem...

transcript.speaker: Therapist
transcript.text: Your problem is that you're ugly. You should drink beer until you feel handsome.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I thought you would say something about my mother.

transcript.speaker: Therapist
transcript.text: Good point. Your mother should drink beer too. She's probably as ugly as you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're over-priced.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: Ooh, "Mister Low Self-Esteem" is unhappy.

setting: A free therapy clinic, including the reception desk and the therapist's office
situation: Dilbert sees a sign for free therapy and learns the therapists are first-year psychology students, but decides he has nothing to lose. In the session, the student therapist insults his looks, recommends drinking beer, and then insults his mother. Dilbert leaves complaining that the service is over-priced, and the receptionist mocks him.
punchline: The free therapy is so terrible and insulting that Dilbert says it is over-priced, implying that even free is too much to pay for worthless advice.
summary: A man takes advantage of a no-cost counseling clinic staffed by novices and gets rude, useless advice in return.
keywords: you get what you pay for

title: Ratbert Spots Flaw in Dilbert's Theory

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then, Ratbert, the weight of the universe collapsed in on itself until all of existence could fit into a thimble!

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Why would there be a thimble in space?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Uh... there wouldn't...

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Boy, it didn't take long to spot the gaping logical flaw in that theory.

setting: Dilbert's desk in his home or office, with Ratbert sitting on the desktop
situation: Dilbert is explaining a theory about the collapse of the universe to Ratbert, claiming everything could shrink to fit into a thimble. Ratbert asks why a thimble would exist in space at all. Dilbert admits it wouldn't, and Ratbert comments that the flaw was easy to spot.
punchline: Dilbert's cosmic theory is undone by a simple question from Ratbert, and the deadpan last line is Ratbert's smug remark that the logical flaw was obvious.
summary: A pet rodent pokes a hole in his owner's grand explanation of the universe with one naive but devastating question.

title: Dogbert's School for Technology Imbeciles

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm going to open a school for people who are technology imbeciles.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll teach people how to use automatic bank machines, microwave ovens, video recorders, CD players, that sort of thing...

transcript.speaker: Father
transcript.text: I thought he was reasonably bright until we got the VCR...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: They can fool you.

setting: Dilbert's living room, then Dogbert's school admissions desk
situation: Dogbert, perched on a footstool beside Dilbert, announces he will open a school for people who can't handle everyday technology like ATMs, microwaves, VCRs and CD players. In the last panel a father brings his young son to the Imbecile Admissions desk, explaining that he thought the boy was bright until the VCR arrived. Dogbert, seated at the desk, reassures him.
punchline: The 'imbecile' being enrolled is a small child whose parent blames him for failing to work the VCR, implying the real problem is confusing technology and a parent who can't use it either, while Dogbert happily profits from the confusion.
summary: Dogbert launches a tutoring school for the technologically hopeless and soon enrolls a toddler whose parent blames him for the baffling VCR.

title: Dogbert's Parenting Advice: TV Listings

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: "Although raising children is difficult, be assured that you will get help from a power greater than yourself."

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: "Teach your children about the higher power and about the 'Great Book' which will give them direction."

transcript.speaker: Parent
transcript.text: They're called "TV listings." Without them, you're just flipping.

setting: Dogbert's desk at a computer, then a living room with an armchair and TV
situation: Dogbert sits at his computer writing a parenting guide that praises a higher power and a 'Great Book' that gives children direction. The scene then cuts to a parent crouched beside a baby in an armchair in front of a TV, holding up a TV guide and explaining what it is.
punchline: The 'higher power' and 'Great Book' that guide a child's life turn out to be television and the TV listings, mocking how much TV has replaced religion and parenting in modern households.
summary: A parenting guide that sounds deeply spiritual is revealed to be about worshipping television and its program guide.

title: Dilbert's List of Annoyances Backfires

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Dogbert, I've found a way to improve the quality of life around here.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've catalogued and prioritized all of the things that bother me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Study the list so you'll know what behaviors are unacceptable.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Wow! Thanks! This is a real bonanza!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You're right. This certainly will improve the quality of my life!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I think I'll do a "top hundred" countdown. This could amuse me for months.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That didn't go as well as I'd hoped.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Number 73: "Clipping my toenails near your soup."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That had better be an onion in there.

setting: Dilbert's home living room, then a dinner table
situation: Dilbert gives Dogbert a long, prioritized list of everything that annoys him, expecting Dogbert to avoid those behaviors. Dogbert instead treats the list as a menu of ideas and plans a "top hundred" countdown of ways to irritate Dilbert. At dinner Dogbert begins performing the items, such as clipping toenails near Dilbert's soup.
punchline: By handing Dogbert a detailed catalogue of his pet peeves, Dilbert has given his tormentor a ready-made list of ways to annoy him.
summary: A man hoping to stop his dog's irritating habits instead supplies the dog with a full script of ways to torment him.

title: Student Microwaves a Video Tape

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert's School for Technology Imbeciles

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Can anybody show me what you do with a microwave?

transcript.speaker: Student
transcript.text: I insert the video tape ... then I set the timer for ninety minutes...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Does anybody know why it isn't working?

transcript.speaker: Another Student
transcript.text: The fool! It's Beta!

setting: Classroom at Dogbert's School for Technology Imbeciles
situation: Dogbert, running a school for the technologically clueless, asks the class to demonstrate how to use a microwave. One student describes putting a video tape in the microwave and setting the timer for ninety minutes, treating it like a VCR. When Dogbert asks why it isn't working, another student confidently blames the tape format being Beta.
punchline: The students are so technologically clueless that they think a microwave is a VCR, and they blame the failure on the wrong tape format (Beta) rather than on using the wrong device entirely.
summary: In a class for the tech-illiterate, a pupil tries to record a show by putting a tape in a microwave, and a classmate blames the tape format.

title: Acronym Soup: Very G, Meaning Good

transcript.speaker: Bald coworker
transcript.text: ...So, either an IBM 586 with 10 meg RAM or maybe a SPARC CPU on a LAN...

transcript.speaker: Bald coworker
transcript.text: ...But with AI and AVR combined with BISDN, well, it's very G.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: G?

transcript.speaker: Bald coworker
transcript.text: Good.

setting: Office, two men talking
situation: A bald coworker rattles off a string of computer hardware and technical acronyms while advising Dilbert on a system choice. He wraps up by calling the combination 'very G'. When Dilbert asks what G means, the coworker admits he just means 'good'.
punchline: After drowning the listener in jargon and acronyms, the speaker abbreviates the simple word 'good' to a single letter, as if shortening it were just as technical.
summary: A techie buries a colleague in hardware acronyms, then confusingly abbreviates the plain word good into a single letter.

title: Boss Misreads Management By Walking Around

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My new style of management is exhausting me.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I heard some people talking about "MBWA" or "Management by Walking Around."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I walked all the way to the park and back. But I can't say that I see much improvement around here.

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle
situation: The Boss stands by Dilbert's desk and complains that his new management style is wearing him out. He explains that he overheard people discussing 'Management by Walking Around' and took it literally, walking to the park and back. He is puzzled that nothing at work has improved.
punchline: The Boss takes the management buzzword 'Management by Walking Around' literally, going for an aimless walk outside instead of engaging with his employees, and wonders why nothing improves.
summary: After overhearing a management buzzword, the boss goes on a literal hike and is baffled that his department hasn't gotten any better.

title: Rewiring the Boss's Shock Headset

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The Boss is making us wear these things on our heads so he can give us painful shocks whenever he wants.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm rewiring mine so it redirects the signal to Wally.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm sure he'll see the humor in that.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay, wise-guy, do you want more of this?!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe one more.

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle
situation: Dilbert tells Dogbert that the Boss is forcing employees to wear head devices that deliver painful shocks on demand. Dilbert rewires his own headset so the shocks are redirected to Wally. The Boss then zaps what he thinks is Dilbert, but Wally is the one frazzled and smoking, and Dilbert asks for one more.
punchline: Dilbert has turned the Boss's punishment device into a way to torment Wally, so the Boss's threats only hurt Wally while Dilbert cheerfully invites more.
summary: A scheming engineer reroutes his boss's shock-delivering headgear onto a coworker and happily asks for another jolt.

title: Ratbert Clings to Dilbert's Leg

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: There's Dilbert... I'll sneak up and hug his leg until he loves me and accepts me in the family.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: A rat is clinging to my leg.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I had that problem till I switched to "Old Spice."

setting: Dilbert's home entryway, then an office or hallway
situation: Ratbert, a lab rat desperate for a home, plans in a thought bubble to sneak up and hug Dilbert's leg until Dilbert loves him. Dilbert comes through the door, Ratbert leaps, and in the last panel Dilbert tells a bald coworker that a rat is clinging to his leg.
punchline: The coworker treats the clinging rat as a personal hygiene problem, cracking that he solved it by switching to Old Spice, as if the rat were drawn by body odor like an unwanted admirer.
summary: A lonely rat's plan to win a family by hugging a man's leg gets reduced by a smug coworker to a cologne-ad quip.

title: Engineers' Acronym Society Gets Mocked

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm joining the S.E.W.L.T.U.I.F.E.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: To the lay dog, it's known as the "Society of Engineers Who Like to Use Initials for Everything."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We use acronyms to set us apart from the unwashed masses who don't understand technology.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: B.F.D.*

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: *Big Furry Deal

setting: Dilbert's desk in an office
situation: Dilbert sits across a desk from Dogbert and announces he is joining an engineering society with an unpronounceable acronym. He explains that it stands for a society of engineers who love initials, and that acronyms exist to separate engineers from people who don't understand technology. Dogbert answers with an acronym of his own.
punchline: Dogbert dismisses Dilbert's elitist acronym club with the deflating acronym B.F.D., which stands for "Big Furry Deal."
summary: A proud engineer explains his society of acronym lovers to a dog who responds with a sarcastic initialism of his own.

title: Bureaucracy Monsters Cling to Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Bureaucracy

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need to buy an upgrade for my computer.

transcript.speaker: Green monster
transcript.text: Rrrr...

transcript.speaker: Green monster
transcript.text: First, you must write a business case and get five signatures.

transcript.speaker: Green monster
transcript.text: Get bids from nine vendors.

transcript.speaker: Green monster
transcript.text: All vendors must be approved by a vote of the Vendor Approval Committee.

transcript.speaker: Green monster
transcript.text: ...Purchase order... Budget transfer... Legal review... Accounting classification... Inventory...

transcript.speaker: Green monster
transcript.text: These steps are necessary to prevent employees from doing something uneconomical.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: ...So you suggested a process "quality audit"?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yeah, that's the one clinging to my buttocks.

setting: A cave labeled Bureaucracy, serving as an office with a computer
situation: Dilbert enters a cave called Bureaucracy to ask for a simple computer upgrade. A green monster demands an ever-growing list of approval steps, and more monsters pile onto Dilbert with each requirement. Dogbert later notes that Dilbert suggested a process quality audit, and Dilbert replies that the resulting monster is clinging to him.
punchline: Proposing a process audit to fix bureaucracy only spawns another bureaucratic monster that attaches itself to the person who suggested it.
summary: A man seeking a routine computer upgrade gets buried under a swarm of clinging monsters, each one an additional approval hurdle.

title: Testosterone Flinging From Bald Pores

transcript.speaker: Bald coworker
transcript.text: Don't get too close-- I found out that my baldness is caused by too much testosterone.

transcript.speaker: Bald coworker
transcript.text: Now with my hair gone I'm afraid the testosterone will start flinging out of my pores.

transcript.speaker: Coworker in blue tie
transcript.text: Hey! You got some on my shirt!

transcript.speaker: Bald coworker
transcript.text: Do you have a problem with that?

setting: Office
situation: A bald, bespectacled coworker warns Dilbert and another colleague to keep their distance because his baldness is caused by excess testosterone. He says the hormone might now fling out of his pores, and when a colleague complains that some landed on his shirt, the bald man responds aggressively and demands to know if he has a problem with it.
punchline: The man's supposedly flung-out testosterone seems to be real, since he instantly turns confrontational and aggressive when the colleague complains.
summary: A balding man jokes that his surplus hormones may spray off him, then proves the point by picking a fight over it.

title: Boss Demands Report Contradict Itself

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Good report... but add a sentence that says micro-robotics is a dead-end technology.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But that's the exact opposite of my point! If I add that, the whole report would be a confusing and senseless waste of time!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's okay. We just won't let anybody else see it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is this a win-win scenario?

setting: The Boss's office
situation: The Boss praises Dilbert's report but orders him to add a sentence claiming micro-robotics is a dead-end technology, which contradicts the report's whole argument. When Dilbert objects that this would ruin the report, the Boss casually says they simply won't let anyone else read it.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically asks if this is a win-win, since the Boss's solution is to bury the now-worthless report so nobody ever benefits from it.
summary: A manager insists on inserting a self-sabotaging claim into an employee's research, then solves the resulting problem by hiding the document from everyone.

title: Heckled During Technical Presentation

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Please excuse the artwork in this next diagram.

transcript.speaker: Audience member (off-panel)
transcript.text: What's that? It looks like Elvis' face on a credenza! Ha ha ha! Or is it a Rorschach test??! Ha ha ha!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And in conclusion, I hate you all.

setting: Conference room during a technical presentation
situation: Dilbert presents to a group, apologizing in advance for the crude artwork in his next diagram. Unseen audience members mock the drawing, comparing it to Elvis' face on a credenza and a Rorschach test. Dilbert, fed up, ends his talk by announcing that he hates everyone.
punchline: After being ridiculed for his diagram despite apologizing in advance, Dilbert drops all professionalism and closes his presentation with open contempt for his audience.
summary: A presenter who warned his audience about a poorly drawn diagram gets laughed at and responds with a hostile sign-off.

title: Budget System Invented By Crazed Monk

transcript.text: Dilbert is assigned to prepare the budget.

transcript.speaker: Woman

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: It was developed 400 years ago by a crazed monk who sealed himself in a wine cask.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Unfortunately, we still have him.

transcript.speaker: Monk in cask
transcript.text: Hey, I've got another idea.

setting: Office, finance department
situation: Dilbert is assigned to prepare the budget, and a female coworker tells him he must learn the company's budget system. She explains that it was invented 400 years ago by a crazed monk who sealed himself in a wine cask. The monk is still alive in the cask and chimes in that he has another idea.
punchline: The company's budget process is so archaic and absurd that its inventor, a lunatic monk in a barrel, is still around and is about to make it even worse.
summary: A coworker reveals that the baffling budget system came from a medieval madman who is somehow still alive in a barrel and cooking up more ideas.

title: No Stupid Questions, Except This One

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Does anybody have any questions about our plan? Ask me anything—there are no "stupid" questions.

transcript.speaker: Meeting attendee
transcript.text: If you crossed the International Date Line on your birthday, would you still get presents?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Oh great... there ARE stupid questions and I don't know the answers.

setting: Conference room during a business meeting
situation: The Boss opens a meeting by inviting questions about the plan and claims there are no stupid questions. An attendee then asks an absurd, irrelevant question about crossing the International Date Line on a birthday. The Boss privately realizes the question is stupid and that he has no answer.
punchline: The Boss's blanket reassurance backfires when he gets a truly stupid question, exposing that he is unprepared and cannot answer even the dumb ones.
summary: A manager promises that no question is foolish, then gets one so silly that it proves him wrong and leaves him stumped.

title: Garbage Man Critiques Dilbert's Spelling

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: Hoo-boy! I hope you're not going to show this to anybody.

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: Oh, it's obviously a first draft. By now you've run it through the spelling checker.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Technologists are concerned with ideas, not spelling.

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: Well, since you brought it up...

setting: Outside near a trash can, apparently where Dilbert's discarded papers are collected
situation: A garbage man pulls a crumpled paper of Dilbert's out of the trash can and reads it, mocking its quality and assuming it is only a rough draft that has been spell-checked. Dilbert defensively claims that technologists care about ideas rather than spelling. The garbage man then begins pointing out the spelling mistakes, since Dilbert raised the subject.
punchline: Dilbert's excuse that technologists only care about ideas is undercut by a garbage man who is a better proofreader than he is, and who happily seizes the opening to criticize his spelling.
summary: A trash collector scrutinizes a crumpled document from the bin and ends up correcting the engineer who wrote it.
themes: being criticized by an unexpected expert

title: Rumors of Lizards and Corn Dogs

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you have a minute?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Uh-oh, it's touchy-feely stuff.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's going to happen to our department? The rumors are flying.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What have you heard?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Rumor has it that flying lizards from the planet Zorb will buy the company.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: They plan to turn the employees into giant corn dogs on sticks.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't worry about rumors. It's business as usual for now.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Gulp.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I think I handled that pretty well.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Are you sure this will impress the Zorbians?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hear they like team players.

setting: The Boss's office
situation: Dilbert asks his boss what will happen to their department amid swirling rumors of a takeover. When the boss asks what he has heard, Dilbert invents an absurd rumor about alien lizards buying the company and turning employees into corn dogs. The boss nervously dismisses it as business as usual, then ends up standing awkwardly with a stick up each side as a corn dog costume, hoping to impress the Zorbians.
punchline: Dilbert feeds the boss a ridiculous rumor and the boss, who is gullible and anxious, ends up dressing as a corn dog on a stick to curry favor with the supposed alien buyers.
summary: A worried employee fabricates an outlandish alien-takeover rumor and watches his gullible boss prepare to be turned into a snack.

title: Computer Eliminates Process of Wishing

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: For only twenty-five thousand dollars I've eliminated many tedious and time-consuming processes.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What would be an example of one of those tedious and time-consuming processes?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, there was the process of sitting around and wishing I had more computer stuff...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Next time don't ask.

setting: Office, beside Dilbert's computer
situation: Dilbert shows off a new computer system he bought for $25,000 and claims it eliminated many tedious, time-consuming processes. The Boss asks for an example, and Dilbert admits the only process eliminated was sitting around wishing he had more computer equipment. The Boss, annoyed, thinks to himself that he shouldn't have asked.
punchline: The only 'process' the expensive computer purchase eliminated was Dilbert's own wishing for more computer equipment, exposing the purchase as a self-serving splurge with no real productivity gain.
summary: After buying pricey new hardware, Dilbert justifies the cost with a feeble answer that leaves his irritated manager regretting the question.

title: Recycled Agenda Is Last Week's

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: First on the agenda is a discussion of the company's new paper recycling program.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We talked about that last time... Hey, this is last week's agenda.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You spotted the one drawback.

setting: Conference room during a meeting
situation: The Boss opens a meeting by announcing the first agenda item is the company's new paper recycling program. Dilbert points out they already discussed it last time and realizes the paper being used is last week's agenda. The Boss admits that Dilbert has spotted the one drawback of recycling paper.
punchline: The recycling program is so literal that the company reuses old agendas, so meetings repeat themselves, and the boss treats this as a minor flaw.
summary: A manager reuses an old agenda from the previous week and shrugs off the repetition as an unavoidable side effect of recycling.

title: Lawyer's Threat Backfires on Dogbert

transcript.speaker: Lawyer
transcript.text: If you do not drop your class action suit, then you'll have to face me in court.

transcript.speaker: Lawyer
transcript.text: And I've never lost a case.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Then how do you know you wouldn't enjoy it.

transcript.speaker: Lawyer
transcript.text: Well... I just wouldn't.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Good argument.

setting: Conference room table during a legal negotiation
situation: A lawyer sits across a table from Dogbert and threatens that Dogbert will have to face him in court if he does not drop a class action suit, boasting he has never lost a case. Dogbert calmly asks how the lawyer can know he wouldn't enjoy losing. The lawyer can only offer a weak 'I just wouldn't,' and Dogbert sarcastically praises it.
punchline: The lawyer, supposedly skilled at argument, can only respond with a feeble 'I just wouldn't,' and Dogbert mockingly calls it a good argument.
summary: A boastful attorney tries to scare Dogbert out of a lawsuit, but a sly question leaves him with nothing but a lame comeback.

title: Rigged Review Motivational Process

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's time for your annual performance review.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The process is the same as usual.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Make your accomplishments fit the trendy categories on this form.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: "1. Estimate the cash value of the empowerment you displayed this year. Cite examples."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Try to make your accomplishments match the raise I've already decided for you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why don't you just tell me what you've decided?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What--and ruin the motivational value of the process??

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How did I get stuck with all the cynical employees?

setting: Dilbert's cubicle in the office
situation: The Boss arrives to conduct Dilbert's annual performance review and explains that Dilbert must fit his accomplishments into trendy categories on a form. He then admits the raise has already been decided and Dilbert should make his accomplishments match it. When Dilbert suggests simply being told the decision, the Boss refuses, citing the process's motivational value.
punchline: The review is a sham in which the raise is predetermined and employees must reverse-engineer justifications, yet the Boss is baffled that his employees are cynical about it.
summary: A manager forces an employee to invent achievements that justify a pay raise already chosen in advance, then wonders why his staff is so cynical.

title: Mission Statement Meets Donuts

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I took a crack at writing a "mission statement" for our group.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: "We enhance stockholder value through strategic business initiatives by empowered employees working in new team paradigms."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you ever just marvel at the fact we get paid to do this?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did anybody bring donuts?

setting: Conference room during a team meeting
situation: The Boss reads aloud a mission statement he wrote for the group, which is full of empty corporate buzzwords. Dilbert quietly remarks on how absurd it is that they are paid for this kind of work, while the Boss, already bored by the whole exercise, asks if anyone brought donuts.
punchline: Even the author of the buzzword-filled mission statement cares more about free donuts than the meaningless document he just wrote, underscoring how pointless the exercise is.
summary: A manager recites a jargon-stuffed group mission statement, then drops the subject entirely to ask about pastries.

title: Dogbert Bribes the Jury Obliquely

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Before you decide who wins this civil suit, remember this...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I can't legally offer you large cash kickbacks for deciding in my favor. But please take a moment to complete a self-addressed stamped envelope.

transcript.speaker: Judge
transcript.text: What are you doing?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm trying to establish "reasonable doubt."

setting: A courtroom, in front of the jury box
situation: Dogbert addresses the jury in a civil suit and says he cannot legally offer cash kickbacks for a favorable verdict. He then hands out self-addressed stamped envelopes as a hint for the jurors to send him bribes. The judge asks what he is doing, and Dogbert claims he is establishing reasonable doubt.
punchline: Dogbert's wink-wink bribe request, an envelope for the jurors to mail him cash, is passed off as a legal strategy by misusing the term 'reasonable doubt'.
summary: A scheming dog in court nudges jurors toward bribing him by handing out return envelopes, then excuses it with legal jargon.

title: Ted Brags About Competitor's Perks

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Have I told you recently that I have a lucrative job offer from our competitor?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: The pay is obscene, they wear casual clothes at work, and Wednesday through Friday is free beer and pizza.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: As the new guy I get to date the masseuse until the company matches me with an attractive co-worker.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sob.

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle
situation: Ted repeatedly brags to Dilbert about a job offer from a competitor, listing high pay, casual dress, and free beer and pizza. He then adds that new hires get to date the masseuse until the company pairs them with an attractive co-worker. Dilbert, who has been listening glumly at his computer, ends up with his head in his hands sobbing.
punchline: The competitor's perks escalate from reasonable to absurd, and Dilbert's sobbing shows how miserable his own job and love life are by comparison.
summary: A smug coworker rubs in the over-the-top benefits of a rival employer until his listener breaks down in tears.

title: Dogbert Teaches Management Zombie Seminar

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert's seminar on management zombies

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The successful zombie knows how to squash the creativity of co-workers.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: When you hear a new idea, adopt a facial expression which conveys both fear and an utter lack of comprehension.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Those of you who work in marketing only need to add the fear part.

transcript.speaker: Audience Member
transcript.text: Why is that?

setting: Conference room during a training seminar
situation: Dogbert leads a seminar teaching managers how to become 'management zombies' who suppress their coworkers' creativity. He points to a drawing on an easel showing the ideal blank, fearful expression to use when hearing a new idea. An audience member asks why marketing people only need the fear part.
punchline: Dogbert implies that marketing staff already have a complete lack of comprehension, so they only need to learn to look afraid.
summary: A canine consultant coaches managers on the art of crushing innovation with a frightened, clueless stare, then takes a swipe at the marketing department's intelligence.

title: Dogbert's Professional Insulter Free Sample

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm going to start a business as a professional insulter.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: For example, I would say to you, you're so ugly you have to wear a disguise on garbage pick-up day.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That was uncalled for.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Well, then no charge.

setting: Dilbert's living room at home
situation: Dogbert, perched on a footstool, tells Dilbert he plans to start a business as a professional insulter. He demonstrates with a sample insult about Dilbert's ugliness while Dilbert reads the newspaper in his armchair. Dilbert objects that it was uncalled for, and Dogbert waives the fee.
punchline: Dogbert treats Dilbert's complaint that the insult was 'uncalled for' as a service-quality objection, so he cheerfully offers the insult for free since it wasn't requested.
summary: A scheming dog launches an insulting business by trying out a sample jab on his owner, then waives payment when the owner complains it was unrequested.

title: Ratbert Outlives Disaster, Wants Shirt

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: You know, as a rat I'm far more likely to survive a major environmental calamity.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: And there's no shortage of potential disasters — you've got global warming, ozone depletion, air pollution...

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Can I try on one of your shirts?

setting: Dilbert's cubicle
situation: Ratbert stands beside Dilbert, who is working at his computer, and cheerfully lists the environmental catastrophes that he, as a rat, is likely to survive. Dilbert never looks up or answers. Ratbert then abruptly asks to try on one of Dilbert's shirts.
punchline: Ratbert's cheerful talk of surviving the extinction of humanity is really a veiled hint that he expects to inherit Dilbert's belongings, which is why he asks for a shirt.
summary: A smug little rat gleefully predicts that he will outlast mankind's ecological collapse, then politely asks to borrow the wardrobe of the person he expects to outlive.

title: Ratbert Learns Bonding Through Insults

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Dogbert insults you all the time and you treat him like your best friend.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Obviously, I need to give you some verbal abuse in order to cement our bond of love and friendship.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're an idiot.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Hey, I just bonded a little bit! This really works... You moron!

setting: Dilbert's living room, with Dilbert seated in an armchair
situation: Ratbert observes that Dilbert tolerates constant insults from Dogbert and treats him as a best friend. He concludes that verbal abuse must create friendship and tries it out on Dilbert. When Dilbert calls him an idiot in response, Ratbert is delighted and insults him right back.
punchline: Ratbert misreads Dilbert's friendship with Dogbert and takes Dilbert's irritated retort as proof that insults create friendship, so he happily escalates the abuse.
summary: A small, well-meaning rodent decides that trading insults is the secret to friendship and cheerfully puts the theory into practice.

title: Dogbert's Envy List Therapy Session

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: One of my co-workers got a much better job at another company. I'm feeling quite envious.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Instead of feeling sad, you should make a list of all the things you have that he doesn't.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: So far, you have a birthmark, a fear of spiders and the list itself.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I had the birthmark removed.

setting: Dogbert's therapy office, with Dilbert reclining in an armchair
situation: Dilbert confides in Dogbert, who is acting as a therapist, that he envies a co-worker who landed a much better job elsewhere. Dogbert advises him to list everything he has that the co-worker lacks. The resulting list is pitifully short, and Dilbert even removes one item from it.
punchline: Dogbert's feel-good exercise backfires because Dilbert's advantages over his successful co-worker amount to a birthmark, a phobia and the list itself, and he has even lost the birthmark.
summary: A therapist dog tries to cure a man's job envy with a list of his advantages, only to find the list is embarrassingly empty.

title: Bioworld Volunteers: Car Salesmen and Ratbert

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've completed the design for Bioworld. Have you selected the volunteers?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So... these are the brave people whose lives will depend on my ability to engineer a balanced ecology.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Seven car salesmen plus Ratbert...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Coincidence.

setting: Dilbert's workspace with a Bioworld terrarium model on a desk
situation: Dilbert tells Dogbert he has finished designing Bioworld, a sealed dome ecosystem, and asks whether the volunteers have been chosen. Reading from the list, he finds the test subjects are seven car salesmen and Ratbert. Dogbert dismisses the odd selection as coincidence.
punchline: Dogbert's volunteer list of seven car salesmen and Ratbert is clearly no coincidence, implying he chose people he dislikes (or finds expendable) for a dangerous experiment, and his deadpan denial makes it obvious.
summary: A dome ecosystem engineer discovers his guinea pigs are a group of salesmen and a small rat, and his dog boss insists the choice was random.

title: Boss Demands 178-Hour Work Week

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I can't keep working these long hours... I deserve a family life.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, Alice, Alice...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This isn't the "me" generation of the eighties. This is the "lifeless nineties." I expect 178 hours of work from you each week.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: There are only... uh, 168 hours in a week.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I expect your family to chip in a few hours.

setting: Office
situation: Alice complains to the Pointy-Haired Boss that her long hours leave no time for a family life. The Boss dismisses her, saying this is the 'lifeless nineties' and demands 178 hours of work per week. When Alice points out a week only has 168 hours, he says her family can cover the difference.
punchline: The Boss's solution to an impossible workload is to conscript Alice's family into working for the company, showing his total disregard for employees' personal lives.
summary: A manager brushes off an employee's plea for a home life by demanding more hours than a week contains and volunteering her relatives to make up the shortfall.

title: Ratbert Welcomes Dilbert's Polluted Demise

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: It used to bother me that the air was getting polluted and unbreathable.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: But I realized that rats are hardier than humans — so we'll get all your stuff after you wheeze your last breath!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think I'll go for a walk.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Hey! Why not drive?

setting: Dilbert's living room
situation: Ratbert sits near Dilbert, who is reading a newspaper in an armchair, and cheerfully explains that air pollution no longer bothers him because rats will outlast humans and inherit their belongings. Dilbert decides to go for a walk, and Ratbert urges him to drive instead.
punchline: Ratbert, eager to inherit Dilbert's possessions, encourages him to drive, which adds to the pollution and hastens his death.
summary: A gleeful rat looks forward to inheriting a human's belongings once smog finishes him off, and nudges him toward the most polluting way to travel.

title: Telepathic Blind Date Thinks Naughty

transcript.speaker: Two-headed woman
transcript.text: Our last blind date was intimidated just because we're two-headed and telepathic.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Must clear my mind. Don't think of anything naughty.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Oops.

setting: A restaurant table on a blind date
situation: Dilbert is on a blind date with a two-headed woman who explains that her previous date was scared off because she is telepathic. Dilbert tries to keep his thoughts clean, but the effort of not thinking about anything naughty backfires. Both of her faces look shocked, showing she has read his mind.
punchline: Telling himself not to think of anything naughty makes him think of exactly that, and his telepathic date picks up on it immediately.
summary: A man on a blind date with a mind-reading, two-headed woman fails to keep his thoughts polite and gets caught.

title: Recognition Fuzzy Mistaken for Lint

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm awarding you a "recognition fuzzy" to commend you for your good work on the project.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Display it proudly on your shirt. It's good for morale.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You have pocket lint on your shirt.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your jealousy is so transparent.

setting: Office
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he is awarding him a "recognition fuzzy" for his work on a project and instructs him to wear it on his shirt to boost morale. Wally then points out that Dilbert just has pocket lint on his shirt. Dilbert dismisses the remark as obvious jealousy.
punchline: The company's cheap employee recognition award is literally a bit of lint, so the only reward for good work is something indistinguishable from trash, yet Dilbert defensively pretends it is a coveted prize.
summary: A boss hands out a worthless fuzzy as a morale-boosting honor, and a coworker's honest observation gets brushed off as envy.

title: Boss's Cryogenic Chamber Coat Prank

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I just arranged to have my body cryogenically frozen before my death.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: In a hundred years I'll be revived and cured. That way, future generations will get the benefits of knowing me.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I hope you have a good warm coat.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Coat? Nobody said anything about needing a coat.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Obviously you need a coat. It's freezing in that cryogenic chamber. You'd better wear long underwear too.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Don't let them tell you otherwise. Remember, the customer is always right!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: (thought) I want a space heater in there too!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That wasn't nice.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I did it for future generations.

setting: Office hallway
situation: The Boss announces that he has arranged to be cryogenically frozen so that future generations can benefit from knowing him. Wally feeds him a series of absurd 'tips' about needing a warm coat, long underwear and insisting that the customer is always right. The Boss falls for it and decides to demand a space heater in the freezing chamber.
punchline: Wally tricks the Boss into making ridiculous demands of the cryonics company, which he claims is a service to future generations, since it keeps the Boss from being revived and spreading his influence.
summary: Wally exploits his boss's gullibility with silly advice about preparing for a cryogenic freeze, all to spare the future from a revived manager.

title: Dogbert Campaigns on Hair Quality

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Thank you all for coming to this emergency board meeting.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: As you know, all promotions to senior management are based on hair. I think we all agree this is the best system.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: But have you noticed that I have a rich lustrous coat, whereas our current president gets a little outside help?

setting: Corporate boardroom
situation: Dogbert, seated at the head of a board meeting table, calls an emergency meeting and gets the board to agree that promotions are based on hair. He then points with a pointer at the company president, implying the president wears a toupee, while his own fur is naturally lustrous. The president looks alarmed.
punchline: Dogbert exploits a shallow promotion criterion to argue that he deserves the president's job because his natural coat beats the president's toupee.
summary: A scheming dog persuades a board that hair determines promotions, then uses that logic to expose the president's hairpiece and make his own bid for power.

title: Dogbert Mocks Dilbert's Outdated Computer

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I just read that a new computer chip is on the market. Your machine is out of date.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You're behind the curve. Technology is racing ahead without you. You're no longer state-of-the-art or leading edge.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Sometimes people like you can get jobs in museums.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I bought this thing yesterday!!

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle
situation: Dogbert tells Dilbert that a newly released computer chip has made his computer obsolete, lecturing him about being behind the curve and no longer leading edge. He suggests Dilbert could get a job in a museum. Dilbert, typing at his desk, protests that he only bought the computer yesterday.
punchline: Technology moves so fast that a computer bought just yesterday is already considered obsolete, fit for a museum.
summary: A dog gleefully informs his owner that the computer he purchased only a day ago is already a relic.

title: Dilbert's Backhanded Rat Compliment

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Is it possible that you're prejudiced against rats because you once had a bad experience with a rat?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Just out of curiosity, what would be a good experience with a rat?

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I believe I've been insulted!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That was kind of a good experience.

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle
situation: Ratbert asks Dilbert, who is working at his computer, whether his dislike of rats comes from a bad experience with one. Dilbert asks what a good experience with a rat would even be. Ratbert concludes he has been insulted, and Dilbert replies that this was kind of a good experience.
punchline: Dilbert admits that insulting Ratbert was the closest thing to a good experience he has ever had with a rat, confirming his prejudice.
summary: A rat probes his coworker's bias against rodents and gets a reply that proves the bias is real.

title: Wally's Testosterone Makes Him Hunt Pigeons

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Gee, Wally, you sure have been popular with women since the testosterone started spewing from your head.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's amazing... I even bought a pickup truck and a rifle so I can hunt after work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What do you hunt around here?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Pigeons are the most convenient... Don't even have to get out of the truck.

setting: Office, with a plain pink background
situation: Dilbert remarks that Wally has become popular with women ever since testosterone began visibly spraying out of his head. A woman clings to Wally's arm as he explains he bought a pickup truck and a rifle to hunt after work. When Dilbert asks what he hunts, Wally says he shoots pigeons without even leaving the truck.
punchline: Wally's sudden macho makeover is undercut by his lazy, unsporting version of hunting, which means shooting pigeons from the comfort of his truck.
summary: A newly hormone-charged Wally attracts women and buys a truck and rifle, yet his hunting turns out to be as effortless and lazy as ever.

title: Crushing the New Hire's Spirit Schedule

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Matt is fresh out of engineering school. You'll be his mentor.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Whatever you do, don't crush his spirit before Wednesday.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why put it off so long?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Because I bet ten bucks we could string him along until Thursday.

setting: Office
situation: The Boss introduces Matt, a new engineering graduate, and assigns Dilbert to mentor him. The Boss warns Dilbert not to crush Matt's spirit before Wednesday. When Dilbert asks why, the Boss admits he has a ten-dollar bet that they can keep Matt's hopes up until Thursday.
punchline: The Boss treats the new hire's inevitable disillusionment as a betting game, showing that management expects the job to destroy his enthusiasm and only wants to time it.
summary: A manager hands a naive new graduate to a mentor with orders to delay his disillusionment, because the manager has money riding on how long it lasts.

title: Dilbert Chokes While Scoffing Dramatically

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Maybe Dilbert can tell us if our plan is technically feasible.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: For dramatic effect I'll scoff loudly.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll just sort of laugh and snort and take a breath at the same time.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Snork

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Oh-no! Some spittle went down my air pipe... I'm choking.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Mmph gaak

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Should we do something?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: We're over our headcount, you know.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...And so I survived, but my professional credibility took a hit.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You knew the risks when you became an engineer.

setting: Conference room, then Dilbert's home
situation: In a meeting, Dilbert is asked if the team's plan is technically feasible and plans to scoff for dramatic effect. He accidentally inhales spittle and chokes, collapsing under the table with his feet in the air. His colleagues, noting they are over headcount, consider not helping him, and afterward he tells Dogbert he survived but lost credibility.
punchline: Dilbert's colleagues treat his near-death choking as a convenient way to reduce headcount, and Dogbert dismisses the humiliation as an occupational hazard of engineering.
summary: A calculated show of derision goes wrong when an engineer nearly chokes to death while managers weigh whether rescuing him is worth the headcount.

title: Crossbow Improves Job Satisfaction

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: My job satisfaction has gone way up since I got this crossbow.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Hey, Russell! Answer your own phone once in a while!

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: FFFT

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: We need to chat.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Chat this.

setting: Office cubicles
situation: Carol sits in her cubicle holding a crossbow and thinks about how much happier she is at work with it. She shouts at a coworker named Russell to answer his own phone and fires a bolt. When a bespectacled coworker holding a folder says they need to chat, an arrow is already lodged in his folder, and Carol silently thinks of the crossbow as her reply.
punchline: Carol's idea of improved job satisfaction is threatening and shooting coworkers, and she answers a request to chat with another implied crossbow shot.
summary: A cubicle worker discovers that arming herself with a crossbow is the secret to enjoying her workplace interruptions.

title: Garbage Man Rejects Engineer's Suggestions

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I wish you'd realize that you're a garbage man, not an engineer. I don't need your suggestions on my designs.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What are you writing? Oh yeah, as if I care.

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: If you need help understanding that, the paper boy will be by soon. I've been working with him.

setting: Dilbert's workplace, beside a trash can
situation: Dilbert scolds the garbage man for offering suggestions on his engineering designs, insisting that a garbage man is not an engineer. The garbage man scribbles notes on paper, and Dilbert dismisses what he is writing. The garbage man then threatens that the paper boy will come by to help Dilbert understand, revealing the two have been working together.

He ends by gloating that his co-workers had to be sick for him to win.
punchline: Dilbert's perfect attendance is really the result of his romantic rejection, social exclusion and lack of meaningful work, and Dogbert points out that he also needs to gloat to enjoy it.
summary: A lonely, sidelined employee accepts a perfect-health prize by turning every one of his workplace and personal failures into a reason he never got sick.

title: Dogbert's Backhanded Pep Talk for Ratbert

transcript.text: Don't feel bad because you're awkward, Ratbert.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Do I have to learn any computer skills?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It seems like a requirement, but it's not.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hey!

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle, at his desk
situation: Dogbert tries to comfort the small, awkward Ratbert while Dilbert works at his computer. His encouragement consists of pointing out that some happy people are awkward, homely and dull. Ratbert asks if he needs computer skills, and Dogbert says it seems like a requirement but is not, which prompts an offended 'Hey!' from Dilbert.
punchline: Dogbert's consolation is really an insult, and his remark that computer skills aren't required for happiness implies that people like Dilbert, who work with computers, are the awkward, homely and dull ones.
summary: A supposedly kind reassurance to a nervous rodent turns into a dig at the nerdy engineer typing away beside them.

title: Total Quality Management Funds Consultants

transcript.text: In the old days, quality was just an empty word meaning "good."

setting: Elbonia, outdoors in a muddy landscape with a flip chart
situation: Dilbert has travelled to Elbonia to teach a group of locals about Total Quality Management. Using a flip chart, he explains that quality originally just meant "good", then reveals a diagram showing money flowing to business consultants.
punchline: Quality management has become less about improving products and more about a scheme to funnel money to consultants.
summary: Dilbert lectures a group of Elbonians on a management buzzword and cheerfully admits it exists mainly to enrich consultants.

situation: During a meeting, the boss announces a ten-minute break and Dilbert panics because he needs the restroom and fears being left out of the mingling groups. A slow air dryer makes him late, so he fakes reading the agenda to hide that he is standing alone, then realizes nobody will believe it. At home, Dogbert asks if work was tough and Dilbert says only the breaks are.
punchline: The meetings themselves are easy, but the unstructured break time is the socially agonizing part for an awkward person like Dilbert.
summary: A socially anxious engineer finds the coffee break far more stressful than the meeting it interrupts.

title: Bioworld Volunteers Doubt Their Own Value

setting: Outside a domed Bioworld habitat, with Dilbert at a laptop and Dogbert and Ratbert on cell phones
situation: Dilbert sits at a laptop monitoring the Bioworld experiment while the volunteers inside run low on oxygen and food. Ratbert, who is inside the dome, phones Dogbert to report that the car salespeople suspect they are considered expendable. Dogbert replies that Ratbert was put in there too, and Ratbert admits he already told them that.
punchline: Ratbert's reassurance that he was also sent into the deadly dome is no comfort, because it only shows that Dogbert treats everyone, even Ratbert, as expendable.
summary: Trapped in a failing experimental habitat, a pet reports the occupants' fear of being disposable, and the supposed proof to the contrary just confirms it.

setting: Office cubicle area
situation: Dilbert admires how productive a temporary contract programmer is as the man types furiously at his computer. Dilbert points out that the programmer's job depends entirely on results, and the programmer becomes ever more frantic, eventually surrounded by a cloud of dust. Dilbert then casually invites a coworker to go blame marketing for the missing requirements, and the coworker asks why the rush.
punchline: Dilbert is hard at work frightening the contract programmer into superhuman speed while idly planning to blame marketing for the vague requirements, so the real 'big rush' is only for the temp, not the permanent staff.
summary: A permanent employee remarks on a contract worker's speed, reminds him how disposable he is, then wanders off to complain about marketing while the temp slaves away.

title: Budget Mockery Backfires With Click

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Ha ha! It must be really exciting work. I mean, gosh, making all those numbers add up.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Ha ha! I'm glad I have a real job!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Not anymore.

setting: Office cubicle with Dilbert at his computer
situation: A smug coworker stands over Dilbert and mocks him for being assigned budget work, laughing that he is glad he has a real job. Dilbert silently keeps typing, then thinks "Not anymore" as he clicks away at his computer, implying he is using his budget access to eliminate the coworker's job.
punchline: Dilbert, now in control of the budget numbers, quietly retaliates against his mocking coworker by cutting the coworker's position.
summary: A taunting colleague gets his comeuppance when the man he ridicules for crunching budgets decides to crunch him out of a paycheck.

setting: Executive's office
situation: Dogbert, posing as the leader of a huge nerd buyers' collective, visits a company executive and demands a twenty percent discount on all products. He threatens to e-mail a million nerds to boycott the company. When the executive doubts him, Dogbert sends a wireless message giving the nerds the executive's daughter's phone number.
punchline: Dogbert backs up his empty-sounding threat by sending a million lonely nerds the executive's daughter's phone number, showing he is ruthless and that nerds are a force to be feared.
summary: A dog claiming to lead an army of nerd customers shakes down a businessman for discounts and proves he means it with a nasty wireless message.

title: Raised by Bumper Sticker Logic

situation: Dilbert lectures Dogbert that people who don't vote have no right to complain. When Dogbert asks why not, Dilbert just restates the slogan as if it were airtight logic. He adds that it's how he was raised, prompting Dogbert to ask if he was raised by bumper stickers.
punchline: Dilbert's 'logical' argument is just a circular bumper-sticker slogan, and Dogbert points out that his whole upbringing seems to consist of such slogans.
summary: A man defends a civic slogan by merely repeating it, and his dog mocks him for apparently learning his values from car decorations.

title: Dilbert Fakes Norwegian at Introductions

setting: Conference room, then a short closing scene outside the meeting
situation: At a meeting, the boss asks everyone to introduce themselves and say which district they work in. Dilbert panics because he can't remember the name of his district, so he pretends to speak only Norwegian and spouts gibberish. Afterward he tells Dogbert he gets paid the same no matter what he does.
punchline: Dilbert's absurd fake-Norwegian act changes nothing about his pay, which reveals that his compensation has no connection to his performance, and Dogbert sarcastically agrees.
summary: Put on the spot to name his department, a flustered engineer fakes a foreign language and then admits his salary never depends on his behavior.

title: Never So Little Measured So Much

transcript.text: Here's my time report, in fifteen minute increments.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And here's my monthly project status, my budget forecast, my key accomplishments, my jeopardy list...

transcript.text: Never has so little been measured so much.

setting: Office, Dilbert handing paperwork to his boss
situation: Dilbert hands his boss a growing stack of reports: a time report in fifteen-minute increments, a monthly project status, a budget forecast, key accomplishments and a jeopardy list. The boss happily collects the papers. In the last panel the boss, clutching the pile, thinks about how much is being measured.
punchline: The boss's own thought admits that the reporting is excessive for the tiny amount of actual work being measured, parodeying Churchill's famous line, yet he enjoys the paperwork anyway.
summary: An employee buries his manager in status paperwork while the manager privately jokes that the volume of measurement far exceeds the work being done.
keywords: never has so much been owed by so many

punchline: Dogbert's grand promise of having something named after Ratbert is cheaply fulfilled by renaming Ratbert himself after existing things, and the naive Ratbert is delighted anyway.
summary: A scheming dog flatters a gullible rat with naming honors that amount to simply borrowing names that already exist.

summary: A manager's attempt to offload a vacationing employee's work turns into a battle of wits that the manager secretly wins with a prize of his own.

summary: A television newscast piles on grim stories and then reveals it manufactured its own local headline by running someone over.

Dogbert, seated on a desk, responds by zapping him with a stun device, leaving him frazzled with storm clouds over his head.
punchline: The radio traffic reporter's cheesy, pun-filled segue is so annoying to Dogbert that he punishes him with an electric shock, taking revenge on behalf of every irritated commuter.
summary: A radio traffic reporter delivers a corny transition line and gets shocked by a vengeful Dogbert tired of such banter.

summary: A worried woman laments that failing schools will leave the country with cleaners instead of engineers, and Dogbert finds the bright side in spotless surroundings.

Dilbert, holding a rolled-up magazine, reads out the readers' responses: male writers want to whack Ratbert with the magazine, and others suggest using power tools on him.
