situation: A coworker named Tim Zumph introduces himself to Wally and Dilbert as the author of a famous memo from 1978. He proudly recalls that his boss complimented the memo outside of a performance review, and says he still carries a copy. Wally, holding his coffee mug, glances at the memo and points out a typo.
punchline: Tim's one career highlight is a decades-old memo he treasures, and Wally deflates it instantly by spotting a typo in it.
summary: A man basks in the glory of a single complimented memo from years ago until a coworker finds an error in it.

title: Wally's Brainstorming Nap Fantasy

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Hey, what are you doing? Are you sleeping?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Zzzzz

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Uh... No, I was brainstorming.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What idea did you come up with?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It involves Irene in Accounting. She's the stern nurse and I'm the incorrigible industrialist.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I already thought of that one.

setting: Office cubicle
situation: The Boss catches Wally asleep at his desk in front of his computer. Wally claims he was brainstorming, and when pressed for his idea he describes a romantic role-play fantasy about a coworker from Accounting. The Boss reveals he has already had the same fantasy.
punchline: Wally's work-hours 'brainstorming' was really a daydream about a coworker, and the Boss's deadpan reply shows he has had the same fantasy himself.
summary: Caught napping, a lazy employee passes off a steamy daydream about a coworker as brainstorming, only for his manager to admit he's already used the idea.

title: Dilbert's Overly Affectionate Computer Upgrade

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Look what I got for my computer! It's a romostatic real-time data compression processor!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Oooh... I can't wait to plug you in, my little darling. I've waited so long.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Oh yes! Yes!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Does the church know about this?

setting: Dilbert's home living room
situation: Dilbert proudly shows Dogbert a new computer component he bought, a data compression processor. He then lovingly coos at the box about plugging it in and gets so carried away that he sounds ecstatic. Dogbert, sitting in an armchair, wryly asks if the church knows about this.
punchline: Dilbert's passionate, romantic enthusiasm for computer hardware sounds so inappropriate that Dogbert jokes it might be a matter for religious disapproval.
summary: A gadget-loving engineer sweet-talks a computer part in terms so amorous that his dog wonders if clergy should be told.

title: Jacked-Up Pickup Truck Problem

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Maybe it's because of my high testosterone levels, but I couldn't resist getting my pickup jacked up.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I thought it would be more frightening to the people I tailgate.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The only problem is that you can't let people see you trying to get in it.

setting: Outdoors next to a pickup truck with oversized suspension
situation: Wally proudly shows Dilbert his pickup truck, which he has had jacked up on enormous tires, blaming his high testosterone. He explains he did it to intimidate the drivers he tailgates. In the last panel he is seen scrambling headfirst into the high cab, admitting the flaw in the plan.
punchline: The macho image of a towering truck is ruined by the undignified, comical effort Wally needs just to climb into it.
summary: A man brags about lifting his truck to scare other drivers, then concedes the vehicle is awkward to climb into.

title: Dogbert Guilt-Trips Dilbert Into Gifts

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: How can this be the season of good cheer when I don't even have my gifts yet?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I mean, what if you get me something stupid? I'll hate you forever and have to run away.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your psychology won't work this year. I will not buy more gifts.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You'll probably find me dead in some snow bank.

setting: Dilbert's desk in an office, at Christmas time
situation: Dogbert sits on Dilbert's desk while Dilbert works at his computer, and complains that he hasn't received his Christmas gifts yet. He tries to manipulate Dilbert with worries about getting a stupid gift and threats to run away. Dilbert, unmoved, refuses to buy any more gifts, so Dogbert escalates to a dramatic guilt trip about dying in a snow bank.
punchline: Dogbert's escalating emotional manipulation fails to work on Dilbert, so he resorts to an over-the-top guilt trip about freezing to death, mocking the pressure of holiday gift-giving.
summary: A scheming dog badgers his owner about presents before the holidays and plays the dying-in-the-snow card when the manipulation is rejected.

title: Sealed Biodome, Plants Left Outside

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The Bioworld dome is now sealed. You must live off its resources for two years.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The edible plants were delivered just before the dome was sealed. They are the key to your survival.

transcript.speaker: Delivery Man
transcript.text: Can somebody open the delivery door? I've got some plants outside.

setting: Outside and inside a sealed Bioworld biodome
situation: Dilbert, holding a clipboard, announces to the volunteers inside the Bioworld dome that it is sealed and they must live off its resources for two years. He stresses that the edible plants, delivered just before sealing, are essential to their survival. A delivery man then appears outside, still holding the plants and asking someone to open the door.
punchline: The plants that the inhabitants' survival depends on were never actually delivered inside, so the dome is sealed with no food.
summary: A sealed two-year biosphere experiment is doomed from the start because its vital food supply is still standing outside with the delivery driver.

title: Phil Summons Demons, Accountant Arrives

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's "Phil, the Prince of Insufficient Light"!

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: I saw you take that chair.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: I summon all the demons and trolls of heck to come forth and punish you now!!!

transcript.speaker: Ed
transcript.text: I'm Ed, from Accounting. The others are at lunch.

setting: Office doorway and hallway
situation: Dilbert recognizes Phil in his red devil costume, and Phil accuses him of taking a chair. Phil waves his pitchfork and dramatically summons all the demons and trolls to punish Dilbert. The only one who answers is Ed, a mild-mannered accountant, who explains the rest are out at lunch.
punchline: The grand summoning of hellish punishers produces only a lone accountant, since all the other 'demons' are on their lunch break.
summary: A devil-costumed coworker's theatrical call for infernal vengeance is answered by one underwhelming accountant while everyone else is eating.

title: Dilbert Sucked Into Cyberspace Pantsless

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Help! Dogbert, I'm being sucked into cyberspace!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Aaaagh!!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Let's hope you don't need pants in cyberspace.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wow! It's like a "Calvin and Hobbes" fantasy but without the artistic look to it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's beautiful! I'm interacting with the minds of brilliant people from around the globe.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can see how all their ideas and knowledge fit together! It's exhilarating!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How can I ever describe this to somebody who hasn't been here?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...And I didn't even need pants!!

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: So, you're some kind of nerd, right?

setting: Dilbert's home computer, then a fantasy cyberspace, then a social gathering
situation: Dilbert is pulled into his computer screen while Dogbert watches, leaving his pants behind. Inside a surreal 1990s vision of cyberspace he marvels at the internet and email as a network of connected minds. Back in the real world he excitedly recounts the experience at a party, mentioning that he didn't need pants.
punchline: After raving about his transcendent internet experience, Dilbert's only boast is that he didn't need pants, so the woman he's talking to concludes he's just a nerd.
summary: A man gets vacuumed into a glowing digital realm, gushes about global connectedness, then loses his audience by bragging about his missing trousers.

title: Infinitely Dense Gym Teacher Cover-Up

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ... As you approached the speed of light you would become infinitely dense.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Then would you be forced to take a job as a high school gym teacher?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The book changes subjects at this point.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Sounds like a cover-up.

setting: Dilbert's living room, in armchairs
situation: Dilbert reads aloud from a physics book about approaching the speed of light while Dogbert listens. Dogbert jokes that becoming infinitely dense would lead to a career as a high school gym teacher. When Dilbert says the book changes subjects, Dogbert suspects a cover-up.
punchline: Dogbert plays on the double meaning of 'dense' as stupid, joking that dense people end up as gym teachers, and then treats the book's silence on the subject as a conspiracy.
summary: A physics book's talk of becoming infinitely dense prompts a dog to insult gym teachers and then suspect the author of hiding the truth.

title: Ratbert Complains About Cheese Traps

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Yeah, I'd say that I've become a loved and respected member of the family.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Sure, you had some initial prejudice because I'm a rat, but love won out.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: So, I was thinking maybe there's a better way to leave little bits of cheese around the house for me.

setting: Dilbert's home, at his desk with a computer
situation: Ratbert, Dilbert's pet rat, talks about how he has become a loved and respected member of the family despite initial prejudice against him being a rat. Dilbert sits at his computer, mostly silent. In the last panel Ratbert is caught in a snap mousetrap by the tail while asking for a better way to leave cheese out for him.
punchline: Ratbert claims to be a beloved family member, yet the cheese Dilbert leaves around the house is bait on mousetraps, showing he is still treated as vermin.
summary: A pet rat boasts of being cherished by his household, then reveals his tail is caught in a trap baited with cheese.

title: Third Date Reveals Mob Boss

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This is it... the critical third date.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This is when they casually mention any hidden deformities or horrible secrets to see if you still like them.

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: Some people say you should stop dating after you marry a mob boss.

setting: Restaurant table during a dinner date
situation: Dilbert sits across from a woman at a restaurant and thinks to himself that the third date is when people confess hidden flaws and horrible secrets. His date then casually mentions that you should stop dating after you marry a mob boss, implying she is married to one.
punchline: The date's offhand remark reveals she is married to a mob boss, a far worse secret than Dilbert was bracing for, and one that makes continuing to date her dangerous.
summary: A nervous man expecting a mild confession on his third date instead learns his companion is already married to a gangster.

title: Bunny Ears Behind the Monkey

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's going to be tough deciding which of you to lay off.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I want to keep the employee who projects the most professional image.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This should make him look pretty stupid.

setting: The Boss's office
situation: The Boss sits across his desk from Dilbert and a monkey, announcing that one of them will be laid off. He says he will keep whoever projects the most professional image. Dilbert smiles and secretly holds up bunny ears behind the monkey's head, planning to sabotage its chances.
punchline: Dilbert treats the layoff as a contest against a monkey and still resorts to sabotaging the monkey, which reveals how low the 'professional image' criterion, and Dilbert's own scheming, really is.
summary: Faced with a layoff decision against a monkey, Dilbert sneaks a prank gesture behind it to make it look unprofessional.

title: Dogbert Emails the President Satirically

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It says the President can now receive electronic mail.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Really?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Dear Mr. President, I would like to make a few suggestions on how to run the country.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: As you know, the citizens are mostly imbeciles.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You should give an executive order for all people to march into the sea.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Then, the few of us who are smart enough to ignore you can divide up their stuff.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: This may seem slightly immoral, but it's better than having a bunch of unwanted people clogging up the country.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: (typing silently at the computer)

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And we won't have to hear your brother sing anymore. Sincerely, Ross Perot

setting: Dilbert's living room
situation: Dilbert reads in the newspaper that the President can now receive email. Dogbert immediately writes the President a message offering suggestions on running the country, proposing that all the citizens be ordered to march into the sea so the smart few can divide up their belongings. He signs it as Ross Perot.
punchline: Dogbert's genocidal proposal is justified by a bonus perk, never having to hear the President's brother sing, and he sends it under the name of political rival Ross Perot.
summary: Upon learning that the President accepts email, Dogbert drafts a monstrous plan to drown the population and signs it with a famous politician's name.

title: Dogbert's Remedies for Annoying Coworkers

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Today you will learn how to deal with people who have personality defects.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Case 1: Todd laughs nervously at every one of his own comments.

transcript.speaker: Todd
transcript.text: Don't hold it against me! Hee hee haw haw!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Remedy: Todd must be relocated to a distant planet.

transcript.speaker: Todd
transcript.text: It sure is lonely! Hee hee!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Case 2: Allen stares at you like a zombie for long periods before responding to questions.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Remedy: Allen must be paired with Virginia (Case 3) who fills all quiet spots with inane chatter.

transcript.speaker: Virginia
transcript.text: Yak yak yak

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Case 4: Matt speaks slowly about amazingly boring topics.

transcript.speaker: Matt
transcript.text: I... ate... a... pickle...

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Remedy: Matt's head can be outfitted with a reading stand.

transcript.speaker: Matt
transcript.text: I... like... pickles...

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Case 5: An engineer. Remedy: Very quietly seal him in his own cubicle.

setting: Office training session, with scenes of a distant planet and a cubicle
situation: Dogbert lectures on how to handle coworkers with personality defects, presenting a case and a drastic remedy for each. Todd is exiled to a distant planet, Allen is paired with the chatterbox Virginia, and Matt's head gets a reading stand. The final case is an engineer, whom Dogbert quietly walls into his own cubicle with bricks.
punchline: Each remedy is an absurdly extreme solution, culminating in bricking an engineer into his cubicle, implying that engineers are the most socially tolerable only when kept out of sight.
summary: A canine trainer offers outrageous cures for irritating coworkers, ending with an engineer being walled in alive.

title: Dogbert's Analogy-Padded Consulting Report

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Here's my consulting report on your company.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I had no insights so I bulked it up by adding witty analogies.

transcript.speaker: Report text
transcript.text: "His head was like a hollow putty ball attacked by two pointy dust bunnies."

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Vivid, isn't it?

setting: The Boss's office
situation: Dogbert, working as a consultant, delivers a thick report on the company to The Boss. He admits he had no real insights, so he padded the document with witty analogies. The Boss reads a sample line, which insults his own pointy-haired head, and Dogbert asks if it is vivid.
punchline: The consultant's expensive report contains no actual insight, just filler analogies, one of which mocks the boss himself, and the boss is too clueless to object.
summary: A consultant dog hands over a hefty report with nothing useful inside except colorful similes, including a rude one about the client's own head.

title: Boss Sends Dilbert to Elbonia

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm sending you to our plant in Elbonia. I want you to teach them "quality."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I selected you because you've been there and you know their language.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: They speak English.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Oh. Then I guess it's because I hate you.

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he is being sent to the company's plant in Elbonia to teach the workers about quality, claiming he was chosen because he knows their language. Dilbert points out that they speak English, so the stated reason falls apart.
punchline: With his excuse debunked, the Boss cheerfully admits the real reason for the assignment is that he hates Dilbert, treating a punitive overseas posting as a punishment.
summary: A manager's flimsy justification for shipping an employee off to a remote foreign plant collapses, leaving only open spite as the motive.

title: Dogbert's Happy News Network

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm going to start-up a television news network that only reports happy stories.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: In sports, fifty percent of the teams won their games yesterday. And all the players are millionaires - most of whom have no serious drug problems.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Our person of the week is Darryl, who, despite his tiny brain, found success through a life of crime.

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle, then Dogbert's mock news anchor desk
situation: Dogbert tells Dilbert, who is working at his computer, that he will launch a TV news network reporting only happy stories. In the following panels Dogbert sits at an anchor desk and delivers sample 'good news' reports about sports and a criminal who became successful.
punchline: Spinning bad news in a positive light only makes it more cynical, since the 'happy' stories celebrate millionaire athletes with drug problems and a successful criminal.
summary: A news anchor dog shows how relentlessly upbeat reporting turns grim facts into darkly ironic cheerfulness.

title: Challenge of Fear Dating Test

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Uh... Lisa, I was wondering if you'd like to go on a date with me.

transcript.speaker: Lisa
transcript.text: I can only date you if you survive the "Challenge of Fear."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What is the "Challenge of Fear"?

transcript.speaker: Lisa
transcript.text: It's a test of your manliness.

transcript.speaker: Lisa
transcript.text: First you must stick your head in the drawer as I slam it shut.

transcript.speaker: Lisa
transcript.text: Then I staple you to the employee bulletin board.

transcript.speaker: Lisa
transcript.text: Live weasels are stuffed in your pants.

transcript.speaker: Lisa
transcript.text: Finally, you must fling yourself down the elevator shaft!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ready.

transcript.speaker: Lisa
transcript.text: The weird thing is that they rule the world.

setting: Lisa's office desk
situation: Dilbert nervously asks a coworker named Lisa on a date. She says he must first pass a 'Challenge of Fear' that tests his manliness, and lists a series of increasingly painful and absurd ordeals: a slammed drawer, stapling, weasels in his pants and jumping down an elevator shaft. Dilbert bends over eagerly, ready to begin.
punchline: Lisa's remark that the weird thing is that 'they' (men, who will endure absurd pain for a date) rule the world is a sarcastic comment on male behavior and the irony that such people hold power.
summary: A hopeful engineer agrees to endure a gauntlet of ridiculous torments just to win a date, prompting his intended to marvel at who runs the planet.

title: Dogbert Loves Rigging Democratic Votes

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now that you've united the electronic mail users of the world, what are you going to do?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll poll them about their needs, then use their collective political and economic power to get them whatever the majority wants.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Couldn't you easily rig the vote to support your own selfish ambitions?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I love the democratic system.

setting: Dilbert's office, at a computer desk
situation: Dilbert asks Dogbert what he plans to do now that he has united all the world's email users. Dogbert describes a noble plan to poll them and deliver whatever the majority wants. Dilbert points out that he could easily rig the vote for his own gain, and Dogbert cheerfully replies that he loves democracy.
punchline: Dogbert's gleeful endorsement of the democratic system is an admission that he intends to manipulate the vote, since democracy is so easy to rig.
summary: A scheming dog announces a fair-sounding plan to serve a vast online electorate, then happily confirms that the system's weaknesses are exactly what he likes about it.

title: Near Diamond Engagement Ring Insult

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Look everyone, I'm engaged!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Hey, it's one of those "near diamond" rings they were selling on the TV shopping channel for $29.95.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Uh... of course it has a list price of over a hundred dollars...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ooh, good save.

setting: Office break area
situation: Carol proudly shows her coworkers her new engagement ring. Wally recognizes it as a cheap imitation diamond sold on a TV shopping channel and blurts that out. Seeing her upset, he awkwardly tries to recover by mentioning its inflated list price, and Dilbert sarcastically praises the save.
punchline: Wally's attempt to rescue his tactless remark by citing the ring's inflated list price barely softens the insult, which Dilbert sarcastically acknowledges as a 'good save'.
summary: A woman happily shows off her engagement ring, only for a coworker to identify it as a cheap TV-shopping knockoff and then clumsily try to backpedal.

title: Boss Gloats Over Last Coffee

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm the boss. I can take the last bit of coffee without making a new pot.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Look at me!! I'm taking the last drop!! Ha ha ha ha ha ha!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: An actual human would feel guilt in this situation.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The pot needs washing.

setting: Office break room with a coffee maker
situation: The Boss reasons that his position lets him take the last of the coffee without brewing a fresh pot, then gleefully celebrates doing exactly that. Dilbert observes that a real human would feel guilty. The Boss misses the point and responds only that the pot needs washing.
punchline: The Boss shows no guilt or self-awareness, interpreting a remark about his lack of humanity as a comment on the dirty coffee pot.
summary: A smug manager gloats about draining the coffee pot without refilling it, and when told a decent person would feel bad, he completely misses the point.

title: Dilbert Steals a Coworker's Chair

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If the warehouse won't replace my broken chair, I'll just take one from somebody else.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Technically, it's not stealing because the chair belongs to the company either way.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's the worst thing that could happen?

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Hold the elevator. ...Over.

setting: Office cubicle area
situation: Dilbert, whose chair is broken and can't be replaced by the warehouse, sneaks into another cubicle to take someone else's chair. He rationalizes that it isn't really stealing since the company owns every chair. As he wheels the chair away and wonders what could go wrong, Phil, dressed as a devil with a pitchfork and a walkie-talkie, calls for the elevator, implying Dilbert is headed to hell.
punchline: Dilbert's self-justifying theft of a chair ends with a devil costume-clad Phil and a ride in the elevator, suggesting he is going straight to hell for stealing.
summary: A man with a busted seat talks himself into swiping a coworker's, only to meet a pitchfork-toting devil who seems to be waiting for him.

title: Digitally Enhanced Dating Photo Service

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert's Digital Dating Service

transcript.text: I'm a loser. Sign me up.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Say "Velveeta."

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Now we digitize your picture for the database.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I could add some digital hair.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Good idea.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Maybe I should bob your nose and give you a tan.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: That's fair.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Whiten teeth? Smooth wrinkles? Hide stomach? Thicken lips?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: I look like Sandra Bernhard.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Yeah, but you have to admit it improves your odds.

setting: Dogbert's office for his digital dating service
situation: A balding man in a red sweater signs up for Dogbert's digital dating service, calling himself a loser. Dogbert photographs him, digitizes the picture, then offers to edit it with digital hair, a smaller nose, a tan, whiter teeth, smoother wrinkles, a hidden stomach and thicker lips. The man agrees to every change and ends up looking like Sandra Bernhard.
punchline: The customer's photo is altered so heavily that he ends up looking like a woman (Sandra Bernhard), and Dogbert cynically points out that the result still improves his chances of getting a date.
summary: A man has his dating profile photo digitally retouched so extensively that he ends up looking like a famous actress, which Dogbert insists is still an upgrade.

title: Boss Sends Dilbert to School

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The local school wants somebody to talk to the kids about a career as an engineer.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm giving this plum assignment to you because you're such a good role model.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Hee hee.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's more sincere sounding when you don't giggle.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Remember, children are our future!

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that a local school wants an engineer to talk to kids about the profession, and says he picked Dilbert as a good role model. The Boss giggles while calling it a plum assignment, and Dilbert points out that the praise would sound more sincere without the giggling. The Boss then ends with a cheerful slogan about children being the future.
punchline: The Boss's giggling reveals that the 'plum assignment' is really an unpleasant chore, and his flattery is insincere, which Dilbert calls out while the Boss keeps up the cliche.
summary: A manager hands off an unwanted school-visit duty to an engineer while snickering through the supposed compliment.

title: Faking Celebrity Photos With Photoshop

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't understand why photographers try so hard to get embarrassing pictures of celebrities.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Heck, I could just scan the celebrity photos into my computer and create any embarrassing situation you can think of.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I think Cindy Crawford should look more repulsed.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This is before we kiss.

setting: Dilbert's home, in an armchair and then at his computer
situation: Dilbert sits in an armchair reading an I Spy book while Dogbert reads beside him. He wonders why paparazzi work so hard for embarrassing celebrity shots when he could simply scan photos into his computer and fabricate any scenario. In the last panel he is doing exactly that, and Dogbert critiques his doctored image of himself with Cindy Crawford.
punchline: Dilbert's digital manipulation is really a lonely fantasy of kissing a supermodel, and Dogbert points out that even in a fake picture she looks too unenthusiastic about him.
summary: A lonely engineer brags that he can fabricate scandalous celebrity photos on his computer, then uses the idea to stage a romance with a supermodel that even his dog finds unconvincing.

title: Company's Cure: Celibacy and Adoption

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I'm working too many hours... I never spend time with my family.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The company cares. That's why we've developed a program to teach you how to cope.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: "Celibacy and adoption — the choice for the nineties."

setting: The Boss's office
situation: A female employee tells the boss she works so many hours that she never sees her family. The boss cheerfully says the company cares and has a program to teach her to cope, handing her a pamphlet. She reads it and finds it recommends celibacy and adoption.
punchline: Instead of reducing overwork, the company's 'caring' coping program simply advises employees to give up on having a family life, showing management would rather change the employee than the long hours.
summary: A overworked staffer asks for more family time and is handed a pamphlet that effectively tells her to forgo relationships and just adopt.

title: Dilbert's Pointer Pen Burns Coworkers

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I boosted the power on the pointer pen light so it's easier to see on the wall.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Look how strong it is now.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Click

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Zzzz

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let me see that. I've got a few things to point out.

transcript.speaker: Woman in meeting
transcript.text: Next.

setting: Conference room during a presentation
situation: Dilbert tells his audience he has boosted the power of his pointer pen light so it shows up better on the wall. When he demonstrates it, the beam apparently burns or zaps something, and the boss, in the third panel, reaches out to take the powerful pointer for himself.
punchline: The boss sees a dangerously powerful laser-like pointer as a tool for making his own points in meetings, and a woman nearby seems ready to use it to dismiss the next person.
summary: After supercharging his presentation pointer into something that sizzles, Dilbert watches his boss eagerly demand a turn to wield it.

title: Doctor Weighs Organs Versus Billing

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is it the flu?

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Hmm...

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: I had the computer run an economic report on the market value of your organs.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: I could make thousands of dollars by selling your parts for transplants.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Of course, this is all moot unless you die in my office while under my care.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: But if I let you die from the flu then my malpractice insurance will go up again.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: But if you live I can continue to bill you for unnecessary tests.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: There's a slight economic advantage to keeping you alive... if you leave three pints of blood and do me a little favor.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then I had to wax his jeep with my clothes.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Apparently he didn't know what kind of fabrics you wear.

setting: Doctor's examination room, then Dilbert's bed at home
situation: Dilbert visits a doctor to ask whether he has the flu. The doctor coldly runs through the financial pros and cons of selling his organs, losing malpractice coverage, or billing him for unnecessary tests, and settles on keeping him alive in exchange for blood and a favor. In the last panel Dilbert lies face down on his bed, reporting that he had to wax the doctor's jeep with his clothes.
punchline: The doctor treats the patient purely as a source of profit, weighing organ sales against billing and insurance costs, and the 'favor' turns out to be Dilbert's clothes used as car-waxing rags.
summary: A money-minded physician calculates whether his patient is worth more dead or alive, then extracts blood and menial labor as the price of treatment.

title: Dogbert Decides to Tax People

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Do you realize the government takes half of all the money you make?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And the majority of people are too young to vote, or didn't bother to vote, or voted for the loser. ...And nobody alive voted for our Constitution.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's never good when you have these insights.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I've decided to levy my own tax on people.

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle, at his desk
situation: Dogbert, sitting beside Dilbert's desk, points out that the government takes half of everyone's income. He then argues the government lacks legitimacy because most people didn't vote for it and nobody alive voted for the Constitution. Dilbert warns that Dogbert's insights are a bad sign, and Dogbert announces he will impose his own tax.
punchline: Dogbert uses a critique of the government's legitimacy to justify taxing people himself, showing his cynical logic is really a pretext for a power and money grab.
summary: After questioning why anyone should accept government taxation, Dogbert concludes he may as well start collecting taxes of his own.

title: Laser Pointer Vaporizes Temp Carl

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Dogbert, do you know how my light pointer pen could have gotten set to maximum power?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You never seem to grasp the humor in these situations. It's not as if you caused any permanent damage in the office.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Actually, I wasted a temp named Carl in the next office.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: A temp - my point exactly.

setting: Dilbert's office
situation: Dilbert, whose clothes are tattered and singed, asks Dogbert whether he knows how his light pointer pen got set to maximum power. Dogbert dismisses his concern, saying no permanent damage was done. Dilbert admits the pen killed a temp named Carl in the next office, and Dogbert says that proves his point.
punchline: Dogbert considers the death of a temp to be no permanent damage at all, since temporary workers are viewed as disposable.
summary: A scorched Dilbert confesses that his tampered pointer pen destroyed a temporary worker, and Dogbert insists that is hardly a real loss.

title: Secretary Hunts Boss Like Moby Dick

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: The "secretary with a crossbow" goes on the hunt.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Moby Dick!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You've been harpooned again, sir.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Yeah, but I capsized her desk.

setting: Office cubicles
situation: Carol, the Boss's secretary, stalks through the office carrying a crossbow, narrating her own hunt. She spots the Boss walking past a cubicle partition and likens him to the white whale. Afterward the Boss has a bolt stuck in his back, and Dilbert points it out, while the Boss claims he got back at her by tipping over her desk.
punchline: The secretary treats her boss as a whale to be harpooned, and he, in keeping with the nautical theme, brags that he retaliated by capsizing her desk, a pitifully petty revenge for being shot.
summary: A crossbow-wielding secretary stalks her boss like a whale hunter, and he shrugs off the bolt in his back by boasting he flipped her desk in return.

title: Shunned Over Budget Questions

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The other engineers shun me because I'm assigned to work on the budget.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Shun.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: They know I could pounce any moment and ask inane hypothetical budget questions.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Shun.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What if you only had half as much electricity next year?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Too late. I shunned you.

setting: Office corridors
situation: Dilbert walks through the office thinking about how other engineers avoid him because he has been assigned to work on the budget. Coworkers cover their faces and think 'shun' as he passes. When he finally approaches Alice with a hypothetical question about halving electricity, she announces that she has already shunned him.
punchline: Dilbert's coworkers are right to avoid him, since he really does ambush people with pointless hypothetical budget questions, and Alice's deadpan 'too late' shows that shunning him is a pre-emptive defence that has now failed.
summary: An engineer saddled with budgeting duties finds his colleagues dodging him in the halls, and the one he corners can only claim she was already ignoring him.

title: President's Brutally Honest Q&A Session

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You all know our president, Mister Goodenrich. He's here to answer any questions you have.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Why aren't there any women or minorities in senior management positions?

transcript.speaker: Mister Goodenrich
transcript.text: We think women are for making babies. As for minorities, we fear them.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: How can you justify your ten million dollar salary when profits are down?

transcript.speaker: Mister Goodenrich
transcript.text: Ha ha! The board of directors are friends of mine and it's not their money they're spending.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why does the company keep talking about employee training while at the same time slashing the training budget?

transcript.speaker: Mister Goodenrich
transcript.text: We think you're too dumb to train. We'll hire people from the outside if we need talent.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I must say, your honesty is kind of refreshing.

transcript.speaker: Mister Goodenrich
transcript.text: And you're all fired for asking questions.

setting: Conference room during a company meeting with the president
situation: The Boss introduces the company president, who has come to answer any questions from employees. Alice, Wally and Dilbert each ask a pointed question about diversity in management, executive pay and the training budget, and the president answers with shockingly candid, insulting honesty. He finishes by firing everyone for asking questions.
punchline: The president's refreshingly honest answers reveal management's real attitudes, and the reward for asking tough questions is being fired.
summary: A company president invited to take employee questions gives brutally truthful answers about discrimination, pay and training, then dismisses everyone for daring to ask.

title: Boring Date Gets Her Knife Taken

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...So I knew it was either a layer three protocol error or else it was time to recalibrate the scope.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ha ha! I'll avoid the obvious pun about D-channel packet addressing!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't think she's done with her knife.

transcript.speaker: Waiter
transcript.text: I know. I lost three engineers this way.

setting: A restaurant table during a dinner date
situation: Dilbert is on a date and drones on about network protocol errors and recalibrating a scope, then laughs at his own joke about D-channel packet addressing. His date sits stone-faced and grows increasingly agitated, until in the last panel she lunges with her knife and a waiter restrains her.
punchline: Dilbert's relentless engineering talk is so unbearable that his date tries to stab him, and the waiter calmly says it has happened before with other engineers.
summary: A man bores his dinner companion into a murderous rage with shop talk, and the waiter shrugs it off as routine for engineer customers.

title: Crying Over Restaurant Prices Backfires

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: I like a man who isn't afraid to cry.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Waah! Waah! The prices here are so high! Waah! Waah!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's not working. She tricked me.

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: I'll just have water, I think.

setting: A restaurant table on a dinner date
situation: On a date, Dilbert's companion says she likes a man who isn't afraid to cry. Dilbert takes this as a cue and loudly sobs about the high menu prices, hoping to get her to order cheaply. She ends up ordering only water, but Dilbert realizes the ploy has not paid off and that she tricked him.
punchline: Dilbert hopes to exploit her stated preference for sensitive men by crying about prices so she orders cheaply, but her frugal choice of water shows his emotional display was used against him, or at least did not pay off.
summary: A man tries to turn a date's praise for emotional openness into a way to cut the dinner bill, only to feel he has been played.

title: Task Force Volunteers Seeking Resume Padding

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Thank you all for volunteering for my task force on "Palmtop Personal Multimedia."

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm sure that you all have a common vision about this project...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Specifically, you think it will look good on your resumes while being too futuristic to generate any real work.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Mother lode.

setting: Office conference room
situation: Dogbert, leading a task force on a futuristic palmtop multimedia project, thanks the assembled volunteers. He then reveals he knows their true motive: they signed up because the project will look impressive on a resume but is too far ahead of its time to require any actual work. Wally privately thinks he has struck a mother lode.
punchline: The volunteers aren't motivated by the project's merits but by the chance to pad their resumes with a trendy initiative that will never demand real effort, and Wally's thought bubble confirms Dogbert's cynical read.
summary: A task force leader exposes his volunteers as résumé-padders drawn to a project too futuristic to produce any actual labor.

title: Dogbert Holds Santa Hostage

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Here's a list of my Christmas demands.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Follow the instructions and nobody gets hurt.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're bluffing. You wouldn't hurt my plastic window Santa.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: One yank and he's off life support!

setting: Dilbert's living room at Christmastime
situation: Dogbert sits on the couch and hands Dilbert a list of Christmas demands, threatening that nobody gets hurt if the instructions are followed. Dilbert dismisses it as a bluff, since Dogbert wouldn't harm his plastic window Santa. Dogbert reveals he is holding the Santa's power cord and threatens to yank it.
punchline: Dogbert treats an inflatable Santa decoration like a hostage on life support, threatening to unplug it to extort Christmas demands.
summary: A scheming dog stages a ransom-style holdup using a holiday lawn ornament's power cord as his leverage.

title: Dogbert Uses Dilbert as Lightning Rod

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I was thinking about how much I enjoy our conversations.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: They're consistently witty and intellectually stimulating.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Then I realized that all of the witty and intellectually stimulating stuff comes from me.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Naturally I started wondering what was the point of even having you along.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Then I thought about lightning and how it always hits the tallest object.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: So there is a slight statistical advantage to having you nearby.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Crack!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You aren't going to be witty now, are you?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How can you say that? I'm shocked!

setting: Outdoor walking path in a park or countryside
situation: Dogbert walks beside Dilbert, first flattering their conversations, then admitting the wit all comes from himself and questioning why he keeps Dilbert around. He concludes that Dilbert is useful because lightning strikes the tallest object, and Dilbert is promptly struck by lightning.
punchline: Dogbert's reasoning that Dilbert is a handy lightning rod comes true instantly, and Dilbert's dazed pun about being 'shocked' is the witty remark Dogbert goaded him into.
summary: A scheming dog explains that his companion's main value is as the tallest target nearby, and a bolt from the sky proves him right.

title: Dogbert's Net Worth Taunts Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Does it bother you that I won fifty million dollars in my lawsuit, whereas you still toil to remain middle class?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Does it bother you to know that I could buy you and sell you... how many times?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: 834 times.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Hey, it's gone up since lunch!

setting: Dilbert's cubicle
situation: Dogbert, sitting at Dilbert's desk, gloats about winning a fifty million dollar lawsuit while Dilbert works at his computer. He asks how many times he could buy and sell Dilbert, and a woman with a calculator supplies the exact figure. Dogbert is delighted that the number has risen since lunch.
punchline: Dogbert treats Dilbert's value as a fluctuating asset price, cheerfully noting that Dilbert's worth has increased since lunch, which is both an insult and a joke about financial quotes.
summary: A wealthy Dogbert taunts Dilbert with a calculated figure for how often he could purchase him, then celebrates a mid-day price rise.

title: Secret Project Gets Gun Drawn

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hi, Tim. What are you working on these days?

transcript.speaker: Tim
transcript.text: A secret project.

transcript.speaker: Tim
transcript.text: Very, very secret. Confidential and proprietary. Real hush-hush.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It sounds important.

transcript.speaker: Tim
transcript.text: Just move along.

setting: Office hallway
situation: Dilbert, holding a coffee mug, casually asks coworker Tim what he is working on. Tim insists it is a very secret, confidential and proprietary project. When Dilbert remarks that it sounds important, Tim pulls out a revolver and tells him to move along.
punchline: Tim's over-the-top secrecy about his project escalates into threatening a curious coworker with a gun, satirizing corporate paranoia about confidentiality.
summary: A coworker's fanatical secrecy about his project ends with him brandishing a pistol at a friendly colleague who simply showed interest.

title: Bob the Dinosaur's Christmas Wedgie Income

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Remember, Bob, it is better to give to Dogbert than to receive... especially at Christmas.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: But I don't have any income... except for the coins people drop when I give them wedgies.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: It seems like exactly the wrong season to pick up the pace on this sort of thing.

setting: Outdoors in a city, with Dogbert sitting on a ledge
situation: Dogbert lectures Bob the dinosaur about giving money to Dogbert at Christmas. Bob replies that his only income is the coins that fall out of people's pockets when he gives them wedgies. In the last panel Bob hoists a startled man by his underwear, thinking that the holiday season is a poor time to step up his wedgie business.
punchline: Bob has been shaking down strangers with wedgies for pocket change, and he realizes too late that stepping up this activity at Christmas is a bad idea, while Dogbert's request for donations is the real scam.
summary: A dim-witted dinosaur explains that his only earnings come from the loose change that falls out of wedgie victims, and wonders whether the holidays are the right time to expand.

title: Dogbert's Shoplifting Christmas Wish List

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Here's my list of Christmas demands, Ratbert.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Since you have no money I included items which can be easily shoplifted.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Thanks.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Or you can check the box where it says you agree to be my personal valet for life.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I need to shoplift a pencil first.

setting: Plain pink background, no specific location
situation: Dogbert hands Ratbert a list of Christmas demands, claiming to be considerate by including items that are easy to shoplift since Ratbert is broke. He then offers an alternative: Ratbert can sign on as his personal valet for life. Ratbert, handed a list he must tick, realizes he has nothing to write with and says he must steal a pencil first.
punchline: Ratbert is so powerless and penniless that even signing the contract that enslaves him requires committing a petty theft first.
summary: A scheming dog presents a small rodent with a gift list full of stealable items, or a lifetime servitude clause, and the rodent can't even sign without stealing a pencil.

title: Garbage Man Lends Dogbert Phaser

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Dilbert won't build a phaser pistol for me. He thinks it's wrong to zap people for fun.

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: Yeah, that would be wrong... unless the people you zap are themselves immoral, in which case you would be on the side of justice.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I guess it's academic since I don't have a phaser.

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: Here, borrow mine.

setting: Outdoors by a garbage can
situation: Dogbert complains to a garbage man that Dilbert refuses to build him a phaser pistol because zapping people for fun is wrong. The garbage man reasons that it would be justified if the targets are immoral. When Dogbert notes he has no phaser anyway, the garbage man casually pulls one from his belt and offers to lend it.
punchline: The garbage man's tidy moral justification for zapping people turns out to be backed by a phaser he happens to own, so the ethical debate instantly becomes practical.
summary: A sanitation worker talks himself into a moral loophole for vaporizing wrongdoers, then hands Dogbert the weapon to try it.

title: Dilbert Tests Dogbert's Homing Instinct

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Where are we now?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can't tell you. That's part of the experiment.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I read in "Reader's Digest" how a dog found his way home from a hundred miles away. I want to test your homing instinct.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay, I think we're ready to begin...

setting: A car and a remote rural dirt road
situation: Dilbert drives Dogbert to an unknown location, refusing to say where they are because it is part of an experiment. He explains he read about a dog finding its way home from a hundred miles away and wants to test Dogbert's homing instinct. After dropping Dogbert off, Dilbert stands on the roadside with a clipboard while Dogbert's own car drives away in the distance, and announces they are ready to begin.
punchline: Dilbert's experiment is undermined because the car, with Dogbert's ride home, is already driving off, so Dogbert has been abandoned in the middle of nowhere; the 'experiment' is really just a cruel and clueless way of stranding him.
summary: Dilbert dumps his dog in the countryside under the guise of a scientific experiment, clipboard in hand, to see whether he can find his own way back.

title: Dogbert's Absurd Archive of Stupid Remarks

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm building a permanent file of all the stupid things you say.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: At least it's only a few pages long.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: This is just the table of contents.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The full database will be compressed on CD ROMs.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I hired Juan and his crew to design the system and type in the data.

transcript.speaker: Juan
transcript.text: We're working overtime.

transcript.speaker: Juan
transcript.text: The new computer center is done... we had to level the neighbor's garage.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: By any chance, are you still upset that I asked you to fetch my slippers?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Did you get that one?

transcript.speaker: Juan
transcript.text: I'll need to hire more people.

setting: Dilbert's living room
situation: Dogbert tells Dilbert he is compiling a permanent file of Dilbert's stupid statements, and Dilbert is relieved it is short until Dogbert reveals it is only the table of contents. Dogbert hires Juan and his crew to build a computer system and enter the data, and they work so much overtime they level the neighbor's garage for a computer center. Dilbert suspects Dogbert's real motive is revenge over being told to fetch slippers.
punchline: Dogbert's petty grudge over fetching slippers has ballooned into an enormous, absurdly expensive project that needs ever more staff, a perfect satire of runaway projects and overkill technology.
summary: A dog's petty revenge turns into a sprawling data-entry empire complete with a purpose-built computer center and an ever-growing headcount.

title: Employees Rank Ninth, Behind Carbon Paper

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've been saying for years that "employees are our most valuable asset."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It turns out that I was wrong. Money is our most valuable asset. Employees are ninth.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm afraid to ask what came in eighth.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carbon paper.

setting: Conference room during a meeting
situation: The Boss addresses his staff at a meeting table and admits that his long-repeated claim that employees are the company's most valuable asset was wrong. He announces that money is the top asset and employees rank only ninth. When Wally nervously wonders what ranked eighth, the Boss reveals it was carbon paper.
punchline: Management's feel-good slogan about valuing employees is exposed as empty, since staff rank just below obsolete office supplies like carbon paper.
summary: A manager cheerfully admits that his staff are actually ranked ninth in importance, just beneath an outdated office supply.

title: Salesman Insults Engineer, Dilbert Plans Karate

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Stan, you promised the customer things that engineering can't possibly deliver. Do you know what this means?!

transcript.speaker: Stan
transcript.text: It means I'm a great salesman and you're a putrid engineer.

transcript.speaker: Stan
transcript.text: Maybe you should consider taking classes at night.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Karate classes.

setting: Office
situation: Dilbert confronts Stan, a salesman, for promising a customer things engineering can't deliver. Stan cheerfully turns the blame around, calling himself a great salesman and Dilbert a putrid engineer, and suggests Dilbert take night classes. Dilbert, fuming, thinks of karate classes.
punchline: Stan shamelessly blames the engineer for his own impossible promises, and Dilbert's thought bubble reveals he would rather use night classes to learn karate and hit him.
summary: A smug salesman shrugs off an engineer's complaint about impossible promises by insulting him, prompting violent thoughts.

title: Dogbert Insults the Company President

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert meets the company president.

transcript.speaker: Company President
transcript.text: You've made quite a name for yourself in the week you've worked here.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It was easy to grab power, once I realized the other executives were just imbeciles with good hair.

transcript.speaker: Company President
transcript.text: I hope you don't think that of me.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: No, that looks like a toupee from here.

setting: The company president's office
situation: Dogbert, who has risen to power after only a week at the company, sits in a chair facing the company president's desk. The president compliments his rapid rise, and Dogbert explains that the other executives were merely imbeciles with good hair. When the president hopes Dogbert doesn't think that of him, Dogbert replies that the president's hair looks like a toupee.
punchline: Dogbert reassures the president that he isn't an imbecile with good hair, only because his hair is obviously fake, which insults him anyway.
summary: After boasting that his meteoric rise was easy because the executives were fools with nice hair, Dogbert backhandedly spares the president by noting his hairpiece is clearly fake.

title: Sleeping Tubes Instead of Commuting

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I borrowed a Japanese work custom — sleeping tubes!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No more wasted time commuting. If you keel over from exhaustion we'll just cram you into a sleep tube.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Which tube is mine?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You don't get a personal tube unless you're Employee of the Week.

setting: Office wall lined with round sleeping tubes
situation: The Boss shows Dilbert a wall of sleeping tubes he has borrowed from Japanese work culture, where exhausted employees can be stuffed in to sleep at the office instead of commuting home. Dilbert asks which tube is his, and the Boss says only the Employee of the Week gets a personal tube.
punchline: Employees are expected to work until they collapse, and even the dismal reward of a personal sleeping tube is handed out like an employee-recognition perk.
summary: Management adopts a foreign practice of in-office sleeping pods to squeeze out more work hours and makes a private pod the prize for top performers.

title: Loud Dogbert Demands Promotion Immediately

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm a loud dog! Give me a job! You must obey me because I'm loud!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay okay.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That was too easy. There must be something wrong with the job. It must be an entry level job...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I want a raise!! Promote me, you imbecile!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Bad trend.

setting: The Boss's office
situation: Dogbert hops onto a chair and shouts at the Boss, demanding a job simply because he is loud, and the Boss immediately gives in. Dogbert then suspects the job must be entry level because it was so easy to get. He jumps onto the desk and loudly demands a raise and a promotion, while the Boss worries about the pattern.
punchline: The Boss caves to anyone who is loud enough, so Dogbert escalates from a job to a promotion in minutes, and the Boss sees the problem only after it is too late.
summary: A noisy dog bullies his way into employment and then straight into demanding advancement from a pushover manager.

title: Dogbert Kicks Ratbert Into Space Hole

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Dogbert! Ratbert! Come quickly, I found a hole in the fabric of space!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We must look inside, but it's too incredibly dangerous.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Thanks.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: No problem.

setting: Dilbert's home living room
situation: Dilbert calls Dogbert and Ratbert, who are watching TV, to see a hole he has found in the fabric of space. He says someone must look inside but it is too dangerous to do himself. Dogbert obligingly kicks Ratbert into the hole.
punchline: Dilbert implies he wants someone expendable to explore the dangerous hole, and Dogbert instantly sacrifices Ratbert, the lowest-status member of the group.
summary: A man wanting a risky job done by someone else gets exactly that when his dog boots the smallest pet into a cosmic rift.

title: Thank Goodness for C Priorities

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There... I've organized all of my tasks into "A," "B" and "C" priorities.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The "A" priorities aren't even worth doing. And the "B" priority stuff would probably get me in trouble.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Are you done with the stapler oil?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Thank goodness for "C" priorities.

setting: Office cubicle
situation: Dilbert sorts his task list into A, B and C priorities and privately concludes the A items are pointless and the B items are risky. His boss then asks whether he has finished the stapler oil, while Wally, oiling a stapler at his desk, is grateful that trivial C priorities exist.
punchline: The only work that is safe and doable is the trivial C-priority busywork, like oiling staplers, because the important tasks are either pointless or dangerous.
summary: After ranking his to-do list, an engineer realizes only the least important chores are safe to do, and a coworker happily proves it by lubricating a stapler.

title: Leftover Project Acronyms: Phlegm and Placenta

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: As you know, all projects are assigned acronyms. Unfortunately, all the good ones have been used.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Any new project will have to use an acronym from this short list of somewhat less desirable choices.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What should I call my new project?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well, you could use "PHLEGM" or "PLACENTA."

setting: Conference room during a meeting
situation: The Boss tells his team at a conference table that every project must be given an acronym, but all the good ones are already taken. He reads from a short list of leftovers, and when Dilbert asks what to name his new project, the Boss suggests the unappealing options "Phlegm" or "Placenta."
punchline: The only acronyms left for Dilbert's project are revolting bodily terms, mocking the bureaucratic obsession with project naming conventions.
summary: Management forces a new project to pick a name from a list of gross, unwanted acronyms because the decent ones have run out.

title: Dilbert Retracts His Disapproval, Carries Dogbert Sign

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: May I have a word with you?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I understand that you hijacked a satellite signal and hypnotized everybody to carry your picture and chant your name. That is not amusing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: In retrospect, I shouldn't have said "That is not amusing."

setting: Dilbert's office, at Dogbert's desk
situation: Dilbert approaches Dogbert, who is seated at a desk, and says he has heard Dogbert hypnotized everyone via a hijacked satellite signal to carry his picture and chant his name. While criticizing this, Dilbert is himself carrying a Dogbert sign, showing he has been hypnotized too. By the last panel he retracts his disapproval, and Ratbert is also seen with a Dogbert sign.
punchline: Dilbert is clearly under Dogbert's hypnosis, since he is carrying the sign himself, and he quickly backpedals on his criticism out of fear or brainwashed loyalty.
summary: A sign-carrying Dilbert confronts Dogbert about a mass-hypnosis scheme, then hastily takes back his complaint.

title: Creativity Seminar Ends in Donuts

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: As your consultant I will unleash the creativity that the company has suppressed.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: We'll begin with word association. I'll say a word then you each say what pops into your head.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Chair.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Donut?

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I say donut too.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Donut

transcript.speaker: Woman with curly hair
transcript.text: I was going to say donut.

setting: Conference room during a consultant's creativity seminar
situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, promises to unleash the company's suppressed creativity and begins a word association exercise. He says 'chair' and the assembled employees, led by the boss, all respond with the same word, 'donut', each one echoing the previous answer.
punchline: Despite being asked for whatever pops into their heads, the employees all give the identical answer, showing that the company's conformity has completely crushed any original thought.
summary: A consultant's brainstorming exercise reveals that every employee in the room can only come up with the same answer as the person before them.

title: Engineer Makes Change Needlessly Complicated

transcript.speaker: Cashier
transcript.text: That's $1.89

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Just for simplicity, I'll give you $7.14

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: As an engineer, I feel a professional responsibility to make things easy for people.

transcript.speaker: Cashier
transcript.text: ...Carry the three.

setting: A shop counter at a cash register
situation: Dilbert is paying a cashier whose total is $1.89. He hands over $7.14 and claims he is doing it for simplicity. The cashier struggles through the arithmetic in his head, muttering about carrying the three, while Dilbert insists he is just being helpful as an engineer.
punchline: Dilbert's supposedly simplifying payment is bizarrely awkward and makes the cashier's job harder, mocking engineers who think they are making things easy when they are actually making them more complicated.
summary: A customer hands over an oddly specific amount of cash, claiming to simplify the transaction, while the confused clerk is left doing difficult mental math.

title: Dogbert Recruits Dinosaur for World Conquest

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Bob, I need your help in my quest to conquer Earth.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: What do I do?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll use my powers of hypnosis to control everybody who sees me on television. You must whack everybody else with your mighty tail.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Did I ever mention that I have sensitive skin?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Start with accountants. They're soft and you can build calluses.

setting: A plain room with a blue wall and tan floor
situation: Dogbert asks his large green dinosaur friend Bob to help him conquer the Earth. Dogbert will hypnotize everyone who sees him on television, while Bob is assigned to whack everyone else with his tail. Bob admits he has sensitive skin, so Dogbert suggests he start with accountants.
punchline: Dogbert cheerfully treats accountants as soft, expendable targets for Bob to practice on, a callous solution to Bob's sensitive skin problem.
summary: A small dog plots world domination with a hulking dinosaur accomplice and picks a convenient group of victims for the dinosaur to practice his tail-whacking on.

title: Dilbert's Honest Career Day Talk

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dilbert talks to a class about career options.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Engineering is one of the best careers available.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: For the next twenty years I'll sit in a big box called a cubicle. It's like a restroom stall but with lower walls.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I spend most of my time hoping the electromagnetic fields from my office equipment aren't killing me.

setting: A school classroom during a career talk
situation: Dilbert addresses a class of students about career options and starts with a positive claim about engineering. He then describes his actual working life, comparing a cubicle to a restroom stall and admitting he worries about radiation from his equipment. The students react with growing alarm.
punchline: Dilbert's supposedly promising career pitch turns into a bleak confession about cramped cubicles and health fears, horrifying the students.
summary: A career day speaker opens with praise for engineering but quickly reveals the grim reality of cubicle life and possible radiation exposure.

title: Ratbert Questions His Family Status

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I was wondering if we're a dysfunctional family.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're not a family member. You're a rat who won't go away.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Suddenly I have the urge to rob a convenience store.

setting: Dilbert's living room
situation: Dilbert sits in an armchair reading the newspaper while Dogbert and Ratbert sit nearby. Ratbert wonders aloud whether they are a dysfunctional family, and Dilbert coldly replies that Ratbert is not family at all, just a rat who refuses to leave. Hurt by the rejection, Ratbert says he now feels like committing a crime.
punchline: Dilbert's cruel dismissal of Ratbert as a mere pest ironically proves the family is dysfunctional, and Ratbert reacts by wanting to turn to crime.
summary: A small pet's innocent question about family dysfunction gets a harsh rebuke that pushes him toward a life of robbery.

title: Bob the Dinosaur Behind the Couch

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Noriko, I'd like you to meet Bob the Dinosaur.

transcript.speaker: Noriko
transcript.text: Hi.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Hi.

transcript.speaker: Noriko
transcript.text: I thought dinosaurs were all extinct.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: No, they were just hiding. We found Bob behind the couch.

transcript.speaker: Noriko
transcript.text: I wish we had one at our house.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Look in your credenza. The Belmonts live in the "Krazy Glue" drawer.

setting: A room with a door and orange walls, likely Dogbert's home
situation: Dogbert introduces a young girl named Noriko to Bob, a green dinosaur wearing sneakers. Dogbert explains that dinosaurs were never extinct, just hiding, and that Bob was found behind the couch. Noriko wishes she had one at home, and Bob replies with a nonsensical tip about where to find the Belmonts in her credenza.
punchline: Bob's deadpan reply implies that dinosaurs, like lost items, can be found hiding in furniture, with the absurd detail of the Belmonts living in the 'Krazy Glue' drawer.
summary: A girl learns that dinosaurs survived by hiding in household furniture and is given an absurd tip about where to find more of them.

title: Ratbert's Three Hundred Thousand Year Wait

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm going to pull Ratbert out of the hole in space before anything bad happens.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: ...Although only a minute passed in this dimension, I've been floating in the other dimension for three hundred thousand years.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wow! It's lucky I didn't reach in there with my watch hand!

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Yes I was bored!!! Thanks for asking!!

setting: Dilbert's home, with a hole in space opening in a wall
situation: Dilbert announces he will rescue Ratbert from a hole in space before anything bad happens. Ratbert emerges and explains that although only a minute passed here, he floated in the other dimension for three hundred thousand years. Dilbert responds only by noting how lucky it is that he did not reach in with his watch hand, ignoring Ratbert's ordeal.
punchline: Dilbert is only concerned about the risk to his own watch, completely ignoring that Ratbert suffered 300,000 years of boredom, and Ratbert sarcastically answers the question nobody asked.
summary: After being fished out of a dimensional rift following an eternity of isolation, a rodent is met with selfish concern about a wristwatch rather than sympathy.

title: Manager Attrition Is Not Fast-Track

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ted, you're part of the company "right sizing" program, effective today.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Thank you! It's nice to get positive feedback from the boss!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's not feedback. I'm saying your position has been "management adjusted."

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Sounds great! Is there a raise involved?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Listen to me!! You're part of "manager attrition" starting right now!

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Wow! Is that the fast-track program for managers?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I heard that Ted got picked for the "manager attrition" program.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why not us?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So unless you put us on the "manager attrition" program too, we quit!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: There's never a flamethrower handy when you need it.

setting: Office cubicle and the boss's office
situation: The Boss tells Ted he is being cut under euphemistic programs like "right sizing" and "manager attrition," but the cheerfully oblivious Ted keeps interpreting each euphemism as good news, a compliment, a raise or a fast track. Dilbert and Wally hear that Ted got picked and, assuming it is a perk, demand to be included or they will quit. The frustrated Boss wishes he had a flamethrower.
punchline: Ted and his coworkers are so fooled by corporate euphemisms for layoffs that they beg to be fired, leaving the Boss wishing for a flamethrower.
summary: A manager's layoff gets dressed up in so much corporate jargon that the victim and his coworkers mistake it for a prize and demand to join him.

title: Jury Awards Dogbert Fifty Million Dollars

transcript.speaker: Juror
transcript.text: The jury has reached a decision in the case of "Dogbert vs. a big corporation."

transcript.speaker: Juror
transcript.text: We award Dogbert fifty million dollars because we hate big companies and we like little dogs with glasses.

transcript.speaker: Judge
transcript.text: I hate my life.

transcript.speaker: Juror
transcript.text: And we award a Maytag dryer to juror Mindy for being "best dressed."

setting: A courtroom, in the jury box and at the judge's bench
situation: A juror stands in the jury box and reads out the verdict in Dogbert's lawsuit against a big corporation. The jury awards Dogbert fifty million dollars purely out of dislike for big companies and fondness for little dogs with glasses. The judge puts his head in his hand in despair as the jury also hands a dryer to a fellow juror for being best dressed.
punchline: The jury decides a huge case on whim and prejudice rather than evidence, even handing out a prize for fashion, which leaves the judge despairing at how arbitrary the justice system is.
summary: A frivolous jury hands a giant payout to a small dog out of pure bias and then gives a household appliance to a well-dressed colleague, to the judge's dismay.

title: Dogbert, Romance Interpreter for Hire

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Here's my new business card. I'm a romance interpreter.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: For a small fee I'll accompany you on dates and translate between male and female language.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Blah blah blah

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: She's telling a pointless story about work. By annoying you in this way she hopes to form a closer bond.

setting: Dilbert's living room, then a restaurant table on a date
situation: Dogbert shows Dilbert his new business card advertising his services as a romance interpreter who will translate between male and female language on dates. In the last panel Dogbert sits at the restaurant table with Dilbert and his date, whispering a translation of her chatter about work.
punchline: Dogbert's 'translation' offers no real insight; it simply confirms that the date's story is pointless and annoying, while claiming the annoyance is meant to bring the couple closer.
