summary: Dogbert launches a paid service interpreting dating talk between the sexes and demonstrates it by decoding a woman's tedious work anecdote for Dilbert.

title: Dogbert Distrusts Context-Free News Reports

transcript.speaker: TV News
transcript.text: The budget for education was cut ten million dollars.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Is that a big percentage? Does it make any difference?

transcript.speaker: TV News Anchor
transcript.text: Congress considered a music safety law after studies showed a ten percent increase in piano-related deaths.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: How does that compare to other health risks? Should I be concerned?

transcript.speaker: TV News
transcript.text: Lawmakers debated a bill to lower capital gains tax rates...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: What do most economists think? Would it stimulate the economy much? Should I care?

transcript.speaker: TV News
transcript.text: A new poll shows that many voters have strong opinions on these issues despite the fact that we provide no useful contextual data.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I've got to stop watching scary shows right before bedtime.

setting: Dogbert's living room, watching television
situation: Dogbert sits on his chair watching a news broadcast. Each story gives a bare statistic or headline with no context, and Dogbert wonders in thought bubbles whether the numbers matter. The final report admits voters form strong opinions without useful data, and Dogbert walks off to bed unsettled.
punchline: Dogbert treats the news as a scary show because it offers alarming facts without any context to judge them, mocking how the media leaves viewers anxious and uninformed.
summary: A dog watching the evening news gets frightened by statistics that are never explained or compared to anything.

title: Dogbert Guilt-Trips Dilbert Into Shopping

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Several shopping hours left, and you just sit there.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Did you really buy enough gifts for Dogbert? You worry. Guilt and doubt begin to gnaw at your gut... the pain... the pain...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I thought it was the thought that counts.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Don't believe the hype.

setting: Dilbert's living room on Christmas Eve
situation: Dilbert relaxes in an armchair reading the newspaper on December 24th while Dogbert lounges nearby. Dogbert deliberately plants guilt and doubt in Dilbert's mind about whether he bought enough gifts for Dogbert. When Dilbert puts on his jacket and says it's the thought that counts, Dogbert dismisses the saying.
punchline: Dogbert manipulates Dilbert into last-minute shopping for his own benefit and rejects the 'it's the thought that counts' adage, revealing he expects actual, plentiful presents.
summary: On Christmas Eve, a scheming dog needles his owner into rushing out to buy more presents for him.

title: Bob's Wedgie-Based Planet Saving

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Take Bob with you, Noriko. You'll need help saving the planet for your generation.

transcript.speaker: Noriko
transcript.text: I have a black belt in karate. What skills do you bring to the party?

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Wedgies, mostly.

transcript.speaker: Noriko
transcript.text: It's not as menacing as karate, but you have to love the expressions on their faces.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Turn him this way.

characters: Man in white shirt and tie
setting: Outdoors on a sidewalk, after a scene beside a wall
situation: Dogbert tells young Noriko to bring Bob the dinosaur along as help in saving the planet. When she asks what skills he has, Bob admits his specialty is giving wedgies. Later, Bob is carrying a man by his underwear over his shoulder while Noriko is satisfied with the result.
punchline: Bob's sole skill is giving wedgies, which Noriko ends up appreciating because of the victims' funny expressions, turning planet-saving into schoolyard bullying.
summary: A girl with a karate black belt reluctantly teams up with a green dinosaur whose only talent turns out to be hanging people by their underwear.

title: Paid Not To Work

transcript.speaker: Finance Employee
transcript.text: I found a typo in the budget spreadsheet... it's too late to fix it.

transcript.speaker: Finance Employee
transcript.text: We transferred one job to another group but accidentally kept the money and headcount.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: ...so, we still pay you but you aren't allowed to do work.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: This is the happiest day of my life.

setting: The Boss's office and an employee's cubicle
situation: A finance employee holding a paper tells the seated boss that a budget spreadsheet typo is too late to fix. A job was transferred to another group, but the money and headcount were mistakenly left behind. The boss then informs an employee that he will still be paid but is not allowed to do any work, and the employee thinks it is the happiest day of his life.
punchline: A budget error accidentally creates the dream job of being paid to do nothing, and the employee is delighted instead of upset.
summary: Thanks to a spreadsheet blunder, a worker is told he'll keep collecting a salary while being forbidden from working, and he couldn't be happier.

title: The Boss Wants Whales Extinct

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sometimes I wonder, how would MY life be different if all whales were extinct?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's not like they do anything for us. You never hear of seeing-eye whales. They can't fetch the paper or drag you out of a burning building...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't you think the world has too many fat, worthless, mammals?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I was just thinking that, sir.

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle
situation: The Boss stands over Dilbert's desk and muses about whether the world would be better off without whales, arguing they do nothing useful for humans. He then asks Dilbert if the world has too many fat, worthless mammals. Dilbert, who is typing at his computer, replies that he was just thinking the same thing.
punchline: Dilbert's deadpan agreement implies he is thinking of the Boss himself as the fat, worthless mammal, while the Boss remains oblivious.
summary: A rambling boss questions the usefulness of whales and asks his employee about worthless mammals, getting an answer with a double meaning.

title: Adult Explains Generational Plunder, Gets Wedgie

transcript.speaker: Girl
transcript.text: Stop right there, Mister Adult! You've got some explaining to do to my generation!

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: It's quite simple, really. Children have no political power. So we adults can plunder the planet, run up huge debts, then die fat and happy!

transcript.speaker: Girl
transcript.text: I've never seen anybody lifted by his briefs and spun in the air like that.

transcript.speaker: Green dinosaur
transcript.text: That's my "Twirling Wedgie."

setting: Outdoor sidewalk beside a grassy hedge
situation: A little girl stops a businessman walking by and demands that he explain himself to her generation. He cheerfully admits that adults exploit the planet and run up debts because children cannot vote. A green dinosaur grabs him and lifts him by his briefs, spinning him in the air.
punchline: The man's smug admission that children are powerless is punished by a dinosaur ally giving him a spinning wedgie, showing the kids do have power after all.
summary: A child confronts a complacent adult about the mess his generation is leaving behind, and her dinosaur friend answers his smugness with a physical comeuppance.

title: Dogbert Exploits Employees Turned Rags

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll be representing you corporate employees in a class action suit. Your company has sucked the life force out of you and turned you into little rags.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: My fee will be on a contingency basis. That means I get the entire settlement plus I'll use you to wax my BMW.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I've found the perfect clients.

transcript.speaker: Employee rag
transcript.text: Sounds fair.

transcript.speaker: Employee rag
transcript.text: Don't make waves.

setting: Corporate workplace, with a field of limp rag-like employees
situation: Dogbert, acting as a lawyer, announces he will represent drained corporate employees in a class action suit against their company. The employees have been reduced to little rags on the floor. He proposes a fee of the entire settlement plus using them to wax his BMW, and they meekly accept.
punchline: The employees are so beaten down by their company that they agree to a terrible deal from their own lawyer, which makes them ideal clients for Dogbert to exploit.
summary: A scheming dog-lawyer offers to sue on behalf of workers so crushed they have become rags, then happily fleeces them because they are too timid to object.

title: Dogbert Becomes Center of Universe

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I've decided to be the center of the universe.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: All of the things in the universe can now be described in terms of their relationship to me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't understand why you're doing this.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That's because your brain is only a half-Dogbert.

setting: Outdoors on a walking path and rocky hillside
situation: Dogbert walks alongside Dilbert and announces he has appointed himself the center of the universe, declaring that everything can now be measured by its relationship to him. Later they sit on rocks, and Dilbert says he doesn't understand the point of this. Dogbert replies that Dilbert's brain is only half the size of his own.
punchline: Dogbert explains Dilbert's confusion by turning his own self-importance into a unit of measurement, calling Dilbert's brain a 'half-Dogbert', which insults Dilbert while proving his self-centered point.
summary: A smug dog declares himself the hub of reality and dismisses his owner's bewilderment by using himself as the yardstick for intelligence.

title: Ratbert Evolving Into Flying Rat

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I think I'm evolving into a flying rat.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I noticed that my arms are flatter than my parents' arms. In a million years this natural advantage will become wings!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: There goes the happiest rat I know.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Too soon.

setting: Dogbert's living room, with Dogbert sitting on a maroon ottoman
situation: Ratbert excitedly tells Dogbert that he believes he is evolving into a flying rat because his arms are flatter than his parents' arms. He proudly spreads his arms and predicts they will become wings in a million years. As he walks away, Dogbert remarks on his happiness, and Ratbert, with arms flapping and tongue out, thinks it is too soon.
punchline: Ratbert's evolutionary 'wings' will take a million years to develop, so his flapping and excitement right now are premature and pointless, as he himself admits in his thought bubble.
summary: A cheerful rat convinces himself that his slightly flatter arms are the first step toward wings, then realizes he is celebrating a million years too early.

title: Ratbert's Impatient Reader Short Story

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I'm writing a short story for people who don't have much patience.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: "Blah, blah, blah. Whatever, blah, blah, etcetera, etcetera."

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: If it's a commercial success, the sequel practically writes itself.

setting: Dogbert's lounging spot on a cushion, at home
situation: Ratbert tells Dogbert, who is reclining on a purple cushion, that he is writing a short story for impatient readers. He reads aloud from his notepad, and the entire story is just filler words like 'blah, blah, blah' and 'etcetera'. He then notes that a sequel would be effortless to write if the story sells.
punchline: The 'story' is nothing but meaningless filler, so any sequel would be identical and need no effort, poking fun at lazy, formulaic content cashing in on success.
summary: A small orange rat reads his ultra-brief story to a lounging dog, then points out that follow-up work would cost him nothing.

title: Refunding Salary for Underperforming Potential

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I didn't work up to my full potential today.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Naturally, I'll be refunding a portion of my salary to the company.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Uh... we don't really have a process for that.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What? That's almost like saying it's okay to work below my potential.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hey guys! You were right! The pay's the same whether you try or not!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That's great! I didn't do squat today!

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: I played "Tetris."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Thanks for the clarification.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's a big time-saver.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Hey, I actually got paid for that!

setting: Boss's office and office hallway
situation: Dilbert tells the Boss he underperformed and offers to refund part of his salary, but the Boss admits there is no process for that. Dilbert then realizes pay is the same regardless of effort and tells his coworkers, who gleefully confirm they do nothing all day. The Boss, watching the whole thing, is pleased with himself.
punchline: The Boss's offhand 'no process for that' confirms that effort has no bearing on pay, and he is oblivious that his own words just wrecked the workforce's productivity, while he gloats about being paid for it.
summary: After a worker offers to repay wages for a lazy day, the boss's reply teaches everyone that slacking costs nothing.

title: Clerk Pretends To Be Mannequin

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Some people might be fooled by your pretending to be a store mannequin.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But I saw you hide your name tag. I know you're a retail clerk who is trying to avoid helping me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hey! You're moving toward the "Employees Only" door. Stop it! You won't get away with this!!

transcript.speaker: Retail Clerk
transcript.text: Ten more feet.

setting: Clothing store with sale racks
situation: Dilbert accuses a store clerk of pretending to be a mannequin to avoid helping him, pointing out that he saw the clerk hide his name tag. As Dilbert complains, the frozen clerk quietly shuffles toward the "Employees Only" door, thinking he only needs ten more feet to escape.
punchline: The clerk stays in mannequin pose and slowly inches toward escape, determined to avoid customer service even while being openly caught.
summary: A shopper calls out a salesman who is posing as a dummy to dodge him, but the stiff employee keeps edging toward the staff-only exit.

title: Employees Drained Into Car Wash Rags

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm from the law firm of Dogbert, Dogbert and Dogbert. I'm suing you for draining the life force out of your employees.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: After being drained of life, employees are forced to leave the company. The lucky ones get jobs as rags for a car wash, like Joey Pishkin here.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Honk honk.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: What Joey? That's Marge from accounting???

setting: The Boss's office
situation: Dogbert, posing as a lawyer, arrives at the Boss's office to sue him for draining the life force from his employees. He claims drained employees are fired and the lucky ones become car wash rags, holding up a limp rag he calls Joey Pishkin. When the Boss blows his nose into the rag, Dogbert protests that it is actually Marge from accounting.
punchline: The Boss blows his nose into a rag that was once a human employee, proving Dogbert's accusation of treating workers as disposable objects.
summary: A lawyer-dog sues a manager for sucking the life from his staff, then catches him using a former employee as a tissue.

title: Promoted for Being Socially Inept

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Peter, you're a brilliant computer programmer and you like your job.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Although you lack any social awareness and cannot communicate with your species, I decided to promote you to management.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't be afraid... it's called a necktie.

setting: Peter's office cubicle with a computer on his desk
situation: The Boss tells Peter, a brilliant and contented programmer who is socially awkward, that he is being promoted to management. Peter cowers and clings to his chair in terror, and the Boss holds out a necktie as if it were what frightens him.
punchline: The Boss promotes a talented, happy programmer into management despite his lack of people skills, and Peter's horror at the promotion is mistaken for fear of a necktie.
summary: A boss rewards a gifted and happy programmer with a management post he clearly doesn't want, and misreads his panic as fear of formal wear.

title: Team Player Blackmail Backfires on Boss

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Your entire staff volunteered to work on my task force. Now I want them and their budgets transferred to me.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why would I agree to that?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: If you don't, I'll tell everybody you're not a team player... Sign here.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So... now I'm on the team, right?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Yeah... the losing team... by yourself.

setting: The Boss's office
situation: Dogbert, acting as a power-hungry task force leader, demands that the Boss hand over his entire staff and their budgets. When the Boss resists, Dogbert threatens to spread word that he isn't a team player, and the Boss signs the transfer paper. He then hopefully asks if he's now on the team, only to be told he's on the losing side, alone.
punchline: The Boss gives up everything to avoid being labeled not a team player, and ends up with no staff, no budget, and no place on the team.
summary: A scheming Dogbert strips the Boss of his people and money by threatening his reputation, then leaves him stranded with nothing.

title: Blame Consultant Exposes Employee Motivation

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert is hired as a blame consultant.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The company's woes are YOUR fault, not senior management's!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Do you realize how much YOU could gain personally by making the company a success?

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I would get a nice plaque in a plastic frame.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Yeah... I was hoping you didn't know.

setting: Office, across a desk from a bald employee with glasses
situation: Dogbert, hired as a blame consultant, tells a bald employee that the company's problems are his fault rather than senior management's. He then suggests the employee could gain personally from making the company succeed. The employee correctly points out that his reward would only be a cheap plaque, and Dogbert admits he hoped the man wouldn't realize that.
punchline: Dogbert's motivational pitch relies on the employee not noticing that the only reward for success is a worthless plaque in a plastic frame.
summary: A consultant hired to assign fault tries to motivate a worker with promised personal gain, only to hope the man never figures out how meagre the payoff is.

title: Ratbert Plans to Pickle Humanity

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I'd miss you if the human race died from pollution but rats lived on.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: So I'm dedicating my life to learning the science of preserving humankind.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Conservation?

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Pickling.

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle
situation: Dilbert sits at his computer while Ratbert, standing on the floor beside his desk, says he would miss humans if pollution wiped them out. Ratbert announces he will devote his life to the science of preserving humankind. Dilbert assumes he means conservation, but Ratbert reveals he intends to pickle people.
punchline: Ratbert's sweet-sounding plan to preserve humanity turns out to mean literally pickling humans like food, not protecting the environment.
summary: A small lab rat vows to save mankind from extinction, but his method of preservation is much less noble than his friend assumes.

title: Special Assignment Is Kiss of Death

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Nervous Ed, I'm assigning you to a special project.

transcript.speaker: Nervous Ed
transcript.text: Special assignment? That means you don't have any real work for me.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Everybody knows that a special assignment is a kiss of death.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You'll be sharing a cubicle with six other employees who are also on special assignment.

transcript.speaker: Nervous Ed
transcript.text: Don't panic yet... maybe it's something important... maybe it's something that could make an impact.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your assignment is to improve employee empowerment.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Thanks for letting us watch.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did you like the part about six in the cubicle?

setting: Office meeting area with a green background
situation: The Boss tells Nervous Ed he has been given a special assignment while Dilbert and Wally look on. Ed knows this usually means there is no real work for him and his fears are confirmed when he learns he must share a cubicle with six others. When the Boss reveals the actual task, Ed faints, and Dilbert and Wally thank the Boss for the show.
punchline: The Boss gives Ed a pointless assignment, improving employee empowerment, and the Boss's cheerful cruelty makes Ed faint, which the coworkers treat as entertainment.
summary: A manager hands a worried employee a dead-end make-work project and relishes the shock while his colleagues enjoy the spectacle.

title: Hijack 3000 Fishing Lure Wink

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm looking for a device that will allow me to take over the satellites of all the major broadcasters.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: It would be illegal to sell something like that. But maybe you'd be interested in an electronic fishing lure instead.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: Wink wink.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: Fish can't resist the "Hijack 3000" lure. And it comes with its own stupid-looking hat!

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: Wink wink.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Clever.

setting: An electronics store
situation: Dogbert walks into an electronics shop and asks the salesman for a device that can take over the satellites of every major broadcaster. The salesman says that would be illegal to sell, then winks and pitches an 'electronic fishing lure' called the Hijack 3000, which comes with a satellite-dish-like hat. Dogbert recognizes the coded sales pitch.
punchline: The salesman thinly disguises an illegal satellite-hijacking device as a fishing lure, using winks and a ridiculous cover story to dodge the law, and Dogbert admiringly acknowledges the transparent ruse.
summary: A shopkeeper dodges the law by dressing up a broadcast-hijacking gadget as fishing tackle, complete with knowing winks.

title: Dogbert's Management Zombie Seminar

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert's seminar on management zombies

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: As a zombie, you must speak in empty generalities.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Your business plan might say "We strive to utilize a variety of techniques to accomplish a broad spectrum of results toward the bottom line."

transcript.speaker: Attendee 1
transcript.text: Hey! My skin is getting clammy and I have the urge to call a meeting!

transcript.speaker: Attendee 2
transcript.text: Me too!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Good... good...

setting: A conference room during Dogbert's seminar
situation: Dogbert teaches a seminar on management zombies and tells attendees that zombies must speak in empty generalities, giving a sample vague business plan statement. As he recites it, the attendees start feeling clammy and get the urge to call a meetings, showing they are turning into management zombies. Dogbert approves of the transformation.
punchline: Spouting empty business jargon literally turns people into management zombies, implying that corporate buzzword-speak and compulsive meeting-calling are signs of the living dead.
summary: A dog lecturing on corporate undead coaches his students in vacuous jargon until they feel an uncontrollable craving to schedule meetings.

title: Dilbert's Career Day Slacker Advice

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dilbert talks to a class about career options.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The goal of every engineer is to retire without getting blamed for a major catastrophe.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Engineers prefer to work as "consultants" on project teams. That way there's no real work, blame is spread across the group,

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: and you can crush any idea from marketing!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...and sometimes you get free donuts just for showing up!

transcript.speaker: Teacher
transcript.text: Get out of my classroom.

setting: School classroom during a career talk
situation: Dilbert gives a class of students a career talk and cynically describes engineering as a way to avoid work and blame. He praises consulting on project teams, where he can squash marketing's ideas and get free donuts. The teacher, appalled, orders him out of her classroom.
punchline: Dilbert's honest, cynical advice about dodging work and blame is so inappropriate for students that the teacher throws him out.
summary: A cynical engineer tells schoolchildren that the ideal career means avoiding blame and real work, until the teacher kicks him out.

title: Dogbert Judges Dilbert's Charity Giving

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I gave five hundred dollars to charity this year.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I believe it's my moral duty to help those less fortunate.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Five hundred dollars? What kind of morality is that?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: People are starving and you still have plenty of money left for your hobbies.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: According to your moral code it's more important for you to have a new computer than for poor people to eat.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Morality? Ha! You spent five hundred bucks to ease your own guilt!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And it worked. I feel pretty good.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How much did you give to charity?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: A thousand. That's why I'm so torqued.

setting: Outdoors on a grassy hillside with a path and rocks
situation: Dilbert mentions he gave five hundred dollars to charity because of his moral duty. Dogbert berates him for not giving more while he still spends on hobbies, until Dilbert points out Dogbert's own hypocrisy and asks how much Dogbert gave. Dogbert reveals he gave a thousand and is irritable about it.
punchline: Dogbert, who lectures others about morality and giving, gave away more than Dilbert and is bitter about it, implying he is motivated by resentment rather than virtue.
summary: Two friends on a walk argue over whose charitable donation is more virtuous, and the self-righteous critic turns out to be the more resentful giver.

title: Life Force Drained by Doomed Project

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your new project will have no budget and no management support. Expect to spend most of your time giving status reports.

transcript.speaker: Employee (thought)
transcript.text: Oh no! The life force has been drained out of me! I'm becoming a damp rag!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's amazing.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's nothing. I did eighteen at once at the employee empowerment brunch.

setting: Office
situation: The Boss tells an employee that his new project will have no budget, no management support, and mostly consist of status reports. The employee imagines his life force being drained away until he becomes a damp rag. Dilbert marvels at the effect, and the Boss casually boasts that he drained eighteen people at once at an employee empowerment brunch.
punchline: The Boss is proud of draining the life force from eighteen employees at once at an event supposedly meant to empower them, exposing how demoralizing management really is.
summary: A manager hands out a hopeless assignment that saps an employee's spirit, then brags about doing the same to a whole crowd at a so-called empowerment event.

title: Defending Dilbert With Temp Worker Law

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I bet I've gone to jail more than the average law-abiding citizen.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I plan to defend you by proving your victim was a temp worker.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's legal to kill a temp? Really??

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Now all we need is a jury of your "peers".

setting: A jail meeting room, with Dilbert in a prison uniform across a table from Dogbert
situation: Dilbert, in jail, meets with Dogbert, who is acting as his defense attorney. Dogbert explains that his legal strategy is to show the murder victim was a temp worker. Dilbert is astonished that killing a temp is legal, and Dogbert says they only need a jury of Dilbert's 'peers'.
punchline: Dogbert implies that temp workers are so disposable that killing one is legal, and that a jury of Dilbert's 'peers' would be other temps, so they would be sympathetic to him.
summary: A lawyer dog plans to get his jailed client off the hook by arguing the victim was merely a contract worker, then wants a jury drawn from the client's own kind.

title: Dogbert Hypnotizes Earth Via Satellite

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: This is Dogbert... You are all under my hypnotic powers...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I am the supreme ruler of Earth. You must all carry Dogbert posters and chant "Dogbert is my king."

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That is all for now. If I think of anything else important I'll let you know.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: ...Is my king.

setting: Dogbert's office with a computer, camera and satellite dish, plus a view of a satellite orbiting Earth
situation: Dogbert sits at a desk with a video camera and satellite dish and broadcasts a message to the entire planet. He announces that everyone is under his hypnotic control and must carry Dogbert posters and chant his praises. After signing off casually, a cat walks by holding a Dogbert poster and obediently chanting.
punchline: Dogbert's world domination is as effortless as it is casual, ending his broadcast with a shrug while a hypnotized cat already carries his poster and chants his praise.
summary: Dogbert beams a satellite message declaring himself ruler of Earth, and a hypnotized cat immediately falls in line.

title: Engineers Mock Obsolete Computer Purchase

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm so mad... I just bought a new computer and it's already obsolete.

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: Don't feel bad. The other engineers won't look down on you just because you're behind the technology curve.

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: Yeah, we will.

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: Not right in front of him.

setting: Office break area, coworkers standing with coffee mugs
situation: Dilbert complains to two coworkers holding coffee mugs that the computer he just bought is already obsolete. One coworker tries to console him by saying the other engineers won't look down on him for being behind the technology curve. The other coworker admits they will, only adding that they won't do it in front of him.
punchline: The supposedly comforting reassurance is immediately undercut by a coworker confirming that the engineers will indeed judge him, just not to his face.
summary: A gadget-obsessed office comforts a colleague about his outdated new computer, then cheerfully admits they'll mock him behind his back.

title: Pants Nobody Could Ever Wear

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Excuse me. Do you have any pants that AREN'T a twelve-inch waist and fifty inches long?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I ask because there are no human beings who could wear these pants, and one of the secrets of retail success is to stock merchandise that somebody might want.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then people would shop here and actually BUY things.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: Wow, that's way harder than what we do.

setting: Clothing store
situation: Dilbert asks a store clerk for pants that are not absurdly narrow and long, holding up a pair from the sale rack. He explains that stocking clothes real people can wear is the key to retail success and would lead to actual sales. The clerk admits that doing so sounds harder than what the store currently does.
punchline: The clerk sarcastically-but-sincerely admits that stocking merchandise people want is too much effort compared with the store's current approach of stocking unwearable pants.
summary: A shopper gently lectures a store clerk on basic retail sense, only to find the clerk considers selling wearable clothes too difficult.

title: Random Cruelty Needs Social Context

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The e-mail votes have been tabulated. The will of the people is that Ratbert shall be spared from getting whacked with a magazine.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: 57% = spared

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I guess there's nothing funny about random cruelty.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: AAAII!!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Right! Cruelty is only funny if administered in a proper social context.

setting: Office, at a computer desk
situation: Dogbert announces the results of an e-mail vote in which 57% of respondents chose to spare Ratbert from being whacked with a magazine. Dilbert, holding a rolled-up magazine, concludes there is nothing funny about random cruelty. A green dinosaur (Bob) then grabs Dilbert from behind and gives him a wedgie, and Dogbert says cruelty is only funny in the proper social context.
punchline: Dilbert concludes that random cruelty isn't funny, only to become the victim of a well-targeted wedgie, which Dogbert says proves cruelty is funny when it is directed at the right person in the right context.
summary: After a poll saves Ratbert from a magazine whacking, Dilbert's moral lesson about cruelty is immediately undercut when he becomes the target of a prank.

title: Dogbert Trades Map for Ambassadorship

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'd like your biggest map of the world for my war room.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'd like this for free. In return, after I conquer the world I'll make you ambassador to France.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: Does that require travel? I get air sick.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: No problem. You'll have diplomatic immunity.

setting: A map store
situation: Dogbert walks into a map shop and asks the clerk for the biggest world map for his war room. He demands it for free, offering the clerk an ambassadorship to France once he has conquered the world. The clerk worries about air sickness from travel, and Dogbert answers with a non sequitur about diplomatic immunity.
punchline: Dogbert responds to the clerk's concern about air sickness by offering diplomatic immunity, which has nothing to do with the problem, showing he is either ignoring the concern or doesn't care about it.
summary: A scheming dog haggles for a free world map by promising a shop clerk a diplomatic post in his future empire.

title: Fingernail Computers Know Too Much

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: Laptop computers are outdated. You want our new fingernail models.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: You glue them permanently to each nail. They sense where each finger is at all times. You don't need a keyboard.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: Of course, some people prefer that their computer not know where their fingers are at all times.

transcript.speaker: Fingernail computer
transcript.text: Dave, about last night...

setting: Computer store
situation: A computer salesman pitches Dilbert on tiny fingernail computers that are glued to each nail and track finger positions, replacing laptops and keyboards. He admits some people might not want their computer knowing where their fingers are at all times. A small voice from the salesman's fingernail then speaks up about something that happened last night.
punchline: The salesman's own fingernail computer has been tracking his fingers all night and pipes up to reference an embarrassing private activity, proving the privacy concern is real.
summary: A salesman touting wearable nail-mounted computers is undermined when his own gadget announces it knows what his hands were up to.

title: Dogbert Studies Engineers Like Gorillas

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: A small band of the creatures were known to live high in an artificial structure.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: On my way to study them I took note of the native vegetation.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Rented.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The younger males were at play. They became self-conscious when watched.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The dominant male had a gray back. He controlled the others by waving little envelopes.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: There were few females in the group. The less dominant males had no chance of mating.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Unlike other species they had no instinct for grooming.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Want to groom?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Drop dead.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: My time was up. But I will miss them, those...

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Engineers in the mist

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: How long are you supposed to microwave popcorn?

setting: Office building, parodying a wildlife documentary
situation: Dogbert narrates a nature-documentary-style study of office workers, treating them as a band of primates. He compares a rented office plant to native vegetation, a worker playing a computer game to young males at play, and the boss paying staff with envelopes to a dominant male. He departs, saying he will miss the 'engineers in the mist'.
punchline: Engineers are portrayed as clueless, socially awkward primates who can't groom, mate, or even cook popcorn, in a parody of 'Gorillas in the Mist'.
summary: Dogbert gives a wildlife-documentary narration of the office, casting engineers as awkward apes in a skyscraper habitat.

title: Consultant Warns Against Wasting Money on Consultants

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert is a creativity consultant

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Here's my final report on your company.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I've concluded that you're doomed. You waste too much money on consultants.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're a consultant.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Ironic, isn't it?

setting: The Boss's office
situation: Dogbert, working as a creativity consultant, hands the Boss his final report on the company. He declares that the company is doomed because it spends too much money on consultants. The Boss points out that Dogbert is himself a consultant, and Dogbert calmly acknowledges the irony.
punchline: Dogbert, who is being paid as a consultant, diagnoses the company's fatal flaw as overspending on consultants, then cheerfully admits the irony without any intention of changing anything.
summary: A hired advisor delivers a report blaming the client's ruin on its habit of hiring advisors like him.

title: Barrel Fun Tests Job Gullibility

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dilbert and Zimbu compete for one job.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This next event tests your humor and creativity.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The objective is to see how much fun you can have in the barrel. Who wants to go first?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This is no fair. Zimbu is a monkey. He has an advantage.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Actually, this is a test of your gullibility.

setting: Office hiring competition with a barrel
situation: Dilbert and a monkey named Zimbu are competing for a single job. The Boss, acting as the interviewer, announces a test of humor and creativity that involves having fun in a barrel. When Dilbert complains the monkey has an unfair advantage, the Boss reveals the real test is how gullible the candidates are.
punchline: The supposed test of creativity is really a test of gullibility, and Dilbert fails it by taking the absurd barrel challenge seriously and arguing about fairness.
summary: A job contest between a man and a monkey turns out to be an exam on how easily the applicant can be fooled.

title: Dogbert's Health Book and Carpet Patch

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I thought of another way to profit from the ignorance of humans.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I wrote "The Dogbert Formula for Health." I recommend a daily dose of food, sleep and exercise.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And for only $19.95 you can buy the patented "Dogbert Joggerobic Carpet Patch" to help you run in place.

setting: Dilbert's living room, with Dilbert in an armchair
situation: Dogbert, perched on an ottoman, announces a new scheme to profit from human ignorance while Dilbert sits reading. He pitches a health book whose advice is just food, sleep and exercise, then tries to sell Dilbert a patented carpet patch for running in place.
punchline: Dogbert's health 'formula' is common sense repackaged as a product, and he then upsells a pointless gadget to do something people can already do for free.
summary: Dogbert cheerfully fleeces humans by selling obvious health advice in a book and then pushing a useless overpriced exercise accessory.

title: Clothes Packed in Pringles Can

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hey, Dogbert! I just discovered I can fit an entire change of clothes into an empty "Pringles" potato chip can.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Most of the fabrics I wear can be rolled up pretty tight... So... Uh...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's funny how the most brilliant idea can sound silly when you tell your dog.

setting: Dilbert's home, with Dogbert sitting nearby
situation: Dilbert excitedly tells Dogbert that he can fit a full change of clothes into an empty Pringles can. As he explains it, he trails off, noticing how pointless it sounds. In the last panel he thinks to himself that brilliant ideas sound silly when said aloud to a dog.
punchline: Dilbert's supposedly brilliant idea turns out to sound ridiculous the moment he says it out loud, and Dogbert's silent, unimpressed presence makes that obvious.
summary: A proud inventor realizes mid-pitch that his clever packing trick sounds foolish when explained to his unresponsive pet.

title: Dogbert Sells Collectible Acorn Plates

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What are you making?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Commemorative collectible plates.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: One of the mysteries of life is that you can put any picture on a plate and hordes of morons will want to own it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wow! An acorn! And it's on a plate!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: What's it like to be a member of a horde?

setting: Office conference table
situation: Dogbert is painting pictures onto plates at a table and tells Dilbert he is making commemorative collectible plates. He explains that any picture on a plate attracts hordes of morons who want to own it. Dilbert then excitedly admires a plate with an acorn on it, and Dogbert asks what it feels like to be part of a horde.
punchline: Dilbert proves Dogbert's point by gushing over a plain acorn on a plate, making himself one of the very morons Dogbert described.
summary: A cynical dog crafts keepsake dishes for gullible buyers and promptly watches his friend become a customer.

title: Ratbert Falls for Infomercial

transcript.speaker: TV
transcript.text: Are you tired of fad diets and fad exercise devices?

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Yes I am!

transcript.speaker: TV
transcript.text: Then buy my book and get the revolutionary joggerobic carpet patch for only $19.95 plus shipping and handling.

transcript.speaker: TV
transcript.text: To prove it works, we photographed an actual athlete.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Pictures don't lie!

setting: Living room, in front of a television
situation: Ratbert watches an infomercial that asks if he is tired of fad diets and exercise gadgets, then pitches a book and a carpet patch as a fitness device. The TV host claims it works because they photographed an actual athlete, and Ratbert is convinced by this flimsy proof.
punchline: Ratbert is so gullible that a mere photograph of an athlete, which proves nothing, is enough to convince him the useless product works.
summary: A trusting little lab animal swallows a ridiculous TV pitch for a worthless fitness gimmick because of a single photo.

title: Ratbert Hugs Dilbert's Dirty Shoe

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sigh...

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Hey hey! What's this? Are we feeling blue?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Go away, Ratbert.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: This could be my chance to bond and become a valued member of the family.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I'm going to hug your foot until you turn that frown upside down.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Now tell me why you feel sad.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I just walked through something disgusting with my new shoes.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: One of us isn't trying hard enough to make this relationship work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Could you do the other shoe now?

setting: Dilbert's home, in his armchair
situation: Dilbert sits sighing in a chair when Ratbert, the pet rat, tries to cheer him up so he can bond with the family. Despite Dilbert telling him to go away, Ratbert hugs Dilbert's foot and asks why he is sad. Dilbert reveals he just stepped in something disgusting with his new shoes, and Ratbert's hugging has been cleaning it.
punchline: Dilbert lets the eager Ratbert keep hugging his foot, then calmly reveals the shoe was covered in filth and asks him to clean the other one too, exploiting Ratbert's desperate need to be accepted.
summary: A needy little pet enthusiastically cuddles his owner's shoe, unaware it's coated in something gross, and ends up being volunteered to clean the second one.

title: Happiness Juice Gets Banned

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've identified the brain chemical that controls happiness.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And I found the exact mix of fruit and vegetable juices that stimulate its production.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you realize what this means?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Yeah. Fruits and vegetables will be banned by the government.

setting: Dilbert's home laboratory
situation: Dilbert works with lab equipment and announces he has found the brain chemical that controls happiness, plus a juice mix that triggers it. When he asks if Dogbert grasps the significance, Dogbert cynically predicts the government will ban fruits and vegetables.
punchline: Dogbert assumes that anything which makes people happy naturally and cheaply will be outlawed, mocking government drug policy and the idea that happiness is treated as a crime.
summary: A scientist's breakthrough in natural happiness is greeted with the cynical prediction that officials would simply prohibit the ingredients.

title: Promotion Requires Personality Disorders

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your engineering knowledge is good, but I can't promote you to "prima donna."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: ...unless you demonstrate a few more serious personality disorders.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can mumble.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sure, but can you do it with disdain for all of humanity?

setting: The Boss's office
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that although he is technically skilled, he cannot be promoted to the status of prima donna without displaying more serious personality disorders. Dilbert offers that he can mumble, and the Boss asks whether he can do it with contempt for everyone.
punchline: The Boss treats being an insufferable prima donna as a skill to be earned, implying that obnoxious behavior and contempt for others, not competence, is what gets rewarded in the workplace.
summary: A manager coaches an engineer on the antisocial traits he supposedly needs before he can be elevated to difficult-genius status.

title: Boss Objects to Alice's Family Time

transcript.speaker: The Boss

punchline: The Boss, who demands unpaid overtime, is so detached from home life that he doesn't recognize his own family members and only guesses they live with him.
summary: A manager criticizes an employee's evenings at home with her family, only to reveal he barely knows he has one himself.

title: Engineering Career Day: Scapegoats and Vacation

setting: A school classroom during a career talk
situation: A teacher introduces Dilbert to a class of students as a speaker on exciting engineering careers. Dilbert then gives a brutally honest account of the job, saying engineers mostly write memos nobody reads. On the rare occasion one is read, he says, you must blame someone else or take vacation and hope the problem disappears.
punchline: Dilbert's career-day pitch cynically reveals that engineering means writing ignored memos and dodging blame, not anything exciting.
summary: Invited to inspire students about engineering, Dilbert instead describes a job of unread paperwork and blame avoidance.

situation: Ratbert stands next to Dilbert's armchair holding a leash, asking to be taken for a walk while Dilbert reads a magazine. Dilbert rolls up the magazine and explains that rats are exercised by being hit with it. punchline: Dilbert coolly treats violence as the correct 'exercise' for a rat, and the strip then turns Ratbert's fate into a reader poll.
summary: A pet rat hoping for a stroll is instead threatened with a rolled-up magazine as readers are invited to decide his fate.

setting: A bank teller window, then outside the bank
situation: Dilbert complains to a bank teller named Ethel about a fee for paying his credit card bill one day late and suggests the bank automate payments instead. Ethel cheerfully admits the bank prefers to set traps for customers to collect penalties. When Dilbert threatens to take his business elsewhere, she fines him a hundred dollars for annoying her, and he leaves the bank in his underwear.
punchline: The bank openly rejects customer service in favor of trapping customers with fees, and even Dilbert's threat to leave gets him penalized and stripped of everything, leaving him without even a moral victory.
summary: A customer protesting a late fee learns that his bank deliberately profits from penalties and ends up fined and left in his underwear.

title: Dogbert Adopts Ratbert at Christmas

situation: On Christmas, Dilbert sits by the tree and remarks that Dogbert has guilt-tripped the family into giving lots of presents. Dogbert is busy tearing into gifts while little Ratbert, holding a small present, asks whether he counts as family. Dilbert welcomes him in and hands him a gift, and Dogbert warns him not to expect much allowance.
punchline: Dogbert gladly takes the family's gifts, but as soon as a new member joins he makes clear that membership comes with no financial perks, showing his stinginess and manipulative streak.
summary: After Dogbert guilts everyone into piles of presents, Ratbert is welcomed into the household, only to be told the perks are meagre.

punchline: Dogbert accuses Dilbert of manipulating him into waiting on him, then manipulates Dilbert into waiting on him by making him feel guilty.
summary: A sick man ends up apologizing to his dog for being ill and then agrees to serve the dog breakfast.

title: Fire-Walking Seminar Sock Excuse

Dilbert claims he is only taking his socks off because he is cold. The instructor, unbothered, tells him to go ahead and walk the coals with his socks on.
punchline: The instructor's absurd permission to walk on hot coals in socks ignores the real danger, showing that seminar leaders care more about going through the motions than about safety or logic.
summary: A nervous attendee at a coal-walking workshop makes an excuse about the cold, and the unfazed instructor cheerfully lets him walk on fire in his socks.

punchline: Ratbert's bodyguard services are nowhere to be seen: Dilbert is the one who is sunk in the mud and has to give the tough-guy line himself, implying the rat is useless or has vanished into the mud.
summary: A tiny lab rat promises to protect his owner on a trip to a muddy foreign land, but the tough talk doesn't survive arrival.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that his own boss wants eunuch programmers, having misheard the term Unix. Dilbert patiently corrects the mix-up and says he already knows Unix. The Boss, who had apparently been about to arrange something drastic, asks Dilbert to tell the company nurse to disregard the request.
punchline: The Boss had been ready to have himself or others surgically altered because he misunderstood a technical term, and only the nurse remark reveals how far he had taken the misunderstanding.
summary: A manager garbles a technical hiring requirement so badly that he seems to have already summoned medical help before being corrected.

punchline: Dilbert's triumph is undercut when he learns the monkey has been promoted into management, implying he's now essentially beaten by a monkey who will outrank him.
summary: After gloating over beating a monkey for an engineering job, Dilbert learns the primate is headed for a fast-tracked management career.

title: Dogbert Returns the Garbage Man's Phaser

punchline: Dogbert gleefully used the weapon, and the garbage man is pleased rather than concerned, implying the phaser is meant for fun and Dogbert's lingering tail wagging is a sign of a job well done.
summary: After borrowing a garbage man's zapping gadget, Dogbert cheerfully reports how much fun he had with it, to the owner's satisfaction.

summary: A boss rigs a meeting so that anyone who looks at him gets stuck with a miserable task, and a quick-witted coworker pins it on a colleague who is hiding his face.

punchline: The Boss's eerie zombie-like invitation shows that he has himself become a buzzword-spouting management zombie, and he wants to recruit Dilbert into the fold.
summary: A boss urges his engineer to attend a seminar that teaches empty jargon, then beckons him in like a creature from a horror film.

summary: A badly drawn presentation graphic gets mistaken for a lightning-struck piece of furniture bearing the King's face rather than the high-tech meeting it was meant to show.

punchline: The Boss is so ignorant that he believes office ink comes from squids, and he dismisses Dilbert's correction with a sarcastic remark that misapplies the cow-glue myth, doubling down on his misunderstanding.
summary: A manager orders all ink removed from the office to rescue squids, then scoffs when an employee corrects his misconception.

punchline: The staff sent on 'one-way business trips' are being lured to a sinister fate in rural Iowa, implying Dogbert is getting rid of employees permanently to boost the stock price.

summary: A frustrated marketer berates a table of engineers for stalling, and they respond with dry sarcasm about his career choice.

summary: A man on a date with a mind-reading, two-headed woman assures her his thoughts are ordinary, until she catches one that clearly isn't.
