punchline: Carol answers the manager's queue-jumping with a crossbow, a violent way of showing she resents being treated as less important.
summary: A secretary hogging the copier responds to a manager's polite request to cut in with an armed threat.

title: Ratbert Sees Dick Clark's Hair

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Ratbert falls into a hole in the fabric of space

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's it look like, Ratbert?

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: It's beautiful... I see the secrets of time revealed... an object approaches...

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: It's Dick Clark's hair.

setting: Dilbert's office desk, then a surreal rift in space and time
situation: Ratbert falls into a hole in the fabric of space while Dilbert asks what he sees. Ratbert drifts through a strange, dreamlike void, describing the secrets of time being revealed as an object approaches. The approaching object turns out to be Dick Clark's hair.
punchline: After building up a profound cosmic revelation, the mysterious object drifting through time turns out to be Dick Clark's famously unchanging hair, implying he never ages.
summary: A tiny traveler tumbles through a cosmic rift expecting enlightenment and instead meets a famously ageless television host's hairdo.

title: Deceptively Small Retirement Offers

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Company headquarters

transcript.speaker: Unseen speaker
transcript.text: Does anybody have a plan for getting rid of the employees?

transcript.speaker: Unseen speaker
transcript.text: Well, they're bad at math; we could offer deceptively small sums of money to people who retire.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hey, this could be good.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's been a long time since I had to calculate the cosine of anything.

setting: Outside the company headquarters building, then the office where employees read the offer
situation: Voices at company headquarters ask for a plan to get rid of employees and decide to offer deceptively small sums of money to people who retire, banking on the workers being bad at math. Dilbert and Wally then read the retirement offer, and instead of seeing through it, they react with interest and even look forward to doing the math. Alice reads her copy nearby.
punchline: The employees fall straight into the trap, treating the lowball retirement offer as a fun math exercise and proving management's assumption that they are bad at math right.
summary: Management schemes to lure workers into leaving with a sneakily stingy payout, and the staff are too delighted by the arithmetic to notice.

title: Temp Workers Go In Dumpster

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I just love hiring these temporary workers!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No employee benefits... no union... just toss 'em in the dumpster when you're done with them!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The dumpster seems a bit inappropriate.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: They're way too big to flush.

setting: Office
situation: The Boss cheerfully hugs a limp temporary worker while praising the advantages of hiring temps, such as no benefits and no union. He says he will simply throw them in the dumpster when finished. Dilbert objects that the dumpster is inappropriate, and the Boss replies that temps are too big to flush.
punchline: The Boss treats temporary workers as disposable garbage, and his only concern with disposing of them is a practical one about size, not any ethical objection.
summary: A gleeful manager explains that temps are ideal because they cost nothing extra and can be thrown away like trash afterward.

title: Bowling Night as Disguised Punishment

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're having a department bowling night tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's my way of rewarding all of you for your performance this quarter.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We hate doing things together at night.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I wasn't happy with your performance.

setting: Office, with a plain blue background
situation: The Boss announces a department bowling night for the following evening and presents it as a reward for the team's performance over the quarter. Dilbert objects that the team hates doing things together at night. The Boss replies that he wasn't happy with their performance, revealing the outing is really a punishment.
punchline: The supposed reward is actually a punishment, since the Boss was unhappy with the team's performance and knows they dislike after-hours group activities.
summary: A manager calls a mandatory evening outing a prize, then admits it is meant as payback for a disappointing quarter.

title: Dogbert's Tax-Funded Prison Infrastructure

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Here are the Dogbert tax forms. Pay promptly or you will be penalized.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's not fair!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You can't just levy your own taxes; what makes you think I'll pay?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: If not, I'll put you in my new prison.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You mean, you built a prison with the taxes you've already collected?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I think of it as "infra-structure."

setting: Dilbert's home or office, with Dogbert seated in a blue chair
situation: Dogbert hands Dilbert a set of tax forms he has invented and threatens penalties for non-payment. When Dilbert objects that Dogbert has no right to levy taxes, Dogbert says he will jail him in his new prison. Dilbert realizes the prison was built with taxes already collected, and Dogbert calls it infrastructure.
punchline: Dogbert uses self-imposed taxes to build a prison to enforce those same taxes, dressing up his coercive scheme as respectable public infrastructure.
summary: A self-appointed tax collector dog threatens his victim with a prison that was funded by the very taxes he is demanding.

title: Dogbert's Self-Help Book Overdose

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You fool! You are nothing compared to me! Ha ha ha ha ha ha!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Have you been speed-reading my self-help books again?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The idiots should put warning labels on those things.

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle
situation: Dilbert sits working at his computer while Dogbert, standing nearby, suddenly starts shouting arrogant insults and laughing maniacally. Dilbert turns and asks if Dogbert has been speed-reading his self-help books again. Dogbert replies that the books should carry warning labels.
punchline: Self-help books have inflated Dogbert's already huge ego into delusional megalomania, so he jokes that they are dangerous enough to need warning labels.
summary: After binge-reading self-help books, Dogbert erupts into gloating about his own superiority, prompting his owner to guess the cause.

title: Dilbert Recites Buzzwords in Review

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So, what have you accomplished this year?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hate performance reviews.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, I used my empowerment to create a new paradigm.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And I teamed across functional boundaries to improve quality.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I dare say I was customer-focused and market-driven!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I proactively found excellence in the midst of chaos!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I re-engineered my core processes and embraced change!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I give you — Dilbert — the perfect employee!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Was that sarcasm?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: To be honest, I don't know either.

setting: The boss's office during a performance review
situation: The boss asks Dilbert what he has accomplished this year. Dilbert, privately hating performance reviews, responds with an escalating stream of management buzzwords and finally presents himself as the perfect employee, gesturing grandly at himself. The boss asks if that was sarcasm.
punchline: Dilbert has been parroting corporate jargon so long and so absurdly that even he can no longer tell whether he is being sarcastic or sincere.
summary: Forced to justify his year, an employee buries his boss in management clichés until neither of them can tell if he is mocking the process.

title: Dogbert's Corporate Zombie Seminar

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Many of you come to my management seminar as optimistic, creative, clear-speaking individuals.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: But with hard work, you can become jargon-spewing corporate zombies, like Carl here.

transcript.speaker: Carl
transcript.text: I want to dialogue with you about utilizing resources.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Good boy! Here's a donut.

setting: Management seminar room with a flip chart
situation: Dogbert leads a management seminar with a pointer, standing beside a flip chart showing a smiling man with a lightbulb. He tells the audience, which includes Dilbert, that hard work can turn them into jargon-spewing zombies like Carl. Carl, a suited man leaning back in a chair, spouts buzzwords, and Dogbert tosses him a donut like a trained pet.
punchline: Dogbert treats the corporate jargon-speaking manager as a trained animal, rewarding buzzword babble with a treat, implying that management seminars train people to be mindless.
summary: A talking dog running a seminar presents a buzzword-spouting executive as proof that his course can strip people of creativity and clear speech.

title: Computers Blamed for Productivity Decline

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Government statistics show that office productivity went down as computers became widely used.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But I didn't believe it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So I wrote a little software program to test that conclusion.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It only took a month, but it produced some impressive data.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: In fact, it was so impressive it took a week to figure out how to print it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But before I could print, my computer crashed and I didn't have backup copies.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So, it seems the government was right; computers are to blame for the decline in productivity.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do you think the employees could be partly responsible?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sure, find a scapegoat.

setting: The Boss's office
situation: Dilbert reports to The Boss that he doubted government statistics claiming computers reduced office productivity, so he wrote a program to test it. He spent a month on it, a week figuring out how to print the results, then lost everything when his computer crashed with no backup. He concludes the government was right.
punchline: Dilbert's own wasted month proves computers hurt productivity, and when the Boss asks whether employees are to blame, Dilbert sarcastically tells him to go ahead and find a scapegoat.
summary: A researching employee unwittingly proves that computers sap productivity by burning weeks on a program that crashes before producing anything.

title: Humans Superior Because They Kill

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The great thing about being human is that I'm superior to all other animals.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: On what do you base that absurd conclusion?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Humans have the ability to kill any other animal. Therefore, we are superior.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You could be slaughtered by chipmunks if they ever decided to gang up.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But they wouldn't decide to do that. That's why humans are superior.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Chipmunks waste their days by eating nuts and playing instead of plotting ways to kill other species.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's futile to argue with you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Thank you.

transcript.speaker: Off-panel voice
transcript.text: I say we kill him. Is anybody with me?

setting: A park or grassy hillside with a path and trees
situation: Dilbert takes a walk with Dogbert and argues that humans are superior to all other animals because humans can kill any of them. Dogbert points out that chipmunks could kill him if they banded together, but Dilbert insists their failure to plot murder proves human superiority. When Dilbert reclines under a tree, a voice from above suggests killing him.
punchline: Dilbert's logic that superiority means being willing to kill is so absurd that Dogbert gives up arguing, and then a voice off-panel proposes killing him, as if the chipmunks have taken him up on his definition.
summary: A man's boast that killing power makes his species supreme gets an ominous reply from somewhere in the trees.

title: Ratbert's Endless Space Hole Memoir

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I'm writing a book about being trapped in the space hole for three hundred thousand years.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Day one: I thought about cheese. Day two: See day one. Day three: See day two...

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Do you know a good editor?

setting: Dogbert's home, with a radio and rug
situation: Ratbert tells Dogbert he is writing a book about being trapped in a space hole for 300,000 years. We see his diary, which is just a lazy chain of 'see the previous day' entries about cheese. In the last panel he has produced a towering stack of paper and asks Dogbert for a good editor.
punchline: The book is a monstrous pile of repetitive filler where every day just refers back to the one before, so it clearly needs a ruthless editor to cut it down.
summary: A rodent author produces a skyscraper-sized manuscript whose entries merely point back at each other and wants someone to trim it.

title: Useless Warnings From Symbiotic Rodent

transcript.speaker: Rodent
transcript.text: As part of our symbiotic relationship I'll shout a warning when danger approaches.

transcript.speaker: Rodent
transcript.text: There's a hole in the ozone layer! Consumer confidence is down a point!

transcript.speaker: Rodent
transcript.text: Angry dinosaur with big tail!

transcript.speaker: Rodent
transcript.text: You call that symbiotic??!

setting: Prehistoric landscape with a tree (no office)
situation: A small orange rodent perched on a dinosaur's back promises to warn it of danger as part of their symbiotic relationship. Instead he shouts about abstract modern concerns like the ozone layer and consumer confidence, and only mentions the angry dinosaur with the big tail when it is too late. The dinosaur has already eaten the dinosaur-sized threat, or is being attacked, while the rodent ends up stuck in a tree complaining.
punchline: The rodent's warnings are focused on trivial or irrelevant threats and he only notices the real danger after it has already struck, making the 'symbiotic' arrangement worthless.
summary: A lookout critter on a dinosaur's back raves about distant, abstract worries while missing the immediate predator that ruins everything.

title: Carpet Patch Kids Product Line

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I think I've hit upon a brilliant new direction for expanding our product line.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I call them "Carpet Patch Kids." Each one is made from carpet and has its own name!

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Don't feel bad, Raquel. I don't think he meant it as a personal attack.

setting: Dogbert's office
situation: Ratbert approaches Dogbert, who is seated in his chair, and pitches an idea for expanding the product line. He shows off a doll made of carpet that he calls a "Carpet Patch Kid." Dogbert's reaction is not shown, but Ratbert walks away cradling the doll and consoling it.
punchline: Ratbert's carpet doll pitch is clearly rejected by Dogbert, and he comforts the doll Raquel as though it had feelings, implying the rejection was harsh and that he is lonely and attached to his creation.
summary: A hopeful inventor presents a handmade carpet doll to his boss, then retreats while comforting the toy over the apparent insult.

title: Cubicle as Sensory Deprivation Chamber

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I prepare to enter the sensory deprivation chamber.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I will experience no mental or physical stimulation for hours.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: All that and I get paid too.

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle
situation: Dilbert narrates his thoughts as if he is about to enter a sensory deprivation chamber, anticipating hours without mental or physical stimulation. The final panel reveals he is simply sitting in his chair in his cubicle at work, where the experience is the same and he is paid for it.
punchline: His dull, unstimulating job is equivalent to a sensory deprivation chamber, except that he gets a paycheck for enduring it.
summary: A man mentally psyches himself up for an isolation tank session, only for the reveal to show he is just sitting bored at his office desk.

title: Dogbert Hypnotizes Ratbert Instantly

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Looks easy enough.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Hi, Dogbert! What are you reading?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Nothing. You will remember nothing.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Who am I? Where am I?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That was a little bit like sandblasting a soup cracker.

setting: Dogbert's home, on his reading cushion
situation: Dogbert reads a book titled 'Hypnosis for World Conquest' and thinks it looks easy. When Ratbert cheerfully asks what he's reading, Dogbert tells him he will remember nothing, and Ratbert is instantly left dazed and amnesiac. Dogbert thinks it was absurdly easy.
punchline: Hypnotizing the simple-minded Ratbert was so effortless that Dogbert compares it to using heavy industrial force on something already fragile, an insult to Ratbert's mental sturdiness.
summary: After skimming a hypnosis manual, Dogbert wipes his tiny friend's memory with a single sentence and finds the feat almost insultingly simple.

title: Dilbert's Laser Pointer Triggers Phasers

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm adjusting the pointer-pen laser light for my presentation tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm boosting the power so it's easier to see.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Watch it while I get the phone.

transcript.speaker: Phone
transcript.text: R-R-R-ING

transcript.speaker: Sleeping Character
transcript.text: zzzzz

transcript.speaker: Voice from computer
transcript.text: The aliens appear hostile, Captain. Set phasers to full power!

setting: Dilbert's home office or lab with an old computer console
situation: Dilbert tinkers with a laser pointer pen at his desk, turning up its power for tomorrow's presentation, while Dogbert sits nearby. When Dilbert leaves to answer the phone, the laser is left aimed at the computer, which appears to be running a Star Trek-style game. A sleeping Dogbert sits at the console as the computer announces hostile aliens and orders phasers to full power.
punchline: Boosting the laser's power and leaving it unattended makes the computer's space game think hostile aliens have appeared and set its phasers to full power.
summary: A man amps up his laser pointer, steps away for a call, and the neglected beam seems to trigger an overreacting space-combat computer.

title: Dogbert Bids Fitness Program For Laughs

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Congratulations, Mister Dogbert. You submitted the lowest bid for creating our corporate fitness program.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The other bidders wanted money. You're the only one who offered to do it just for the laughs.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Although I don't see what's so funny about it.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Engineers... aerobics... think about it.

setting: The Boss's office
situation: The Boss congratulates Dogbert for winning the contract to create the company's corporate fitness program because he submitted the lowest bid. The Boss notes that Dogbert alone offered to do it just for laughs, though he can't see what is funny. Dogbert answers by pointing out the absurd image of engineers doing aerobics.
punchline: Dogbert is bidding low simply because he finds it hilarious to imagine the company's out-of-shape engineers doing aerobics, and the oblivious Boss doesn't get the joke.
summary: A clueless executive awards a fitness contract to the dog who underbid everyone, never realizing the real payment is the amusement of watching engineers exercise.

title: Dogbert's Commemorative Plate Scam

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You already own the "Acorn Series" of Dogbert's commemorative plates...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: For a limited time you may also purchase my new issue: the "French Guy with a Hat" series.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My acorn plates are missing.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Tomorrow I'll introduce my new series: "Russian with French Hat."

setting: Dilbert's living room at home
situation: Dogbert pitches Dilbert a limited-time collectible plate series while Dilbert sits reading in an armchair. Dilbert then discovers that his acorn plates have disappeared. Dogbert, who has apparently taken them, is already planning the next series to sell.
punchline: Dogbert is stealing Dilbert's existing collectible plates and will resell them to him as a new series, a never-ending scam.
summary: A scheming dog peddles collectible plates to his owner after quietly swiping the ones the man already had.

title: Alice Squeezes the Boss's Hair

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Squeeze squeeze squeeze

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: In retrospect, that was exactly the kind of temptation I should just ignore.

setting: Office coffee station
situation: The Boss pours himself a cup of coffee while Alice walks up holding her own mug. Alice reaches out and repeatedly squeezes the Boss's pointy hair, which stays bent out of shape afterward. She then admits she should have resisted the urge.
punchline: Alice gave in to the irresistible temptation to squeeze the Boss's pointy hair and immediately recognizes it was a mistake she should have ignored.
summary: A coworker succumbs to the urge to fiddle with her supervisor's odd hair and then wishes she had held back.

title: Donut Rationing Amid Billion-Dollar Shortfall

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The company is a billion dollars below its earnings projections.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: From now on, only the managers at my level or above may eat donuts at company meetings.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This won't be easy for any of us. Heck, I don't even know if I can eat this many donuts.

setting: Conference room during a company meeting
situation: The Boss tells his staff at a meeting that the company is a billion dollars short of its earnings projections. His response is to ban everyone below his own management level from eating donuts at meetings. He then claims the hardship is shared, while worrying about whether he can eat all the donuts himself.
punchline: The Boss presents a petty perk-cutting measure as shared sacrifice when it actually benefits only the managers, who now get all the donuts.
summary: Facing a huge financial shortfall, a manager hoards the meeting pastries for himself while pretending everyone is suffering equally.

title: Ratbert Slaps Head Singing Manilow

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I figured that you would respect me more if I had some sort of talent.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: So I taught myself to sing Barry Manilow's greatest hits while slapping my head rhythmically.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: A-a-a-at the Copa (slap) Ow! Copa Cabana (slap) Ow!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm actually enjoying this and it deeply disturbs me.

setting: Dilbert's cubicle
situation: Ratbert stands on top of Dilbert's computer and explains that he wants Dilbert's respect, so he has developed a talent. He then performs Barry Manilow's 'Copacabana' while slapping himself on the head, yelping 'Ow!' with each slap. Dilbert watches and admits he is enjoying it despite himself.
punchline: Dilbert genuinely enjoys the absurd, painful performance and is disturbed by his own enjoyment.
summary: A little lab-rat tries to win a coworker's admiration by performing a pop song while hitting himself, and succeeds in an unsettling way.

title: Psychic Consultant Senses Dead Coworker

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the psychic business consultant

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I sense death...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's coming from here. Yes, he's definitely dead.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You should bury him. He already smells bad.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'll bet this isn't heaven.

setting: Office cubicle
situation: Dogbert, wearing a turban and posing as a psychic business consultant, walks through the office with the Boss and claims to sense death. He leads them to Wally, who is sitting motionless at his computer, and declares him dead and in need of burial. Wally then mumbles that this surely isn't heaven.
punchline: Wally is so inactive and lifeless at his desk that a psychic mistakes him for a corpse, and Wally's deadpan reply implies his dull office existence is the afterlife he has been stuck with.
summary: A turbaned dog mystic pronounces a sedentary office worker deceased, only for the worker to quip that his surroundings are far from paradise.

title: Secretary With a Crossbow

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I sit innocently in my low-wall, clerical style cubicle.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: One copy, no staple.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Men with Ivy-League degrees walk past the copier and ask me to make copies.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I am... Secretary with a crossbow

setting: Office cubicle area
situation: Carol, the boss's secretary, sits in her low-walled cubicle narrating her thoughts. A man in a white shirt and tie hands her a document and asks for a single copy with no staple, even though the copier is right there. In the last panel she imagines herself brandishing a crossbow.
punchline: Carol's fantasy of being a crossbow-wielding avenger shows her simmering resentment at being treated as a personal copy machine by overeducated men who could easily do the task themselves.
summary: A secretary silently seethes while colleagues with fancy degrees make her do their photocopying, and daydreams of violent revenge.

title: Replacing Engineers With Decorative Plants

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Dilbert, I need you to stop everything and do this emergency budget exercise.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Estimate the budget impact of replacing all the engineers with decorative plants.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Later, I'll summarize everybody's inputs into a bullet point, like "Oxygen is good."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Would these be rented plants?

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle
situation: A manager interrupts Dilbert with an urgent budget exercise and asks him to estimate the cost of replacing every engineer with decorative plants. She explains that she will later boil everyone's input down to a trivial bullet point. Dilbert responds by calmly asking a practical question about the plants.
punchline: Dilbert treats an absurd, insulting proposal as a legitimate budgeting task, asking whether the plants would be rented, while the manager's summary of everyone's input is a meaningless platitude.
summary: A manager tasks Dilbert with costing out a plan to swap the engineering staff for potted plants, and he responds with a straight-faced question about leasing.

title: Dogbert Hovers Through Virtual Basketball

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You might as well admit I'm a better basketball player, Dogbert.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Never!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No fair! You're hovering!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's just the illusion of "hang time."

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I learned it from Michael Jordan.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's a combination of great leaping skill plus the way I move my legs.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There! Right there! That's definitely hovering!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think you tampered with the virtual reality program!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Play the game.

setting: A virtual reality basketball court, revealed at the end to be a simulation in Dilbert's home
situation: Dilbert boasts that he is a better basketball player than Dogbert, but Dogbert leaps and floats impossibly high toward the hoop, claiming it is just the illusion of hang time learned from Michael Jordan. Dilbert protests that Dogbert is hovering and finally realizes the game is a virtual reality simulation that Dogbert has tampered with.
punchline: Dogbert beats Dilbert by secretly rigging the virtual reality program so he can literally hover and dunk, then smugly tells him to just play the game.
summary: A boastful game of one-on-one turns out to be a rigged simulation in which the dog floats to victory.

title: Baffling Form Tricks Employees Into Quitting

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: All employees must fill out this form.

transcript.speaker: Form
transcript.text: "Employee election to not rescind the opposite action of declining the reverse inclination to not discontinue employment with the company."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're trying to trick us into quitting, aren't you?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Use ink.

setting: Office hallway
situation: The Boss hands Dilbert a mandatory form for all employees. The form's wording is a tangle of stacked negatives that makes it impossible to tell what is being agreed to. Dilbert suspects it is a trick to make people quit, and the Boss only tells him to fill it out in ink.
punchline: The Boss neither denies the scheme nor addresses the confusing wording, and his curt instruction to use ink implies the trick is deliberate and that mistakes can't be undone.
summary: A deliberately convoluted company form seems designed to make staff accidentally resign, and the boss's only concern is that they sign it permanently.

title: Ratbert Wonders If He's a Yam

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: How can I be sure I'm a rat?

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: What if I'm really something else — like a potato — and I just think I'm a rat?

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I think, therefore I'm a yam.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It would explain a lot.

setting: A plain green space where Dogbert sits on a purple cushion
situation: Ratbert stands in front of Dogbert, who sits on a cushion, and begins questioning how he can be certain he is really a rat. He wonders whether he might actually be a potato who only believes he is a rat, then concludes he is a yam. Dogbert calmly replies that this would explain a lot.
punchline: Dogbert's deadpan agreement that Ratbert being a yam would explain a lot is a jab at Ratbert's obvious lack of intelligence, deflating his mock-philosophical musing.
summary: A rodent playing at philosophy decides he might be a root vegetable, and his canine companion insultingly finds the theory convincing.

title: Dilbert's Minimal New Hire Training

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dilbert the Mentor

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This is your computer.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: When you hear footsteps it's a good idea to move this thing around and click it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

situation: Dilbert is assigned to mentor a new coworker and shows him his computer. punchline: Dilbert's idea of technical training is teaching the new hire to look busy at the computer, then guilt-tripping him out of asking for any real help.
summary: A reluctant mentor gives a newcomer the bare minimum of instruction, focused on appearing productive, and warns him not to bother him with questions.

punchline: Dilbert's idea of muscular fitness is being worn out from mouse use, which proves the stereotype of out-of-shape, oblivious engineers that the calendar claimed to dispel, and Dogbert plows ahead with the photo shoot anyway.
summary: A camera-wielding dog recruits a desk-bound engineer for a muscle calendar, and the engineer's proof of fitness turns out to be sore mousing muscles.

punchline: Ratbert takes the 'absence makes the heart grow fonder' advice literally, hiding in the trash while Dilbert is not even there, so there is no absence to notice and the plan is hopeless.
summary: A lonely lab rat takes a proverb about absence at face value and tries to win affection by lurking in the garbage.
keywords: absence makes the heart grow fonder

setting: Training session in Elbonia, with a flip chart and a small audience of Elbonians
situation: Dilbert teaches the Elbonians about quality management, using a fishbone diagram on a flip chart to demonstrate root cause analysis. He applies the technique to them and concludes their root problem is that they are a nation of imbeciles. punchline: Dilbert's insult backfires because the Elbonians point out that he needed a silly diagram to reach his conclusion, so they declare him one of their own.
summary: A consultant's quality lesson ends with him insulting his audience, who cheerfully turn the tables and induct him into their fold.

title: Boss Obsesses Over Fake Microfleem Statistic

transcript.text: This is going to be painful.

transcript.speaker: The Boss

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay, okay. I acknowledge your incredible grasp of technology issues.

transcript.speaker: The Boss

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle
situation: The Boss walks up to Dilbert and proudly shares a supposedly technical statistic about microfleems being subradiante. Dilbert dreads the conversation and considers hiding under his desk, then finally flatters the Boss's technical knowledge to end it. The Boss then reveals he has no idea what a microfleem actually is.
punchline: The Boss has been trumpeting the 'implications' of a statistic about something he doesn't even understand, and his trivially obvious inference (20% means 80% are not) is passed off as technical insight.
summary: A manager triumphantly recites a meaningless statistic and its blindingly obvious corollary, only to admit he doesn't know what the thing he's talking about even is.

setting: Outdoors, with Dilbert and Wally standing in a pink-background scene holding Dogbert picture signs
situation: Dilbert and Wally each hold a sign bearing Dogbert's picture, as required by their new ruler. Wally credits Dogbert's world conquest with ending wars and improving the economy, while Dilbert points out that Dogbert's only orders so far are to carry his picture and wear bras. punchline: Dilbert sarcastically undercuts Wally's defense of the new regime by noting that Wally is a man who obviously isn't a "D" cup, exposing the absurdity of the bra-wearing order.
summary: Two coworkers argue over whether their canine overlord deserves credit for global peace while they are forced to wear undergarments and carry his portrait.

situation: Two armed government agents in suits and sunglasses stand over Dilbert at his computer and force him to delete the formulas for his happiness potion under threat of jail. punchline: The government deliberately keeps citizens uncomfortable because it claims unhappiness makes them productive, and it follows through by giving Dilbert a wedgie.
summary: Armed officials make an inventor destroy his joy-producing recipe, insisting that misery keeps people useful, then prove the point with a humiliating prank.

Dilbert admits he votes straight party tickets, and Dogbert says that proves he could finish the conquest before lunch.
punchline: Dilbert's confession that he votes a straight party ticket, without really thinking, confirms Dogbert's insult that voters use hardly any brain power, so conquering them would be trivially easy.
summary: A dog sizes up the human race as pushovers for world domination because voters hardly think at the ballot box, and his owner's voting habits prove the point.

setting: Office, in front of the employees
situation: The Boss announces a monthly 'Open Door Day' where employees can come complain to him. He demonstrates the concerned face he will wear, says he'll then explain why everything is fine, and boasts that morale, profits and his stock options will all rise. When Dilbert asks to comment on the plan, he gives up, and the Boss merely asks if he looks concerned.
punchline: The Boss's open-door policy is purely performative: he intends to ignore all feedback, and he cares more about looking concerned than about listening or hearing criticism of his plan.
summary: A manager rolls out a feedback day that is really a staged show of sympathy designed to dismiss complaints and pad his own payout.

punchline: Wally's absurd belief in his testosterone-driven magnetism seems to work, and he smugly dismisses the woman's attraction as helpless submission to his hormones.
summary: A bald man's boast about his hormonal powers inexplicably succeeds in winning over a coworker and scaring off his rival.

situation: Dilbert sits in an armchair and boasts to Dogbert that he survived a fire-walking seminar unharmed thanks to asbestos-lined socks. punchline: Dilbert's smug vindication reveals that he has long been irrationally paranoid about his backside catching fire, and his preparation for it is absurdly thorough.
summary: A smug Dilbert gloats about his flame-proof underwear while his dog calmly probes the odd anxiety behind it.

situation: The Boss tells his staff he wants to find unnecessary and unproductive employees in order to cut costs. punchline: Anyone with spare time to volunteer for the task force has just identified himself as unproductive, so the Boss is unknowingly collecting the list of people to cut.
summary: A manager hunting for slackers asks for volunteers with free time, and an employee proudly exposes himself as the first candidate for layoffs.

summary: A manager's new peer-review pay policy turns the staff against each other almost as soon as it is announced.

situation: The Boss tells his staff they can succeed if everyone gives 110 percent. Dilbert and Wally calmly dismantle the idea, subtracting vacation, sick days, meetings and interruptions until they arrive at 43 percent, which they say is only an estimate rather than a commitment.

transcript.text: Really? It didn't look awkward?

setting: Dogbert's home, then a park
situation: Ratbert admits to Dogbert that he can't remember which hand is his dominant one and worries about looking awkward if someone tosses him a ball in the park. In the last panel, a ball has flattened him against the grass and a passerby compliments his catch.
punchline: Ratbert's fear of looking awkward comes true in the worst way, since he has been crushed by a huge ball, yet he is still concerned about how the catch looked.
summary: A tiny rodent frets about fumbling a thrown ball, then ends up pinned beneath one while a stranger praises his technique.

title: Scent of Success Is Baloney

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My patent application is complete. Soon the other engineers will come sniffing around.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: They are attracted by the scent of success. They want their names on my patent.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: The scent can't be coming from here.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: We may be getting a false positive from his baloney sandwich.

setting: Office cubicles
situation: Dilbert finishes his patent application and imagines that other engineers will be drawn to him like animals sniffing out success, hoping to get their names added to his patent. In the final panel, coworkers gathered nearby dismiss the idea, suggesting the smell is just his baloney sandwich.
punchline: Dilbert's coworkers are drawn to his desk by the smell of his lunch, not by any scent of success, deflating his inflated view of his own achievement.
summary: A proud engineer assumes his colleagues are sniffing around his finished patent, but they are really just noticing his lunch.

title: Blinding Flash of the Obvious

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Whoa whoa! I just got an idea that could change everything...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What if we lowered expenses and increased revenues? That could help our financial situation.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Aaagh! I can't see!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sounds like a blinding flash of the obvious, sir.

setting: Conference room during a company meeting
situation: The Boss excitedly announces an idea he believes will change everything. He then proposes lowering expenses and increasing revenues to improve the company's finances. He clutches his eyes as if blinded, and Dilbert dryly remarks that it sounds like a blinding flash of the obvious.
punchline: The Boss treats the most basic business common sense as a groundbreaking revelation, and Dilbert sarcastically points out how obvious it is.
summary: A manager breathlessly unveils the decidedly unrevolutionary plan of spending less and earning more, and an employee mocks him for stating the obvious.

title: Ratbert Threatens Life as Accountant

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: If I don't get some love and support around here, I might turn to a life of heinous crime...

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Or worse, I could become a certified public accountant...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Stop it. You're scaring me...

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I'm good with numbers.

setting: Dilbert's living room couch
situation: Ratbert sits beside Dilbert, who is reading a book, and complains that he needs more affection or he may turn to a life of crime. He escalates the threat by saying he could become a certified public accountant. Dilbert, frightened, asks him to stop, and Ratbert notes he is good with numbers.
punchline: Becoming an accountant is presented as a worse and more frightening fate than a life of heinous crime, and Ratbert's aptitude with numbers makes the threat sound credible.
summary: A neglected lab rat warns his owner that without affection he might choose crime, then tops it with an even scarier career in accounting.

title: Salesman Promises Star Trek Technology

transcript.speaker: Stan
transcript.text: And our product has a thirty terabit RAM cache, just like your company needs. Tell him, Dilbert.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It has no RAM.

transcript.speaker: Stan
transcript.text: And it's capable of detecting tachion field emissions.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're confusing us with "Star Trek" again, Stan.

transcript.speaker: Stan
transcript.text: We'll build that stuff into the next free upgrade.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: We'll take it!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Beam me up, Spock. There's no life on this planet.

setting: Conference room during a sales meeting with a customer
situation: Stan, a salesman, pitches his product to a customer, claiming it has a huge RAM cache and can detect tachyon field emissions. Dilbert corrects him, pointing out the product has no RAM and that Stan is confusing it with Star Trek. Stan then promises to add those features in the next free upgrade, and the customer eagerly buys it.
punchline: The customer is so gullible that blatantly impossible, science-fiction features and promised free upgrades seal the deal, leaving Dilbert wishing to escape a planet devoid of intelligent life.
summary: A salesman invents absurd capabilities for a product, and even after the engineer exposes the lies, the client happily buys it on the promise of future free updates.

title: Defantalator Fixes Daydreaming Coworker

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: There's another unproductive man, daydreaming about attractive women.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: A short burst from my "Defantalator" should set him straight.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Wusss

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Hey! I think I'm starting to like figure skating!

setting: Office cubicle area
situation: Alice spots a male coworker, Ted, sitting at his desk daydreaming and assumes he is fantasizing about attractive women. She zaps him with her ray-gun-like invention, the "Defantalator," to cure him of his fantasies. Ted is left suddenly declaring an interest in figure skating.
punchline: Alice's device "straightens" Ted out by making him gay or at least stereotypically interested in figure skating, which is a joking, stereotype-based twist on what 'set him straight' means.
summary: A woman blasts a daydreaming coworker with a gadget meant to cure his fantasies and instead leaves him newly fascinated by figure skating.

title: Team Player Shoulder Massage Gone Wrong

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll give Albert a male bonding shoulder massage to show I'm a team player.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hey, Al! Keep up the good work, buddy!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Oops... That might have been the Vulcan death grip.

setting: Office cubicle
situation: Dilbert decides to show he is a team player by giving his coworker Albert a friendly shoulder massage while Albert types at his computer. Dilbert squeezes Albert's shoulder and praises his work. Albert then slumps unconscious on his desk, and Dilbert realizes he may have used the Vulcan death grip.
punchline: Dilbert's clumsy attempt at friendly male bonding accidentally knocks his coworker out, or possibly kills him, with a Star Trek-style nerve pinch.
summary: An awkward attempt at coworker camaraderie leaves a colleague slumped lifeless at his desk after a Star Trek-style nerve pinch.

title: Boss Wants Credit for Dismissed Idea

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Add my name to your patent application to acknowledge my contribution.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What contribution?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You said it was a stupid idea by a stupid employee. You ordered me to stop working on it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Devil's advocate!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You also said I was ugly.

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle
situation: The Boss demands that his name be added to Dilbert's patent application to acknowledge his contribution. Dilbert points out that the Boss's only input was calling the idea stupid and ordering him to stop working on it. The Boss claims he was playing devil's advocate, and Dilbert retorts that he also called him ugly.
punchline: The Boss's excuse of playing devil's advocate to claim credit is undercut by Dilbert's sarcastic implication that his other insults must have been just a role-playing exercise too.
summary: A manager tries to claim credit on an invention he once belittled, and the employee exposes the absurd excuse with a dry retort.

title: Daydreaming Cure Backfires on Coworkers

transcript.speaker: Bald coworker
transcript.text: My productivity is shot. I can't stop daydreaming about Irene in Accounting.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Do what I did. Try to phase out of it by daydreaming of Laura in Engineering, then move to the ordinary-looking Betty in Marketing.

transcript.speaker: Bald coworker
transcript.text: Now I'm daydreaming about all three of them.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Same thing happened to me.

setting: Office break area where coworkers stand around holding coffee cups
situation: One coworker complains that he can't stop daydreaming about a woman in Accounting, hurting his productivity. Another coworker advises him to wean himself off by daydreaming about other women in different departments. The advice backfires, and the first man now fantasizes about all three, which the adviser admits also happened to him.
punchline: The supposed cure for daydreaming about one coworker just multiplies the distraction, and the adviser reveals his own method failed him the same way.
summary: Two men trade a laughably flawed remedy for office infatuation that only leaves them distracted by even more colleagues.

title: Elbonians Struggle With Total Quality

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dilbert teaches Elbonia "Total Quality" methods.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You start by identifying problem areas.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: Hmm... Sometimes our mittens get stuck to our noses and we can't breathe.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Sniff

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: Yorgi! Try to breathe with your mouth!

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: Mmm! Mmm!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: People! Let's talk metrics, please!

setting: Elbonian mud flat, with the Elbonians sunk in mud up to their chests
situation: Dilbert is teaching a group of Elbonians Total Quality management methods and tells them to start by identifying problem areas. The Elbonians cite their problem that mittens get stuck to their noses and block their breathing, and one is visibly suffocating while the others offer basic advice. Dilbert tries to steer them back to discussing metrics.
punchline: While Dilbert wants to discuss abstract quality metrics, the Elbonians have an urgent, literal problem (a man suffocating on his own mitten) that makes management jargon irrelevant.
summary: A consultant's quality-improvement lesson is derailed when his students reveal a real problem, one of them is suffocating because his mitten is stuck to his nose.

title: Acquitted for Being Clueless

transcript.speaker: Juror
transcript.text: We find the defendant innocent by reason of being generally clueless.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I know I should be happy, but it's so insulting... What will all my friends think?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...Not that I have any.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I call that a win-win scenario.

setting: A courtroom, then at a desk with Dogbert (likely Dilbert's lawyer)
situation: A juror reads a verdict finding Dilbert innocent on the grounds that he is generally clueless. Dilbert, sitting with Dogbert at the defense table, complains that the verdict is insulting and worries what his friends will think, then admits he has no friends. Dogbert calls the outcome a win-win.
punchline: Dilbert is acquitted but insulted, and since he has no friends to judge him, Dogbert declares that a win-win scenario.
summary: A jury clears Dilbert by declaring him hopelessly oblivious, and his sulking over lost reputation collapses when he admits nobody is around to care.

title: Ratbert's Fading Plague Glory Days

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Sometimes I think I'm not reaching my full potential as a rat.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're right. In the Middle Ages, disease-carrying rats wiped out half of the human population of Europe.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I think I've got a little temperature. Feel my forehead.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Face it, your glory days are past.

setting: Dilbert's desk in an office, in front of his computer
situation: Ratbert sits on Dilbert's desk and muses that he is not reaching his full potential as a rat. Dilbert agrees and points out that rats once wiped out half of Europe's population during the Middle Ages. Ratbert, now feeling unwell, asks Dilbert to feel his forehead, and Dilbert dismissively tells him his glory days are over.
punchline: Dilbert's pep talk reminds Ratbert of the bubonic plague, and when Ratbert then feels feverish, Dilbert coldly jokes that the rat's disease-spreading heyday is long gone.
summary: A self-doubting pet rat is reminded of his ancestors' deadly historical feats and then brushed off when he complains of feeling sick.

title: Ratbert's Fate Decided By Email Vote

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Ratbert's fate depends on the kindness of readers who are voting by electronic mail.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Don't worry, Ratbert. You won't get whacked unless people think senseless cruelty is somehow "funny."

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Although I admit it would have a certain visual appeal.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: You're not helping!!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Conclusion Nov. 29

setting: Dilbert's home, near a computer
situation: Dilbert stands holding a rolled-up newspaper over Ratbert while a caption explains that readers are voting by email on Ratbert's fate. Dogbert tries to reassure the nervous Ratbert, then undercuts himself by admitting that whacking him would look appealing. The strip ends with a teaser for the conclusion on Nov. 29.
punchline: Dogbert's attempt at comfort collapses when he admits that Ratbert getting whacked would be visually appealing, which makes Ratbert even more terrified.
summary: Readers get to vote on whether a cartoon rat gets squashed, and his canine friend's pep talk turns into unhelpful honesty.

title: Cheap Firewalking Seminar Means Burns

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I found a seminar that will teach firewalking as a way to build confidence.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Each of you will have to walk barefoot over burning coals while I watch!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: But amazingly, we learn how to do it without injury, right?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, that seminar costs a lot more.

setting: Office hallway
situation: The Boss announces he has booked a firewalking seminar to build team confidence. He explains that employees will have to walk barefoot over burning coals while he watches. Alice asks whether they will at least be taught to do it without injury, and he admits the seminar that teaches that costs more.
punchline: The Boss picked the cheapest seminar, which skips the safety training, so employees will simply get burned because he refuses to pay for the version that prevents injury.
summary: A manager signs his staff up for a bargain-priced coal-walking course that conveniently leaves out the part about not getting hurt.

title: Blonde Joke Gets Logical Rebuttal

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Hee hee! How many blondes does it take to change a tire?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: One?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: No, thirty-seven to lift the car and one to pin the diaper on the tire!!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Ha! Ha!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Couldn't they just use the jack?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I wondered about that too.

setting: Office
situation: Wally tells Dilbert a blonde joke and laughs at his own punchline about thirty-seven blondes lifting a car. Dilbert responds by pointing out the obvious flaw that a jack could be used. Wally admits he had wondered the same thing.
punchline: The joke only works if you don't think about it, and even Wally, who is telling it, realizes it makes no logical sense.
summary: A co-worker's stale joke collapses when the listener applies simple common sense and the teller concedes the point.

title: Car Salespeople Trapped in Bioworld Dome

transcript.speaker: Trapped man

transcript.speaker: Trapped man
transcript.text: We pray there was no sadistic intent when you chose only car salespeople for the experiment... Please... at least let some air in...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Gee, I really want to help. I'll go try to convince my boss to see it your way.

transcript.speaker: Trapped man
transcript.text: Hey! I'm a "Saturn" dealer - I'm different!

setting: Outside and inside a sealed Bioworld experiment dome
situation: A group of men in yellow jumpsuits are trapped inside a sealed dome, calling Dogbert on a mobile phone to beg him to end the experiment because they are running out of food and air. They suspect Dogbert deliberately chose only car salespeople as subjects. Dogbert pretends he will go lobby his boss, and from inside the dome one man protests that he sells Saturns and is different.
punchline: Dogbert's fake promise to help and the salesman's desperate plea that his brand is different show that the experiment was a deliberate punishment of car salespeople, and that even they believe their own sales pitches.
summary: Dogbert lets a domed experiment full of suffocating car dealers plead for rescue, only for one of them to cling to his brand's reputation as an exception.

transcript.text: Hoo-ha ha ha ha ha ha ha

transcript.speaker: Waitress

transcript.speaker: Dogbert

setting: A restaurant table
situation: Dilbert orders a meal and the waitress doesn't write anything down. He accuses her of deliberately planning to get the order wrong, explaining in detail how she will deny it, give him a look, and offer a slow replacement. She laughs maniacally, then turns to take Dogbert's order.
punchline: Dogbert's order of 'hold the demonic hatred' implies the waitress really is a malevolent, gleeful saboteur, confirming Dilbert's paranoia about restaurant service.
summary: A diner's suspicion that a waitress is plotting to botch his order is confirmed when she cackles evilly and Dogbert orders without the hatred.

title: Profit Bucket Disconnected From Budget

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My patent will make fifty million dollars for the company, so I thought maybe you could afford to give me a raise.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Unfortunately, the profit bucket is not connected to the budget bucket, so there's no money for a raise.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think some recognition of a job well-done is appropriate here.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Thanks. It was one of my better excuses.

setting: The Boss's office
situation: Dilbert tells his boss that his patent will earn the company fifty million dollars and asks for a raise. The boss explains that the profit bucket and budget bucket are not connected, so no money is available. Dilbert asks for at least some recognition, and the boss accepts the thanks for his excuse.
punchline: The boss responds to a request for recognition by taking credit for the quality of his own excuse for denying the raise, showing he is proud of dodging payment rather than rewarding good work.
summary: A boss turns down a deserving employee's raise with an invented budget technicality and then proudly accepts praise for the excuse itself.

title: Layoff Decided by Staple Chase

setting: Office
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert and a coworker that instead of choosing who to lay off, he will hold a contest between them. The first event is a "staple chase," and in the last panel Dilbert is pinned against a corkboard with staples stuck into his shirt while the Boss scores the round.
punchline: The Boss resolves a layoff decision by turning it into a violent, absurd game where employees are shot with staples, treating people's livelihoods as entertainment.
summary: Too indecisive to pick who gets fired, a manager stages a gladiator-style competition in which staples are fired at his employees.

title: Defantalator Zaps Boss's Naughty Thoughts

situation: Alice pitches her ray-gun-like "Defantalator" to the Boss, claiming it can wipe out the unproductive and naughty thoughts of male employees. She says men have stopped acting like men but must also stop thinking like men. When she points it at the Boss, he is shown daydreaming about giving her a makeover, which prompts her to snap at him.
punchline: Even while being pitched a device to stop inappropriate thoughts, the Boss immediately has one, showing the invention is needed and that he is oblivious.
summary: A female engineer demonstrates a gadget meant to purge men's inappropriate thoughts, and her clueless boss instantly proves why it's needed.

title: Dogbert Profiles People With Too Much Time

situation: Over three panels, a series of captions lists habits of people with too much free time: obsessively cleaning their cars, writing indignant letters to the newspaper editor, and rereading the same book. In the last panel Dogbert stands by an armchair and sums up that these are the people with way too much time on their hands.
punchline: The outraged letter complaining that the funny pages have no place for sarcasm is itself delivered in a sarcastic comic strip, and the ones with time to complain are the people who don't have enough going on in their lives.
summary: A comic lists the quirks of idle folks, from spotless cars to angry letters about humor in the comics, before a dog declares they simply have too much spare time.

title: Ratbert Tries to Fly

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Flap flap

setting: Dilbert's office desk
situation: Ratbert, perched on a desk, announces he intends to fly. Dilbert explains that evolution takes millions of years and rats won't develop flying skills in his lifetime. Ratbert counters that people said the same to the Wright Brothers, and he ends up flapping his arms pointlessly while Dilbert watches.
punchline: Dilbert points out that the Wright Brothers built an airplane rather than flapping their arms, so Ratbert's flapping attempt is the obviously failed approach that earlier inventors would have tried first.
summary: A determined rat compares his dream of flight to aviation pioneers, only to be told that arm-flapping was the method they would have discarded long ago.

He gives each side a one-minute turn to talk. The date ends with her telling Dilbert she sees him as just a friend, and Dogbert declares it a score.
punchline: Treating a date like a sports game with a referee ends with Dilbert being friend-zoned, which Dogbert cheerfully calls a score for the other side.
summary: Dogbert officiates a dinner date like a sporting match, throwing penalties until the woman delivers the classic brush-off.

title: Government Agents Seize Happiness Drug

setting: Dilbert's doorway
situation: Armed government agents in suits and sunglasses show up at Dilbert's door to confiscate his supposed happiness drug. Dilbert protests that it is only fruits and vegetables, and the agents point guns at his face. One agent concedes the point, but his partner dismisses the argument by saying the first agent is new.
punchline: Government enforcement is not swayed by logic, so an agent who sees sense is waved off as inexperienced, implying that reason is something you unlearn on the job.
summary: Gun-toting officials raid a man's home over a cheerful fruit-and-vegetable concoction, and when one of them admits the law makes no sense, his partner writes it off as rookie naivety.

title: Ratbert Rides Dinosaur for Love

situation: Ratbert sits on the head of Bob, a green dinosaur, and proudly declares they make a great team. He explains his plan to borrow the affection people naturally have for dinosaurs so he no longer has to act pathetic. When they meet someone, the person is disgusted, seeing only a huge lizard with a talking zit.
punchline: Ratbert's plan to piggyback on people's love for dinosaurs fails because Bob just looks like a repulsive giant lizard with Ratbert as a talking zit on its head.
summary: A little rat perched on a dinosaur's head hopes its popularity will earn him affection, but onlookers are simply grossed out.

title: Kid Blames Adults, Dilbert Obliviously Asks

transcript.speaker: Noriko

situation: Noriko, a young girl, angrily rants to Dogbert about the state of the planet, including the environment, crime and poverty, and demands to know who is responsible. Dogbert points out that adults are to blame, just as Dilbert walks up. Dilbert cheerfully asks what's wrong, unaware that he is part of the problem.
punchline: Dilbert, an adult, innocently asks what is wrong without realizing that the girl's tirade is about adults like him, so she answers with a sarcastic 'Duhhh!'
summary: A furious child and a talking dog agree that grown-ups wrecked the world, right as an oblivious grown-up wanders over to ask what's bothering her.

title: Stolen Credit Card, Strangled Owner

transcript.speaker: Cashier

transcript.speaker: Cashier
transcript.text: This card was reported stolen. The real owner was strangled with his own pants just minutes ago on aisle six...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That would explain why these were on the floor by the chalk outline.

setting: Store checkout counter
situation: Dilbert waits at a store register with a pair of pants he is happy to have found, holding a credit card. The cashier reports the card was stolen and its real owner was just strangled with his own pants in aisle six. Dilbert realizes the pants he picked up came from the murder scene on the floor by the chalk outline.
punchline: Dilbert unknowingly took the murder weapon, the dead man's pants, from the crime scene and tried to buy them with the victim's stolen credit card.
summary: A shopper's successful pants hunt turns grim when the checkout clerk reveals the card he's using belongs to a murder victim.

title: Boss's Karoshi Safety Advice

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: In Japan, employees occasionally work themselves to death. It's called karoshi.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't want that to happen to anybody in my department.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The trick is to take a break as soon as you see a bright light and hear dead relatives beckon.

setting: Conference room during a department meeting
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert and Wally at a meeting about karoshi, the Japanese phenomenon of working oneself to death. He says he doesn't want that to happen in his department, then offers advice on when employees should take a break.
punchline: The Boss's idea of work-life balance is to rest only when you are already dying, showing his indifference to overwork until it is nearly fatal.
summary: A manager voices concern about overwork deaths, then sets the threshold for taking a break at the moment you glimpse the afterlife.

title: Wally's Cubicle Roof Is Dilbert's Wall

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hey, Wally, how did you get a roof for your cubicle?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: This stuff is all modular. You just take some idiot's wall and make it your ceiling.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: By any chance, do you know what happened to MY wall?

transcript.speaker: Unseen coworker
transcript.text: What did it look like?

setting: Office cubicle area
situation: Dilbert notices that Wally's cubicle has a roof and asks how he got it. Wally explains that the cubicle parts are modular and he simply took some idiot's wall and used it as a ceiling. Dilbert, whose own wall has gone missing, asks if Wally knows where it went, and a voice from under the new roof asks what it looked like.
punchline: Wally casually admits to stealing a coworker's cubicle wall, and the wall he took turns out to be Dilbert's, with the unseen occupant under the roof feigning ignorance.
summary: A coworker's missing partition ends up as the neighbour's brand-new roof, and the thief plays dumb.

title: Lawyer Defends Temp Worker Killing

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Yes, my client did accidentally slay a "temp" worker... emphasis on "temp."

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: But who among us can say they haven't slain innocent people when the situation called for it?

transcript.speaker: Judge
transcript.text: I can.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Well, great... so much for getting a fair trial.

setting: Courtroom
situation: Dogbert, acting as defense lawyer, addresses the jury and admits his client killed a temp worker, stressing that the victim was only a temp. He then appeals to the jury by suggesting everyone has killed innocent people when necessary. The judge says he never has, so Dogbert realizes the judge will be biased against his client.
punchline: Dogbert's cynical argument that everyone kills innocents when needed backfires when the judge, the one person who must be impartial, declares he has not, undermining the trial's fairness.
summary: A canine attorney's callous plea for sympathy toward his client's killing of a temp is ruined when the judge turns out to be the lone person who disagrees.

title: Ratbert Flaps His Way Airborne

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Dilbert says it's impossible to fly by flapping your arms. Is he right, Bob?

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: It just depends how hard you flap.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It must be embarrassing to be you.

setting: A room with a desk or table; Dilbert's home or office
situation: Ratbert asks Bob the dinosaur whether Dilbert is right that you can't fly by flapping your arms. Bob says it depends on how hard you flap, so Ratbert flaps his arms wildly and ends up hovering in the air. Dilbert, reading a newspaper in an armchair, doesn't look up and insults Ratbert for being gullible.
punchline: Ratbert actually manages to fly by flapping, proving Dilbert wrong, but Dilbert nonchalantly insults him anyway, implying it's still embarrassing to be someone who would try this.
summary: A gullible rat takes a dinosaur's advice literally, flaps his arms until he floats, and is met with a flat insult from the unimpressed man reading the paper.

title: Dilbert Seeks Costly Unwanted Project

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But not something important, because that would draw attention to me at a time of staff cuts.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What can I do that costs a lot but nobody wants?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: "Empowerment" sure made them quiet.

setting: Office cubicle
situation: Dilbert sits at his computer thinking through how to look busy and justify his job during staff cuts. He wants a big project that is not important enough to draw attention, and he wonders what expensive thing nobody wants. The Boss, passing by, muses to himself that 'empowerment' has made employees quiet.
punchline: Dilbert's search for a costly, unwanted project is exactly the kind of wasteful self-preservation that management buzzwords like 'empowerment' produce, while the Boss is pleased that it has merely silenced people.
summary: A worker schemes to look indispensable during layoffs by picking a pricey but unwanted task, while his boss congratulates himself on a hushed workforce.

title: Occam's Razor and Dilbert's Love Life

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe I'm unlucky in love because I'm so knowledgeable about science that I intimidate people.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Their intimidation becomes low self-esteem, then they reject me to protect their egos.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Occam's razor.

transcript.text: What is "Occam's razor"?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: A guy named Occam had a rule about the world.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Basically, he said that when there are multiple explanations for something, the simplest explanation is usually correct.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The simplest explanation for your poor love life is that you're immensely unattractive.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe Occam had another rule that specifically exempted this situation, but his house burned down with all his notes.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then he forgot.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Occam's razor.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm an idiot?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I don't think we can rule it out at this point.

setting: A bedroom, then a grassy hillside outdoors
situation: Dilbert suggests he is unlucky in love because his scientific knowledge intimidates women. Dogbert invokes Occam's razor and explains that the simplest explanation is that Dilbert is unattractive. Dilbert tries to invent an exception to the rule, and Dogbert counters that the simplest explanation might be that Dilbert is an idiot.
punchline: By using Occam's razor against Dilbert's convoluted self-flattering theory, Dogbert shows that the simplest explanation for his failures is that he is unattractive, and even his rationalizing suggests he may be an idiot.
summary: A dog uses a famous scientific principle to puncture his owner's flattering excuse for being single, then doubles down when the owner argues back.

title: Dogbert Trains Dilbert's Disdain

transcript.text: Your boss won't promote you to "technical prima donna" until you learn disdain for others.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Pretend this inflatable dummy is a co-worker asking a question. See how long you can ignore it. I'll check back later.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Psst. Nothing personal, buddy. This is just practice.

transcript.speaker: Inflatable dummy
transcript.text: Hey! Hey!

setting: Dilbert's office desk
situation: Dogbert tells Dilbert that he won't be promoted to "technical prima donna" until he learns to look down on others. He sets up an inflatable dummy as a stand-in co-worker asking a question and tells Dilbert to ignore it for as long as he can. Dilbert awkwardly whispers an apology to the dummy while it keeps calling for his attention.
punchline: Dilbert is too polite to ignore even an inflatable dummy without apologizing to it, showing he lacks the contempt needed to be a technical prima donna.
summary: Dogbert coaches Dilbert on cultivating arrogance by having him snub a blow-up doll, but Dilbert can't help being courteous to it.

title: Pringles Can Luggage Prototype Wrinkles

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's a prototype for my tubular luggage invention.

transcript.speaker: Coworker

setting: Office hallway or doorway
situation: A female coworker asks Dilbert why his shirt and clothes are so wrinkled and rumpled. Dilbert explains he kept them rolled up inside a Pringles potato chip can for a week as a test of his tubular luggage invention. She responds by telling him never to speak to her again.
punchline: Dilbert's proud explanation that his badly wrinkled clothes are the result of a silly invention experiment is so absurd that the coworker cuts off all contact.
summary: A wrinkled Dilbert admits his rumpled outfit came from testing a snack-can suitcase idea, which drives his coworker away.

title: Dishes Stacked on Gaming Dilbert

transcript.text: Poor guy.

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle
situation: Dilbert sits at his computer, absorbed in a video game, with a tall stack of dishes balanced on his head. Ratbert asks about the dishes, and Dogbert explains he is running an experiment on whether Dilbert notices anything around him. Ratbert then walks away feeling sorry for Dilbert, with a stack of dishes balanced on his own head.
punchline: Ratbert's sympathy for 'poor guy' is undercut by the fact that he has unknowingly acquired dishes on his own head, showing he is just as oblivious as Dilbert.
summary: A small pet pities a gamer with crockery stacked on his skull while unknowingly wearing a stack of his own.

title: Naked Engineers Audience Visualization Backfires

transcript.text: Whoa! Cancel that. I just pictured four hundred naked engineers.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Too late.

setting: Dilbert's bedroom
situation: Dilbert is getting dressed in front of a mirror and mentions he is nervous about giving a speech to the Society of Engineers. Dogbert, sitting on the bed, offers the classic tip of imagining the audience naked. Dogbert then pictures the 400 engineers himself and is horrified, but Dilbert has already had the same mental image.
punchline: The common public-speaking trick of imagining the audience naked is a terrible idea when the audience is a room of engineers, and the mental image can't be undone.
summary: A comforting bit of stage-fright advice turns into a mutual mental scar when the audience in question is hundreds of engineers.

title: Kids Plan Penal Colony on Mars

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There's no oxygen on Mars.

transcript.speaker: Girl
transcript.text: Oh, now you learn to plan ahead.

setting: A grassy hillside outdoors
situation: A young girl with a notepad confronts Dilbert, who is sitting on a hill, blaming adults for ruining the planet for her generation. She threatens to take down names and exile all adults to a penal colony on Mars once kids have power. Dilbert points out Mars has no oxygen, and she sarcastically retorts that now he learns to plan ahead.
punchline: Dilbert only shows foresight when it's his own punishment at stake, which proves the girl's point that adults fail to plan ahead about the planet.
summary: A child warns the grown-ups she'll banish them to Mars someday, and when one finally thinks about consequences, she mocks his sudden concern for planning.

title: Boss Threatens Retribution Over Performance Review

setting: Office, the boss's workspace
situation: The Boss announces a new policy in which employees evaluate their manager's job performance. Dilbert immediately gives him a D minus, and the Boss responds by hinting at retribution. Dilbert then points out the Boss's tie is hanging by a thread.
punchline: The Boss's supposedly open feedback policy is undermined by his instant threat of retribution, so Dilbert's honest appraisal gets a hollow, snarky reply about the boss's own precarious position.
summary: A manager introduces upward reviews, then threatens payback the moment his employee grades him poorly.

title: Engineer Savant Legal Defense
