situation: Dogbert, acting as a defense lawyer, addresses a jury and announces that although an insanity defense is unavailable, he has an equally good alternative. He describes Dilbert as an "engineer savant" who grasps technology but nothing else. He then presents Dilbert's white socks, complete with the sock protector and pens, as evidence.
punchline: The stereotypical engineer dress habits (white socks, pocket protector-style sock protector, extra pens) are offered as courtroom proof that engineers are technologically gifted but otherwise socially clueless.
summary: A canine lawyer argues that his client is not crazy but merely a tech-obsessed savant, citing the man's nerdy socks as proof.

Dilbert asks if that includes lunch together, and she says she would schedule it and then cancel at the last minute.
punchline: The offer of friendship is hollow, since she promises only the appearance of friendship (plans she will always cancel) in exchange for a share of credit for his invention.
summary: A coworker tries to buy her way onto a patent with the promise of a friendship that exists in name only.

punchline: Dilbert's pompous vocabulary prompts Dogbert to sarcastically link it to his bad breath and to call out his smug, self-absorbed bubble.
summary: A man who dismisses his television with a fancy word gets verbally deflated by his dog, who is using his feet as a pillow.

summary: A cocky young MBA graduate turns out to be the new senior vice president, instantly turning the staff's disdain for his résumé into servile compliance.

punchline: The legal department is so self-protective and resentful that it not only rejects the proposal but also sues the employee who submitted it.
summary: A bitter in-house lawyer admits he'll shoot down an employee's idea purely to protect himself, then goes further and takes legal action against the employee.

situation: Dilbert tells his boss that his chair is broken and the warehouse has no engineer chairs left. punchline: The boss treats a request for a better chair as an outrageous power grab, mocking the idea that employees are really empowered by comparing it to wanting a screen door, a luxury for a cubicle.
summary: A worker invoking his newfound empowerment to swap a busted chair for a fancier one is met with sarcasm from his boss about his inflated sense of privilege.

summary: A freshly promoted programmer is defeated by the simple task of putting on his new management suit and plans to phone a help line.

punchline: Wally's after-shave ignites in the flames, and the instructor deadpans that the lesson from his example is to avoid alcohol-based after-shave, treating a painful accident as a training takeaway.
summary: A manager-training instructor draws a lesson from a volunteer's fiery mishap on the hot coals.

summary: A departing employee pretends his fancy new position is humble, only to boast about having a pony and a private office.

summary: Dogbert answers a request for a product name with a blunt pun that mocks the inventor himself.

Dilbert and Wally then discuss the new buzzword-laden task force, with Wally noting it will fill up fast.

summary: A scheming Dogbert plans to turn a trendy-sounding committee into his personal fiefdom, and his coworkers are already lining up to join.

summary: A hopeful bachelor's blind date turns out to be a two-headed woman who can read minds, undermining his optimistic plan.

transcript.text: I can top that.

setting: Conference room during a meeting
situation: A man at a conference table announces that he will make funny faces and tell a long rambling story, then launches into a pointless anecdote about monthly versus daily reports. As he drones on, Dilbert and the other attendees sit by, and a man in a gray suit thinks he can tell an even longer, more tedious story.
punchline: Instead of being bored or annoyed by the rambling, a listener is competitive and plans to out-ramble the speaker, showing how meetings become contests of self-indulgent storytelling.
summary: A colleague announces his intention to bore the room with an aimless tale, and a rival listener silently plots to deliver an even worse one.

title: Blame Consultant Blames the Boss

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've seen him before.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm a "blame consultant."

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: For a large fee I will tell the workers that the problems in the company are their fault, not yours. It's the latest management fad.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Won't they see right through that?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Is that my fault??!

setting: The Boss's office
situation: Dogbert, working as a consultant, pitches his services to the Boss. For a large fee he will convince employees that the company's problems are their own fault rather than management's. When the Boss worries the workers will see through it, Dogbert responds as if the Boss is blaming him.
punchline: Dogbert demonstrates the blame-shifting technique he sells by instantly deflecting the Boss's doubt back onto him, showing the consulting service is just scapegoating.
summary: A consultant offers to persuade staff that management's failures are really theirs, then immediately uses that same trick on the skeptical boss.

title: Smile Costs Him a Zapping

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: Hey, little dog, smile. It only takes two muscles!

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: ZAP

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: AAAIII!!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That took a few extra muscles, but I think it was worth it.

setting: Outdoors on a grassy hillside path
situation: A cheerful stranger walking past tells Dogbert, who is lying on a mound holding a small stun device, to smile because it only takes two muscles. Dogbert zaps the man, who screams and ends up frazzled with his hair on end and his tongue out. Dogbert then comments on the muscles involved.
punchline: Dogbert answers the stranger's smile-more cliche by electrocuting him, noting that the resulting spasm used many more muscles than a smile and that it was worth it.
summary: A passerby's unsolicited advice to smile earns him a jolt from Dogbert's stun gun and a lecture on muscle usage.

title: Salesman Refuses to Sell Cheap Part

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Electron Hut

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm looking for a P-connect adapter post.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: We don't have any.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There's a whole shelf of them right behind you.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: They're only five cents apiece. I can't waste my time selling them.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm the only customer in the store! Besides, why do you stock something you don't want to sell?

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: Here! Take three! And stop wasting my time!

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: While you're here, have you seen our fine line of computers?

setting: Electron Hut, a computer and electronics store
situation: Dilbert goes into an electronics store looking for a cheap adapter post. The salesman claims they have none, then admits they are on a shelf behind him but are too low-priced to bother selling. After throwing three of the parts at Dilbert and scolding him for wasting his time, the salesman immediately tries to upsell him on computers while Dilbert crawls on the floor picking up the parts.
punchline: The salesman treats a customer as a nuisance for wanting an inexpensive item, yet instantly switches to a sales pitch for high-priced products as soon as he has humiliated him.
summary: A shopkeeper pelts a customer with the tiny parts he came for, then cheerfully tries to sell him a computer.

title: Executive Burrito Burp Strategy Meeting

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: I'm told by a reliable source that our senior vice president made a sound like "yurp" at lunch.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What does it mean? Does it signal a new set of priorities? We must demonstrate our commitment to this vision.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What was the context of this vision?

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: All we know is he was eating a burrito.

setting: Conference room during a management meeting
situation: At a meeting, a manager reports that the senior vice president made a "yurp" sound at lunch. The Boss treats it as a strategic vision and insists everyone must show commitment to it. Dilbert asks about the context and learns the executive was simply eating a burrito.
punchline: Management over-interprets a random bodily noise from an executive as strategic direction, when it was just a burp from a burrito.
summary: A boardroom solemnly debates the corporate meaning of an executive's lunchtime belch.

title: Dogbert Funds Bioworld, Picks Volunteers

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...So I thought you might use some of your newly won millions to fund my "Bioworld" science experiment.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's a complete ecology enclosed in an airtight dome. The survival of the volunteers would depend on my foresight and engineering skills.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Gee, I thought it would be harder to talk you into it.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I get to pick the volunteers myself.

setting: Dogbert's office, across a desk
situation: Dilbert pitches Dogbert on funding his Bioworld experiment, a sealed dome ecosystem where volunteers' survival depends on his engineering skills. Dogbert, who has newly won millions, agrees almost instantly because he gets to choose who goes inside the dome.
punchline: Dogbert is eager to fund the risky experiment because he gets to pick the volunteers, implying he will send people he wants to get rid of into a potentially deadly dome.
summary: A scientist seeking funding for a sealed-dome survival experiment finds his wealthy patron far too happy to help once he's allowed to choose the test subjects.

title: Retail Clerk Despises the Public

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can you help me?

transcript.speaker: Sales Clerk
transcript.text: No, I'm afraid I can't.

transcript.speaker: Sales Clerk
transcript.text: You see, I get paid the same low hourly wage whether you buy that shirt or not. And after years in this business I've learned to despise the general public.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Please... I have exact change.

transcript.speaker: Sales Clerk
transcript.text: I have no way of knowing if that's true.

setting: Clothing store
situation: Dilbert, holding a blue shirt, asks a store clerk for help. She refuses, explaining that her low hourly wage is the same whether he buys or not and that years in retail have taught her to despise customers. Dilbert pleads that he has exact change, and she coldly says she cannot verify that.
punchline: The clerk's total indifference and contempt for customers is so complete that she won't even believe the customer's claim that he has exact change, making any sale impossible.
summary: A shopper trying to buy a shirt is stonewalled by a bitter, underpaid store clerk who refuses to help or even trust him.

title: One-Way Business Trips Boost Stock

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: What?? The presidents of other companies make way more money than I do!!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'd better make some short-sighted spending cuts. That should raise our stock price and make my stock options worth millions.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: ... All business trips are one-way from now on... And you're all required to take a trip this afternoon.

setting: Company president's office, then a meeting with employees
situation: Dogbert, acting as company president, reads the newspaper in his armchair and is annoyed that other company presidents earn more than he does. He decides to make short-sighted spending cuts to raise the stock price and inflate his stock options. He then tells the assembled employees that all business trips are now one-way and that everyone must take a trip that afternoon.
punchline: Dogbert's cost-cutting is so shortsighted and callous that it amounts to stranding employees on one-way trips, all to boost his own stock options.
summary: A self-interested executive plans to enrich himself with cost cuts and then cheaply eliminates his staff by sending them away on tickets with no return.

title: Shrinking Into Becoming Smallest Company

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've got good news and bad news.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The bad news is that huge companies like us can't compete against small, nimble companies. The good news is that at this rate we'll be the smallest company around.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What am I doing wrong here?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: We're number one!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We're number one!

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Yes!!

setting: Conference room during a staff meeting
situation: The Boss tells his staff at a meeting that large companies can't compete with small, nimble ones, and announces the 'good news' that at the current rate of decline his company will become the smallest around. The employees respond by cheering and pumping their fists, which leaves him wondering what he is doing wrong.
punchline: The staff gleefully cheer the prospect of their company shrinking, and the Boss, who intended it as a pep talk, is baffled that no one understands the downsizing is bad news.
summary: A manager's attempt to spin impending corporate shrinkage as a positive is met with enthusiastic cheers that leave him baffled.

title: Doubling Workload, Promising Promotions

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I just realized I can double your workload and there's nothing you can do about it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're lucky to have jobs in today's economy! You'll gladly sacrifice your personal lives for no extra pay!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But at least our hard work will lead to promotion opportunities.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're so cute. I wish I had a camera right now.

setting: Office, in front of the cubicles
situation: The Boss gathers Wally, Dilbert and Alice and gleefully announces he is doubling their workload, reminding them they are lucky to have jobs and must give up their personal lives for no extra pay. He then claims their hard work will lead to promotions. When the employees stare back in disbelief, he tells them they are cute and wishes he had a camera.
punchline: The Boss is so delighted by his own power over his employees that he finds their stunned, helpless reactions adorable, even as he piles on work and offers hollow promises of promotion.
summary: A smug manager heaps extra work on his staff, dangles vague promotion prospects, and then gets amused by their crushed expressions.

title: Dogbert Questions Opposing Attorney's Lingerie

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: For my first witness, I call the defendant's attorney.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Is it true that you're wearing women's lingerie right now?

transcript.speaker: Attorney
transcript.text: No!

transcript.speaker: Judge
transcript.text: Is this relevant to your case?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I wonder why you're so touchy about this subject.

setting: A courtroom
situation: Dogbert, acting as a lawyer in court, calls the opposing side's attorney as his first witness. He asks the attorney whether he is wearing women's lingerie, and the attorney denies it sharply. When the judge asks if the question is relevant, Dogbert deflects by suggesting the attorney's defensiveness is suspicious.
punchline: Dogbert admits the question has nothing to do with the case, yet turns the witness's indignant denial into supposed evidence of guilt.
summary: In court, a dog lawyer grills the rival attorney with an absurd personal question and then treats his angry denial as suspicious.

title: Two-Headed Date Votes Against Kissing

transcript.speaker: Two-headed woman
transcript.text: You're wondering how to handle the good night kiss...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Uh

transcript.speaker: Two-headed woman
transcript.text: By a vote of two to zero we've decided not to kiss you. And Debbie has threatened a filibuster on the handshake issue.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's a bluff.

transcript.speaker: Two-headed woman
transcript.text: Nice weather today. Have you seen any good movies? How about the economy, huh?

characters: Two-headed woman (Debbie and her other head)
setting: Outside a woman's front door at the end of a date
situation: Dilbert stands awkwardly at the door of his two-headed date, who anticipates his worry about the good night kiss. The two heads announce they have voted against kissing him, and one head, Debbie, threatens a filibuster over even a handshake. Dilbert thinks it's a bluff and offers his hand, and the woman stalls with small talk about the weather, movies and the economy.
punchline: The two heads run their date like a legislature, complete with votes and filibusters, and when Dilbert calls the bluff they stall with small talk exactly as a filibustering politician would.
summary: A man's date with two heads settles the kiss question by committee vote, then stalls a handshake with idle chatter like a senator.

title: Broken Chair Requires Promotion

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My chair is broken. Can you send a new one from the warehouse?

transcript.speaker: Warehouse Clerk
transcript.text: No can do, my friend. All we have is chairs with deluxe armrests. They're only for managers who are one level higher than you.

transcript.speaker: Warehouse Clerk
transcript.text: What do I suggest? I dunno... maybe take some classes at night. I'm sure you can get promoted eventually.

setting: Dilbert's cubicle and the warehouse clerk's desk, connected by phone
situation: Dilbert phones the warehouse to request a replacement for his broken chair. The clerk says the only chairs in stock have deluxe armrests reserved for managers one level above Dilbert. He then suggests Dilbert take night classes and aim for a promotion.
punchline: The only way to get a working chair is to be promoted, and the clerk offers this absurd advice as a helpful suggestion for a basic office supply problem.
summary: A simple request for a replacement chair gets blocked by a rigid hierarchy of furniture entitlements, leaving an employee told to climb the corporate ladder just to sit comfortably.

title: Dilbert Bores Coworker to Death

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...Then I said "What about an optical disk file server."

transcript.speaker: Woman (thought)
transcript.text: So boring, falling asleep...

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Whump

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't know how she died. I was telling her about an optical...

transcript.speaker: Police Officer
transcript.text: Zzzzzz

setting: Office doorway and hallway
situation: Dilbert chats about an optical disk file server to a woman holding a watering can, who thinks to herself that it is so boring she is falling asleep. She collapses out of view with a thud, and Dilbert later tells a police officer he does not know how she died, only that he was describing optical storage. The officer is asleep on his feet while taking notes.
punchline: Dilbert's technical talk is so dull that it literally put his coworker to death, and it is now putting the investigating police officer to sleep too, while Dilbert remains oblivious.
summary: A man's tedious tech chatter makes a woman fall over lifeless, and then lulls the cop questioning him into a nap.

title: Elbonian Quality Teams Halve Productivity

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: Thank you for teaching us "quality" techniques.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: Manufacturing defects are down fifty percent since we all joined "quality teams."

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: Yes!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How's our productivity, Yorgi?

transcript.speaker: Yorgi
transcript.text: Down fifty percent.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: They're on to me.

setting: Muddy Elbonian village or work site, outdoors
situation: Dilbert visits Elbonia with a briefcase, where the locals thank him for teaching them quality techniques. They proudly report that manufacturing defects have dropped by half since forming quality teams. When Dilbert asks Yorgi about productivity, he learns it has dropped by the same amount.
punchline: Defects fell by fifty percent only because productivity fell by fifty percent, since producing half as much means making half as many mistakes, and Dilbert realizes the Elbonians have caught on to the quality-team game.
summary: A consultant's quality program in Elbonia appears to work until it turns out the lower defect count simply mirrors a collapse in output.

title: Blame Consultant Blames Word Processor

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert is hired as a blame consultant.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The company's problems are your fault, Willy.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You blame the senior executives, but it is you — the individual employee — who must build innovative new products and pioneer new markets.

transcript.speaker: Willy
transcript.text: But I'm just a word processor. I was hired to type.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I've seen your typing. That stinks too.

setting: Office cubicle
situation: Dogbert, hired as a blame consultant, tells a word-processor employee named Willy that the company's problems are his fault. He lectures that individual employees, not senior executives, must create innovative products and pioneer new markets. When Willy protests that he was only hired to type, Dogbert insults his typing too.
punchline: The blame consultant pins the company's failures on a lowly typist, and when the typist points out his job is limited, Dogbert simply finds another thing to blame him for.
summary: A consultant paid to assign blame pins a firm's troubles on a lowly typist and, when challenged, just criticizes his typing as well.

title: Alice's Brainstorming Exercise Insults Everyone

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's start with a brainstorming exercise. Alice, you go first.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I imagine myself not surrounded by dull, unattractive, and largely clueless men.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Mmmm...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think she just insulted you guys.

setting: Conference room during a meeting
situation: The Boss opens a meeting with a brainstorming exercise and asks Alice to go first. She describes imagining herself away from dull, unattractive, clueless men, which is a dig at the men seated around her. Dilbert, after a pause, points out to the others that she just insulted them.
punchline: Alice's brainstorming answer is a thinly veiled insult to her male colleagues, and the men are so clueless that Dilbert has to point out they were just insulted.
summary: Asked to join a team creativity session, Alice uses her turn to daydream about escaping her male coworkers, who need a reminder that they were the target.

title: Counting Law Students as Fractional People

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I can't decide if it would be better to conquer the world by building an army or starting a religion.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Which one would have the least loss of life?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That's what I'm trying to calculate on this spreadsheet.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why are you counting law students as two-tenths of a person?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It doesn't drop to zero until they pass the bar.

setting: Office desk with a computer
situation: Dogbert, seated at a computer, muses about conquering the world either with an army or by founding a religion. Dilbert asks which option would cost the fewest lives, and Dogbert is building a spreadsheet to work that out. Dilbert notices that Dogbert is counting law students as a fraction of a person.
punchline: Dogbert values law students at two-tenths of a human, claiming they only become worthless once they pass the bar, a jab at lawyers.
summary: A scheming dog runs the numbers on world domination and cheerfully discounts the humanity of future lawyers in his casualty estimates.

title: Rat Pitches Teamwork to Dinosaur

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Listen to me, Bob. Individually, we're nothing but a rat and a dinosaur...

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: But if we team up we'd have your mighty strength plus my...uh...my...

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Brain?

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: No, that doesn't sound right.

setting: An open area with a ledge, featuring a small rat and a large green dinosaur
situation: Ratbert pitches a partnership to Bob the dinosaur, offering to combine Bob's strength with his own contribution. He struggles to name what he brings and Bob suggests brains. Ratbert rejects that answer as not sounding right.
punchline: Ratbert can't think of anything useful he contributes, and he implicitly admits that the dinosaur is the one with the brains, so the pitch undermines itself.
summary: A small rat tries to recruit a hulking dinosaur into a partnership but cannot figure out what he himself would bring to it.

title: Learning a Personality Disorder for Promotion

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have a chance to be promoted to "technology prima donna" if I can develop a personality disorder.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't know how a person can learn that sort of thing.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's easy.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Imagine Dustin Hoffman in "Rain Man." Now add a dash of Sean Penn meeting a paparazzi.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Grrr... Mumble... Grrr...

setting: Dogbert's therapy office, with Dilbert seated and Dogbert acting as the therapist
situation: Dilbert tells Dogbert, who is playing therapist, that a promotion to 'technology prima donna' depends on developing a personality disorder. Dogbert claims it's easy and coaches him to imitate Dustin Hoffman's Rain Man mixed with an angry Sean Penn confronting a photographer. Dilbert immediately tries it, growling and mumbling with a clenched fist.
punchline: The company rewards erratic, antisocial behavior in technical staff so heavily that Dilbert must deliberately cultivate a personality disorder to get ahead, and he picks it up instantly.
summary: Seeking a promotion that requires being difficult, Dilbert gets acting tips from Dogbert on how to fake a personality disorder.

title: Dogbert Questions Free Will and Brain

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Do you think the chemistry of the brain controls what people do?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Of course.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Then how can we blame people for their actions?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Because people have free will to do as they choose.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Are you saying that "free will" is not part of the brain?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Of course it is. But it's the part of the brain that's out there just being kind of free.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: So, you're saying the "free will" part of the brain is exempt from the natural laws of physics.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Obviously. Otherwise we couldn't blame people for anything they do.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Do you think the "free will" part of the brain is attached or does it just float nearby?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Shut up.

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle
situation: Dilbert sits at his computer while Dogbert questions him about whether brain chemistry determines behavior. As Dilbert defends the idea of free will so that people can be blamed for their actions, Dogbert keeps poking holes in his reasoning until Dilbert runs out of answers.
punchline: Dilbert's defense of free will requires a magical part of the brain exempt from physics, and when Dogbert mockingly asks if it floats nearby, Dilbert can only tell him to shut up.
summary: A philosophical debate about blame and brain chemistry collapses when Dogbert exposes the absurd logic behind Dilbert's view of free will.

title: Psychic Consultant Reads Boss's Puce

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I am Dogbert the psychic business consultant. I can read minds.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If you can read minds, what's my favorite color?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Your favorite color is puce, but you are mistakenly thinking of a primary color because you don't know what puce is.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Whoa... I just got a shiver.

setting: The Boss's office
situation: Dogbert, wearing a turban, introduces himself to the Boss as a psychic business consultant who can read minds. The Boss tests him by asking his favorite color, and Dogbert answers with an elaborate claim about the Boss's thoughts. The Boss is amazed and shivers.
punchline: Dogbert's answer is a nonsense claim that can't be disproven, since the Boss doesn't know what puce is, yet the gullible Boss is convinced of his psychic powers.
summary: A turbaned Dogbert dazzles his client with a mind-reading answer that is really just a clever insult about his ignorance.

title: Dogbert's Insult-o-gram Requires a Tip

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I have a Dogbert insult-o-gram from your ex-wife...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You're so ugly, weather satellites won't photograph your town unless it's cloudy.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The smarter people recognize this as a tipping situation.

setting: Dilbert's home doorway
situation: Dogbert shows up at Dilbert's door to deliver an insult-o-gram supposedly sent by Dilbert's ex-wife. He recites an insulting joke about Dilbert's ugliness, and Dilbert responds with a stern, unamused look. Dogbert then hints that a tip is expected for the service.
punchline: Dogbert insults the customer and then shamelessly demands a tip for the insult, as if a delivery service were owed gratuity for abuse.
summary: A talking dog delivers a nasty singing-telegram-style jab from an ex-wife and then fishes for gratuity from the very person he just belittled.

title: Dilbert Mentors on Meeting Avoidance

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dilbert the Mentor

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This is called a "meeting."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The objective is twofold: Talk as much as possible and leave with no new assignments.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's okay... I thought your talking went very well.

setting: Conference room and office doorway
situation: Dilbert acts as a mentor to a new coworker, explaining that a meeting's goals are to talk as much as possible and avoid getting any new assignments. In the last panel, the coworker is stuck carrying a huge stack of papers, having failed to dodge the work. Dilbert consoles him by praising his talking.
punchline: The mentee followed the 'talk a lot' advice but still got buried in assignments, and Dilbert offers only a hollow compliment on his talking.
summary: A veteran explains the cynical purpose of meetings to a newcomer, who ends up loaded down with a mountain of work anyway.

title: Ratbert's Desperate Cable TV Channel

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What are you filming?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Ratbert got his own cable TV channel.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Now that cable TV has a thousand channels they're desperate for original programs.

transcript.speaker: Man on couch
transcript.text: Back in the six-hundreds I saw a rat slapping his head to a Barry Manilow tune.

transcript.speaker: Woman on couch
transcript.text: That's worth a second look.

setting: Dilbert's home or office floor, then a living room couch
situation: Dilbert asks Dogbert what he is filming, and Dogbert explains he is recording Ratbert, who has landed a cable TV channel. Dogbert says that with a thousand channels, cable networks are desperate for any original programming. A couple channel-surfing on their couch stops at the channel, drawn in by a rat slapping his head to Barry Manilow.
punchline: With so many cable channels to fill, even a rat slapping his own head to Barry Manilow music counts as must-see programming.
summary: A pet's absurd home video ends up on cable because networks with endless channels will air anything, and a bored couple actually stops to watch.

title: Chair Thief Sentenced to Accounting

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's the penalty for stealing a chair??

transcript.speaker: Devil
transcript.text: You are sentenced to sit in the break room used by the accounting department.

transcript.speaker: Accountant
transcript.text: I like to type the number six.

transcript.speaker: Accountant
transcript.text: Cripes! This is my Tuesday lunch bag.

setting: Hell's elevator and an accounting department break room
situation: Dilbert, leashed by a tie-like cord, asks a pitchfork-wielding devil what the punishment is for stealing a chair. The devil sentences him to sit in the accounting department's break room. There, the accountants make painfully dull small talk about typing the number six and mixing up their lunch bags.
punchline: Spending eternity listening to accountants' mind-numbing small talk is portrayed as a punishment worthy of hell.
summary: A devil's idea of eternal torment for office furniture theft turns out to be lunch with the tedious accountants.

title: Ratbert Hot Tubbing in Spaghetti Pot

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The water for my spaghetti should be boiling by now.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Oops! You caught me. I usually finish hot tubbing before you get back.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It raises a big question mark about the capers.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Capers?

setting: Dilbert's kitchen at home
situation: Dilbert, wearing an apron, wonders why the water for his spaghetti isn't boiling yet. He looks into the pot and finds Ratbert soaking in it, admitting he usually finishes his hot tubbing before Dilbert gets home. Dogbert, sitting in a chair, then remarks that this raises questions about the capers, leaving Dilbert confused and unsettled.
punchline: Dogbert implies that Ratbert has been bathing in Dilbert's cooking water, and that the capers (small, pea-like pickled buds) might have been used in some unsavory way or be something other than capers.
summary: A man preparing pasta discovers his pet rat lounging in the cooking pot, prompting his smug dog to raise an unappetizing doubt about one of the ingredients.

title: Airline Snack Cuts Reach Burping

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm starving. Is there a meal on this flight?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's probably just a snack. The airline is cutting back on frills.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: When you say "snack," do you mean a small but well-balanced culinary experience?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's peanuts. We get nine peanuts apiece.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And a soda... but not a whole can, just a little cup... unless they cut back on that too.

transcript.speaker: Flight Attendant
transcript.text: Now we just drink a soda ourselves and burp your seat number.

transcript.speaker: Flight Attendant
transcript.text: Glug glug glug

transcript.speaker: Flight Attendant
transcript.text: 7B

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's actually kind of refreshing.

setting: Aboard a commercial airplane in flight
situation: Dogbert asks Dilbert whether there is a meal on their flight, and Dilbert explains the airline has cut back to nine peanuts each and a tiny cup of soda. The flight attendant then reveals that the airline has cut even that, so she drinks a soda herself and burps out each passenger's seat number. Dilbert, being burped on, decides it is refreshing.
punchline: Airline cost-cutting becomes so extreme that the flight attendant drinks the soda herself and burps the seat number at passengers, and Dilbert resignedly finds it refreshing.
summary: As an airline strips away every last perk, the crew's idea of in-flight service shrinks to a belch aimed at your seat.
